findings.title: Η πειρατεία ως απειλή κατά της διεθνούς ειρήνης και ασφάλειας
findings.evidence_excerpt: Η ενασχόληση του ανθρώπου με πειρατικές δραστηριότητες είναι ένα φαινόμενο τόσο παλιό όσο και η ίδια η ναυσιπλοΐα. Τόσο παρελθοντικά όσο και στη σύγχρονη εποχή η πειρατεία αποτελούσε μια εναλλακτική “διέξοδο” απόκτησης κέρδους και τα άτομα που την ασκούσαν έδειχναν αδιαφορία για το ηθικό μέρος της και τα προβλήματα που προκαλεί σε πολλαπλούς τομείς. Ο αξιόποινος χαρακτήρας της πράξης δεν είναι κάτι νέο, εάν σκεφθούμε ότι από την αρχαιότητα οι πειρατές αντιμετωπίζονταν από τα εκάστοτε κοινωνικά συστήματα ως «εχθροί της ανθρωπότητας». Η πειρατεία πέρασε από διάφορα στάδια ανά τους αιώνες, άλλοτε μεγάλης ακμής και άλλοτε όχι τόσο, ακολούθησε διαφορετική εξελικτική πορεία από περιοχή σε περιοχή και διαφορετικές τακτικές δράσης. Παρ’ όλες τις κατά τόπους και κατ’ εποχήν ιδιαιτερότητες ωστόσο, πάντοτε υπήρχαν άνθρωποι που λόγω των κοινωνικοοικονομικών συνθηκών λάμβαναν το ρίσκο της ενασχόλησής τους αυτής, προκειμένου σε πρώτο επίπεδο να βελτιώσουν το βιοτικό τους επίπεδο. Στην παρούσα εργασία η πειρατεία εξετάστηκε υπό το πρίσμα της «απειλής» που μπορεί να αποτελέσει για τη διεθνή ειρήνη και ασφάλεια και ειδικότερα αναλύθηκε σε τρία κεφάλαια. Στο πρώτο εξετάστηκε ιστορικά, έπειτα προσεγγίστηκε πολιτικά και τέλος νομικά και επιχειρησιακά. Αρχικά αναλύθηκε η ιστορική πορεία του φαινομένου από την αρχαιότητα μέχρι και τα τέλη του 17ου αιώνα ενώ στα άλλα δύο η ανάλυση εστίασε στη σύγχρονη εποχή και τις προκλήσεις που έχουν διαμορφωθεί από τα τέλη του 20ου αιώνα μέχρι και σήμερα.Δείτε περισσότερα

findings.evidence_excerpt:
SIGNIFICATION HISTORIQUE DE LA PIRATERIE GRECQUE 
 La piraterie antique a déjà fait l'objet de plusieurs travaux de synthèse : notamment de J.-M. Sestier en 1880 (La piraterie dans l'Antiquité), de HA. Ormerod en 1924 (Piracy in the Ancient World), d'E. Ziebarth en 1929 (Beitràge zur Geschichte des Seeraubs une Seehandels imalten Griechenland). Mais ce qu'on y trouve, c'est un récit anecdotique de son développement (toujours utile par la documentation mise en œuvre) plutôt qu'une véritable explication historique de ce phénomène (telle du moins que nous en ressentons aujourd'hui le besoin) (1)*. 
 Pour Sestier, l'histoire de la piraterie antique est celle du passage de la barbarie à la civilisation, dont les principales étapes sont marquées par la formation, dans le bassin méditerranéen, de « nations » distinctes, puis par l'extension de l'Empire romain, et enfin par la diffusion du christianisme, « à qui il sera donné de transformer, de civiliser par sa divine morale, par l'enseignement du respect des biens et de la liberté d'autrui, ces Barbares accoutumés jusqu'alors à ne vivre que de pillage, de violence et de brigandage » — histoire qui ne devait se terminer qu'« au jour où le glorieux drapeau de la France fut victorieusement planté sur les murailles d'Alger, le repaire suprême de la piraterie sur les bords de la Méditerranée » (p. VI- VII). Ormerod, de son côté, insiste sur les facilités offertes aux pirates (compte tenu de la technologie contemporaine) par la navigation côtière : en l'absence, tout au moins, d'empires maritimes ou terrestres susceptibles d'y mettre temporairement bon ordre. Quant à l'ouvrage de Ziebarth, il ne tient nullement les promesses de son titre : on y trouve mécaniquement juxtaposées une présentation événementielle de la piraterie - de cas particuliers imputables au « tempérament » grec et à l'insuffisance des mesures de protection — et une présentation moderniste du commerce, qui manifeste une totale incompréhension des thèses naguère soutenues par J . Hasebroek (2) . 
 Aux yeux de ces historiens « humanistes », la piraterie antique se nourrit donc de cette part de nature (mauvaise) qui subsiste, à la faveur des conditions géographiques, sur les marges et dans les interstices de l'ordre établi et que les États gréco-romains, précurseurs des puissances coloniales modernes, étaient seuls à même d'éliminer par la répression (autrement dit : par la « pacification »). Pour eux, il s'agit essentiellement d'un phénomène de remanence, qui entrave le développement de la civilisation (souvent identifiée, de manière significative, à la « liberté » du commerce). La principale fonction qu'ils lui reconnaissent est, en conséquence, de caractère négatif. 
 Certains historiens occidentaux ont réagi contre ce genre d'interprétation en signalant les liens organiques qui unissaient la piraterie antique à tel ou tel autre aspect des sociétés contemporaines — aux modes d'organisation politique, aux coutumes régissant les rapports entre États, au fonctionnement de l'économie et particulièrement à l'esclavage —, tandis que d'autres, par leurs articles d'érudition, précisaient notre connaissance des faits sur quelques

findings.title: Piracy in the Early Hellenistic Period: a Career Open to Talents
findings.evidence_excerpt: Pirates were frequently employed by the Diadochoi and the Epigonoi of Alexander as an auxiliary military or naval force, and some examples are given below. Unfortunately, the surviving evidence does not allow us to do more than make the general statement. The evidence for piratical activity is largely in the form of personal anecdotes, and the evidence for the nature of Hellenistic military and naval establishments is nothing more than a record of a few persons and/or positions. The authors of our scant literary sources, especially those who wrote many generations after the events which they describe, were not attempting to analyse the role of pirates for posterity, thus they often use the word ‘pirate’ with a notable lack of precision, if they use it at all. Nevertheless, a review of the existing evidence suggests a rather remarkable degree of social and occupational mobility in the third century B.C.

findings.title: Διαπολιτισμικές συναντήσεις στη Μεσόγειο: οι Οθωμανοί μέσα από το βενετικό βλέμμα
findings.evidence_excerpt:
δραστηριοτήτων των Καθολικών πειρατών και των Ορθόδοξων εμπόρων, μας αναλύει τον τρόπο
με τον οποίο αυτές οι διαφορετικές ομάδες συνεργάστηκαν και περιηγήθηκαν στη Μεσόγειο.
Λειτουργώντας υπό την προστασία των χριστιανικών δυνάμεων, οι Καθολικοί πειρατές συχνά
συνεργάζονταν με μουσουλμάνους, σχηματίζοντας συμμαχίες με βάση το αμοιβαίο συμφέρον.
Ομοίως, Ορθόδοξοι έμποροι έκαναν εμπόριο πέρα από θρησκευτικά σύνορα, χρησιμοποιώντας
τα εμπορικά τους δίκτυα για να διευκολύνουν τις οικονομικές ανταλλαγές μεταξύ χριστιανικών
και μουσουλμανικών εδαφών39. Η ανάλυση της Green υπογραμμίζει την πρακτική φύση αυτών
των αλληλεπιδράσεων, όπου τα οικονομικά συμφέροντα συχνά υπερτερούσαν ενάντια στις
θρησκευτικές και ιδεολογικές διαφορές.
Επιπροσθέτως η Greene σκιαγραφεί τον πολύπλοκο ιστό των διαπολιτισμικών σχέσεων που
τροφοδότησαν τη Μεσόγειο του 17ου αιώνα. Χρησιμοποιώντας πρωτογενείς πηγές της εποχής,
υφαίνει με συναρπαστικό τρόπο μια ιστορία ανταλλαγής και συνεργασίας μεταξύ των
χριστιανών και των μουσουλμάνων αυτών των περιοχών που βρίσκονται σε ένα σκηνικό
συνεργασίας και πόλωσης. Ως παράδειγμα, εξηγεί πώς το εμπόριο έφερε κοντά ανθρώπους από
διαφορετικούς πολιτισμούς και υπόβαθρα. Συμπληρωματικά, ισχυρίζεται ότι οι θρησκευτικές
ομάδες δεν ήταν ενοποιημένες στη Μεσόγειο καθώς υπήρχαν υπο-ομάδες, με αρκετά
διαφορετικές στάσεις, οι οποίες συχνά αλληλεπιδρούσαν μεταξύ τους και μοιράζονταν κοινές
πρακτικές και πεποιθήσεις 40. Συνολικά με βάση τα επιχειρήματα της Greene έχουμε ένα όραμα
για την Μεσόγειο ως ένας περίπλοκος πολυπολιτισμικός κόμβος που γίνεται κατανοητός μέσα
από την αλληλεξάρτηση που χαρακτηρίζει τους κατοίκους της τόσο σε οικονομικά όσο και σε
πολιτικά πλαίσια.
Ο Cyprian Broodbank προσφέρει μια εξίσου εις βάθος ανάλυση για τη Μεσόγειο,
παρακολουθώντας την ανάπτυξή της από την προϊστορία έως την ανάδυση του αρχαίου κόσμου.
Ο Broodbank επικεντρώνεται στον ρόλο των θαλάσσιων δικτύων εξηγώντας όχι μόνο την
εμπορική χρήση τους αλλά και την συνεισφορά τους στις διαπολιτισμικές ροές. Παρακολουθεί

findings.evidence_excerpt: Τις τελευταίες δεκαετίες, η πειρατεία έχει επανέλθει στο επίκεντρο της συζήτησης της διεθνούς κοινότητας, καθώς όλος και περισσότερος λόγος γίνεται για την εκθετική αύξηση των περιστατικών πειρατείας σε περιοχές ιδίως όπως η Ανατολική Αφρική. Η παρούσα εργασία στόχο έχει να αναλύσει το φαινόμενο της πειρατείας, εξετάζοντας το διαχρονικά και συγχρονικά. Επιπλέον, αν και η πειρατεία είναι προφανές ότι έχει σημαντικές κοινωνικές και περιβαλλοντικές συνέπειες, στην παρούσα μελέτη θα εστιάσουμε στις οικονομικές συνέπειες της πειρατείας, σε όλες τις οικονομικές δραστηριότητες, με έμφαση στον αντίκτυπο της πειρατείας στη ναυτιλιακή βιομηχανία.

findings.title: Με αφορμή τον θάνατο του Creveliers στην Αστυπάλαια. Ο ρόλος του νησιού στις καταδρομικές επιχειρήσεις των καθολικών κουρσάρων κατά τον 17ο αιώνα Occasioned by the death of Creveliers off Astypalaia: The island's role in the raids by Catholic corsairs during the 17th century
findings.evidence_excerpt: Between shortly before midnight of the 24th and early morning of the 25th of September 1679, the life of French corsair Hugues Creveliers, leader of the most important corsair company active in the Aegean sea in the 1670s, came to an inglorious end off the coast of Astypalaia, due to the blowing up of his ship by a member of his crew. The present study takes a closer look at the details of the event and attempts to portray the role that Astypalaia played in the raids of Catholic privateers against the Ottomans during the seventeenth century; raids which had become a regular occurrence because they could find provisions there (such as bread, wine, etc.) and stock up with drinking water, but also because the island provided plenty of safe anchorages. The names of Astypalaia's havens in French and Italian portolan texts, along with other information of the time (testimonies about corsair contrac ts written on the island and marriages between privateers and local Greek women), attest not only the strong relationship that the corsairs built with Astypalaia, but also the degree of appropriation of the place by them. In the last part of this study we examine the role of the bay of Vathy in the corsair raids, since this is most likely where the explosion of Creveliers' ship took place. This particular bay has similar traits to other anchorages in the Cycladic islands where we know that corsairs repaired their ships, since they had built small forts of batteries at the narrow entrances to these lairs so that no enemy ship could approach. In-situ research conducted by the author on the south side of the narrow straits of Vathy bay led to the discovery of similar built structures which semm to be relevant to the frequent corsair presence there.

but also to extend the scope of research into eras and regions where textual evidence is silent or absent. It is precisely this imbalance between the dominance of historical approaches and the relative reticence of archaeology
that calls for a methodological shift, bringing material evidence to the forefront of the investigation.
An effort to address the archaeological approach to piracy in antiquity lay at the core of the research project
“From Archaeology of Piracy to Pirate Archaeology: Piracy in the Greek Seas from Prehistoric to Roman
Times” (A.P.Pir.A.). The project was funded by the Hellenic Foundation for Research and Innovation (H.F.R.I.)
under the “2nd Call for H.F.R.I. Research Projects to Support Post-Doctoral Researchers” (Project Number:
34). Hosted by the Department of History and Archaeology of the National and Kapodistrian University of
Athens (N.K.U.A.) from January 2021 to June 2024, the A.P.Pir.A. project was brought to fruition by the editor
of the present volume as Principal Investigator, alongside a dedicated team of early-career researchers: Orestis
Goulakos, Nadia Giagkoudaki, Panagiotis Gounelas, Alexandra Malliou, Konstantinos Pantzouris and Dimitris
Sakkas.
In the final stage of the project, the international hybrid conference “The Archaeology of Piracy in A
­ ntiquity”
was held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the N.K.U.A., and the present
volume constitutes the proceedings of that conference. Almost all papers presented during the sessions are
included here; regrettably, a small number could not be finalized in time for this publication. However, the
collection is enriched by two significant contributions that were not originally presented at the conference. I am
deeply grateful to Adam Dawson, Nicholas Rauh and George Koutsouflakis for their willingness to contribute
to this volume. Their papers, focusing respectively on the Phournoi archipelago and Cilicia, two areas with a notorious pirate past, offer crucial insights through significant methodological approaches, including underwater
archaeology, surface survey and GIS-based analysis.
It is evident that the archaeological investigation of piracy represents an arduous undertaking marked by
multiple conceptual and methodological challenges, both as a general concept and specifically within the context of antiquity. Piracy is elusive by nature, often leaving behind ambiguous or indirect material traces that
resist straightforward interpretation. It was never the intention of a small research team, nor the goal of a single
conference, to exhaustively cover such a vast subject or to provide definitive answers. Rather, the aim was to
initiate a meaningful scholarly dialog, stimulate critical reflection and encourage a broader range of researchers
to engage with the archaeological dimensions of piracy. The emphasis was placed on raising questions rather

In a collective endeavor such as this, the contribution of many individuals is indispensable. I extend my
sincere thanks to all the conference participants and the authors of this volume, each of whom contributed,
through their unique perspective, to initiating an academic dialog on the archaeology of piracy in antiquity. I
am also indebted to the anonymous external peer reviewers for their careful and constructive comments, which
contributed significantly to the high scholarly standard of the volume. Special thanks are due to the members of
the A.P.Pir.A. Advisory Committee for their unwavering support from the very outset: Professor Emerita Nota
Kourou, Professor Emerita Nagia Sgouritsa, Professor Yiannis Papadatos, Professor Lefteris Platon, Associate
Professor Stelios Katakis, Assistant Professor Marlen Mouliou and the late Professor Panos Valavanis (all of the
N.K.U.A.). All the aforementioned also served on the Scientific Committee of the conference, which was further
distinguished by the participation of: Professor Emerita Pavlina Karanastasi (University of Crete), Professor
Konstantinos Kopanias (N.K.U.A.), Professor Eleni Manakidou (Aristotle University of Thessaloniki), Professor Alexandros Mazarakis Ainian (University of Thessaly), Professor Diamantis Panagiotopoulos (Heidelberg University), Professor Dimitris Plantzos (N.K.U.A.), Professor Manolis Stefanakis (University of the Aegean), Professor George Vavouranakis (N.K.U.A.), Professor Andreas Vlachopoulos (University of Ioannina),
Associate Professor Nikolas Dimakis (N.K.U.A.), Associate Professor Eurydice Kefalidou (N.K.U.A.), Associate
Professor Antonis Kotsonas (New York University), Assistant Professor George Koutsouflakis (University of
Thessaly) and Assistant Professor Vassilis Petrakis (N.K.U.A.). I would like to thank Prof. Dimitris Plantzos,
Dr. Photeini Ball and Dr. Michel Roggenbucke (N.K.U.A.) for their kind willingness to assist with the practical
administration of the A.P.Pir.A. project. I would also like to thank the members of the A.P.Pir.A. team, Orestis,
Nadia, Panagiotis, Alexandra, Konstantinos and Dimitris, for accompanying me on this journey. Finally, my
heartfelt gratitude goes to Katerina Boukala, who, with exceptional professionalism, dedication and patience,
succeeded in transforming our collective effort into this book.
A few months before the completion of this volume, the archaeological community lost Panos Valavanis.
Long before the A.P.Pir.A. project took its final form, he had been one its most enthusiastic supporters, firmly
believing in both the scholarly relevance and the wider potential of what we come to call the “archaeology of
piracy”.
Those who had the privilege of working with him will remember not only his academic stature, but also his
exceptional ability to inspire younger scholars to think boldly and independently. For this reason, the iconic
final scene of the film Dead Poets Society offers a particularly fitting image: Panos Valavanis was among that
rare breed of mentors who inspire their students to stand upon their desks in a gesture of profound respect and
tribute.
Farewell, my Captain.
Vangelis Samaras
January 2026

This study serves as the introduction to the volume The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity and aims to survey
­scholarship on ancient piracy, while primarily assessing the possibilities and limitations of an archaeological approach to
the ­phenomenon. The paper is structured in two main parts. The first part offers a concise overview of research on ancient
piracy from the late 19th century to the present and addresses a series of key issues, including the definition of piracy
and the fluidity of its boundaries, the range and forms of pirate activity, the social and ethnic heterogeneity of pirates,
the complex relationship between piracy and trade, the varied responses of official authorities and social perceptions of
piracy in the ancient world. The second part focuses on the archaeology of piracy. It begins by outlining the history of
­archaeological research in this field and the methodological challenges posed by the difficulty of linking pirate activity to
specific archaeological evidence. It then introduces the A.P.Pir.A. project, which sought to develop a framework for the
meaningful integration of piracy into archaeological discourse through the study of the phenomenon in the Greek seas
from the Final Neolithic to the Roman period (ca. 4000 BCE – 330 CE). The paper further explores the ways in which
piracy can be approached archaeologically by drawing on different categories of material evidence, such as settlements,
­fortifications, funerary assemblages and iconography, in direct dialog with the individual contributions to the volume. It
concludes with reflections on future directions of research, emphasizing that, despite inherent methodological ­challenges,
piracy can be documented through material culture. From this perspective, archaeology is shown to contribute not only
to the identification of piracy as a historical phenomenon but also to a deeper understanding of its social and economic
impact in the ancient world.

INTRODUCTORY REMARKS
“Pirates always used to harass those who sailed the sea, even as brigands did those who dwelt on land. There was
never a time when these practices were unknown, nor will they ever cease probably so long as human nature
remains the same” (Cass. Dio 36.20.1, trans. E. Cary, London and New York, 1914). The accuracy of Cassius
Dio’s remark is borne out even today: despite the existence of powerful state and transnational organizations
with the technological capacity to eradicate piracy altogether, pirate activity persists unabated in critical sealanes throughout the globe. The present volume addresses aspects of the earliest phases in the long history of
piracy, with a particular emphasis on assessing the potential of an archaeological approach to the phenomenon.
This introductory chapter outlines the emerging field of the archaeology of piracy. It first provides a concise
survey of the numerous studies on piracy in antiquity, from the late 19th century to the present. Attention is
then drawn to specific issues that are essential to the scholarly investigation of piracy, both ancient and more recent. This is followed by an overview of the development of the archaeology of piracy, tracing its trajectory from

section presents the A.P.Pir.A. project (full title: “From Archaeology of Piracy to Pirate Archaeology: Piracy
in the Greek Seas from Prehistoric to Roman Times”), which provided the basis for the preparation of this
volume. The A.P.Pir.A. project represents part of a broader initiative, launched in the current century, to address
piracy systematically through the analysis of archaeological evidence. The introduction concludes with a brief
­discussion of specific categories of material culture that preserve traces of ancient piracy and related activities,
as illustrated by the contributions to this volume.
Although the main focus is placed on antiquity, the volume closes with two studies, one by George
­Koutsouflakis and one by George Koutzakiotis, that address piracy in the early modern era. Owing to their
­comparatively abundant body of material and textual evidence, these studies offer insights that are of considerable value for the investigation of ancient piracy and its archaeological dimensions. Finally, it should be
mentioned that, in the case of collective volumes devoted to ancient piracy, references have been provided not
only to the volumes themselves, but also to nearly all the individual chapters they contain. The advantage of this
editorial decision is to make this introduction a comprehensive point of departure and a useful guide for future
research into the phenomenon of piracy in antiquity.

PIRACY IN ANTIQUITY: A CENTURY AND A HALF OF SCHOLARSHIP
Research on piracy in antiquity dates back roughly a century and a half to Jules M. Sestier’s pioneering study
La piraterie dans l’antiquité (1880). Most early works (e.g., Sestier 1880; Ormerod 1922, 1923, 1924a, 1924b;
­Ziebarth 1929) attempted to present broad historical overviews of ancient piracy based on Greek and Latin
­textual information. Others, such as Ellen C. Semple (1916) and John A. Davison (1930), analyzed ancient
piracy along more specific lines: Semple examined the geographical and economic conditions that fostered
­Mediterranean piracy, while Davison briefly considered Cicero’s role in the promulgation of the Lex Gabinia,
the law that granted Pompey extraordinary and unprecedented powers to suppress piracy in 67 BCE. He treated
it more as a vehicle of Roman Republican politics than as piracy per se. This pioneering phase of research was
characterized more by comprehensive treatment of the source tradition than by critical methods of analysis;
the works tend to furnish narrative descriptions, often echoing ancient authors’ moralizing tones and treating
­“piracy” as a transhistorical phenomenon that warranted little explanation. Ormerod’s synthesis (Ormerod
1942a) at least attempted to identify typologies of maritime predation and regional patterning, whereas Semple’s
geographical lens foreshadowed later attention to the environmental and economic constraints on piracy.
A second phase of research, extending from the 1960s to the end of the 20th century, comprises more
s­ ynthetic treatments, such as the studies by Yvon Garlan (1978, 1987), Benedetto Bravo (1980) and William
K. Pritchett (1991), as well as the studies by David Tandy (1997) and Alastair H. Jackson (1973, 1995, 2000)
on ­pirates in Early Iron Age (EIA) and Archaic Greece, respectively. The bulk of scholarly attention, however,
tended to focus on the Hellenistic and Roman periods (e.g., Dell 1967; Maróti 1968, 1970; Hassall et al. 1974;
Ward 1975, 1977; Lintott 1976; Crawford 1977; Brulé 1978, 1999; Clavel-Lévêque 1978; Sumner 1978; Mattingly
1980; ­Ducrey 1983; Gabbert 1986; Marasco 1987; Braund 1993; Tramonti 1994a, 1994b, 1995; Herz 1995; Ferone
1997; Ager 1998; Günther 1999; Perlman 1999). Here the analysis becomes more analytical, with scholars interrogating legal categories, state responses and the political economy of violence. Micro-regional case studies,
such as piracy in Crete, Cyclades and Cilicia (e.g., Brulé 1978; Ducrey 1983; Marasco 1987; P
­ erlman 1999),
likewise began to replace trans-Mediterranean narratives.
A milestone in the treatment of ancient piracy occurred with the publication of Philip de Souza’s Piracy in the
Graeco-Roman World (1999), the first systematically argued and critically documented synthesis to map p
­ iracy
from the Archaic period through Late Antiquity. De Souza integrated literary and epigraphic evidence with
historiographical reassessment, to reframe “piracy” less as a fixed social phenomenon than as a p
­ ropagandistic

The study of ancient piracy has now advanced beyond its treatment as a timeless scourge or a minor footnote
in naval history. The field increasingly understands piracy as a historically contingent and context-dependent
repertoire of practices, shaped by shifting political economies, security regimes and cultural perceptions. This
reframing has freed scholarship from uncritical reliance on ancient authors’ moralizing narratives, simplistic
stereotypes and prejudices, allowing instead for more nuanced analyses of how communities, poleis and empires
constructed, negotiated and instrumentalized the label of piracy.

cannot be said for the term piracy (on the language of ancient piracy see, for instance, MacDonald 1984; Ferone
1997, 43–67; 2008; de Souza 1999, 2–13; Pianezzola 2004). The earliest known occurrence of the word appears
in a mid-3rd century BCE inscription from Rhamnous in Attica (SEG XXIV 154, line 22; de Souza 1999, 3–4;
for a translation and comprehensive analysis see https://www.atticinscriptions.com/inscription/AIO/823). This
does not imply, however, that the practice of piracy did not exist prior to that time. For example, both Homer
and Thucydides describe individuals who, in modern terminology, would be characterized as pirates, even
though the term they employ is robbers (ληϊστῆρες, e.g., Hom. Od. 3.73, 17.425, or λῃσταὶ, e.g., Thuc. 1.8.1, 6.4.5;
for piracy in the Homeric epics see Samaras and Gounelas forthcoming, with further references). In several
instances, even this term is omitted and the pirate nature of the behavior has to be inferred from the context.
Not long after its first attestation, the term pirate acquired a distinctly negative connotation. Almost
­invariably the pirate is portrayed as the “other” – the outsider, the foreigner, the villain. Rarely does an individual define himself as a pirate, while conversely there are numerous instances in which third parties apply
the term selectively, depending on their relationship with the person in question. A striking example is Nabis,
king of Sparta in the late 3rd and early 2nd century BCE. While ancient authors such as Polybius (13.8.2) and
Livy (34.32.18, 34.36.3) describe him as a pirate, the demos of Delos in an honorary decree proclaims him a
proxenos and benefactor (IG XI.4 716, lines 9–10; for further discussions on Nabis see Mendels 1979; Karafotias
1998; Brulé 1999; see also Tsaravopoulos and Kroustalis, this volume). This discrepancy is not unique. Similar
dynamics appear in other contexts, such as in the varying depictions of Cilician seafarers, who are alternately
presented as pirates, allies or even clients, depending on the political alignment of the sources (see Dawson and
Rauh, this volume). Such examples demonstrate how piracy, far from being a fixed category, is part of a contested vocabulary of power, legitimacy and control of mobility.
The selective application of the label pirate underscores its fundamentally relational and perspectival nature:
in ancient written sources (and in later ones as well) it operates less as an objective descriptor and more as a
rhetorical and ideological tool. Thus, any scholarly engagement with ancient piracy must not only catalog instances of the term’s usage, but also interrogate the sociopolitical stakes embedded in those usages. Acts should
be evaluated as piracy (or not) according to clearly defined parameters, rather than merely based on whether
ancient observers classified them as such.

In studies focusing specifically on ancient piracy, the problem of defining piracy is far more pronounced.
In some instances, no definition is provided, presumably because the concept is taken for granted; in others,
definitions are provided but vary widely, as each scholar attempts to create a unique working framework, often
out of dissatisfaction with existing ones. For instance, Henry A. Ormerod (1924a, 60) cites the English legal
definition of piracy as an act of robbery and violence at sea, which, if committed on land, would constitute a
felony because it lacks the authorization of a sovereign state. Philip de Souza (1999, 1) describes pirates more
concisely as “armed robbers whose activities normally involve the use of ships”. Such inconsistency highlights
the conceptual and methodological challenges involved in the study of ancient piracy. If the phenomenon is
difficult to define, it logically follows that placing it in its proper historical context is equally challenging.
During the initial stages of the A.P.Pir.A. project (see below), it became clear that while existing definitions
address key aspects of piracy, none could fully encompass the complexity and variability of the phenomenon.
One of the first steps of the project, therefore, was to adopt a working definition – one that is informed by earlier
scholarship, but one that is also tailored to the specific aims of the investigation. According to this definition, an
act qualifies as piracy when it fulfills the two following criteria: as is widely acknowledged in the literature (e.g.,
de Souza 1999, 1–2; Bradford 2007, xi; Skowronek 2016, 4), piracy must constitute an act of robbery inherently
linked to the maritime sphere, regardless of whether ships are directly employed; in addition, the primary
­motive of piracy must be private economic gain (Samaras 2015, 191; see also Knapp 2018, 36).
This definitional framework proves useful in addressing two major conceptual challenges for the study of
piracy. The first concerns the nature of a pirate’s relationship to the sea. Contemporary perceptions –heavily
influenced by literary and cinematic representations– associate pirates inextricably with ships and seafaring
life. Historically, however, this connection was not universal. While pirates frequently utilized ships to launch
attacks against other vessels or to conduct coastal raids, there are documented instances in which they operated
without ships. Practices such as the looting of shipwrecks –a common occurrence in antiquity, particularly in
regions prone to maritime accidents (e.g., Strabo 5.4.2; 7.6.1; Arr. Peripl. M. Eux. 37; Tsetskhladze 2000–2001,
13; see also Rougé 1966; Mataix Ferrándiz 2022)– and, even more strikingly, the deliberate orchestration of
shipwrecks for the purpose of plunder, constitute a peculiar form of “land-based” piracy (see more in Samaras
and Gounelas forthcoming).
The second major issue addressed by the proposed definition is the distinction between piracy and ­warfare.
Numerous recorded instances concerned raids that transpired during military conflicts, however much they resemble piracy in both their tactical execution and their underlying motivation. The difficulty in distinguishing
between these two forms of organized violence (piracy and warfare) has already been noted by several scholars
(e.g., Wachsmann 1998, 317–21; de Souza 1999, 31–6; Emanuel 2021, 24–9). As previously argued (Samaras
2015, 189–91), the fundamental difference lies in the nature of the action: war, even when e­ conomically motivated, is essentially political in character, whereas piracy belongs to the economic realm and lacks any clear
­political agenda. This conceptual distinction is by no means modern. Fernand Braudel (1973, 867) ­characterized
piracy as “a means of making a living,” noting, in his discussion of the Algerian corsairs, that “if the corsairs
came home empty-handed there would be famine in Algiers”. Much earlier, Aristotle had similarly identified
raiding (ληστρικὸς βίος) as one of the fundamental modes of subsistence, alongside pastoralism, fishing, hunting
and agriculture (Pol. 1256a–b; see also Xen. Cav. 8.8). Of course, this differentiation between piracy and war
exists primarily at a theoretical level. In reality, the boundaries between the two are often blurred. Nevertheless, the distinction remains analytically useful, as it emphasizes that regardless of the ideological or political
­justifications that were sometimes attached to it, piracy was, first and foremost, an economic pursuit.
It should be noted that, although the contributors affiliated with the A.P.Pir.A. project (Nadia Giagkoudaki,
Panagiotis Gounelas, Konstantinos Pantzouris and Dimitris Sakkas) base their analyses in this volume on the

From opportunistic acts to pirate fleets: the spectrum of ancient piracy
Piracy in antiquity can be categorized according to several distinct forms, depending on both the nature of
the operation and the profile of its targets. These include direct attacks by one ship against another in open
waters; raids launched from multiple ships against unprotected coastal or near-coastal targets, such as isolated
farmsteads, rural shrines or pastoral groups; full-scale assaults on larger settlements or even urban centers;
and the plundering of shipwrecks – whether resulting from natural causes or deliberately orchestrated by local
inhabitants along treacherous coastlines. Some of these activities, particularly shipwrecking and opportunistic
raiding, occurred in a gray area between piracy, salvage and subsistence predation, especially in economically
marginal regions (see below).
Beyond this typology, it is important to consider the range and degrees of organization within pirate activity.
At the most rudimentary level, piracy could consist of isolated and opportunistic acts, such as a merchant vessel
abducting a lone shepherd or fishermen appropriating cargo from a wreck. Such events were neither systematic nor premeditated, but rather ad hoc responses to immediate prospects of gain. At a more complex level,
however, piracy could assume forms of semi-permanent, structured organizations. Ancient literary sources
describing the Cilician pirates of the late Hellenistic period (ca. 139–67 BCE) attest to the existence of pirate
flotillas, fortified bases and long-range operations targeting major maritime routes and wealthy sites, including
prominent sanctuaries (e.g., Strabo 14.5.2; App. Mith. 14.92–93; Plut. Pomp. 24.2–5; see more in Dawson and
Rauh, this volume). Earlier examples include the Cretan and Aitolian poleis of the 3rd and 2nd centuries BCE,
which are portrayed as having incorporated piracy into their formal diplomatic and economic practices (on
Cretan and Aitolian piracy, see Brulé 1978; de Souza 1999, 70–6, 80–4; Perlman 1999; on “state” piracy by
Phalasarna and its colony Aigilia, see Tsaravopoulos and Kroustalis, this volume). These examples challenge
simplistic dichotomies between statehood and criminality and invite a more dynamic understanding of ancient
piracy as a phenomenon operating across multiscalar social, economic and political environments.

Who were the pirates? The social and ethnic heterogeneity of pirate crews
The conventional portrayal of a pirate as a marginal and socially deviant figure –rejected by or alienated from
the norms of settled society– is problematized by both archaeological and historical evidence from antiquity and
subsequent periods. Rather than existing entirely outside the social fabric of settled communities, pirates frequently lived within them, resided in ordinary dwellings and participated to varying degrees in local economic
and social life. From a socio-economic perspective it seems clear that piracy was not necessarily a p
­ henomenon
restricted to a particular social stratum. Individuals from across the social spectrum could engage in pirate
­activity, either directly or indirectly. The participation of elites –whether aristocratic landowners, military leaders
or hinterland warlords– should not be regarded as exceptional. On the contrary, access to ships, crews and extensive political or military contacts often made it easier for members of higher social orders to initiate and to
sustain maritime raiding. A characteristic example is Polycrates, the tyrant of Samos in the third quarter of the
6th century BCE, whose naval power and pirate activity are explicitly noted by Herodotus (3.39.3–4). Polycrates
not only used piracy to amass wealth, but he also used it to project power across the eastern ­Aegean and beyond,
thus illustrating how piracy could be incorporated by elite figures into broader strategies of state-building and
regional dominance. Similar dynamics are evident with the late H
­ ellenistic Cilician pirate n
­ etworks mentioned
above, where pirate bands, according to several ancient authors (e.g., Strabo 14.5.2; App. Mith. 14.92), operated
under the protection or with the complicity of local rulers and by drawing support from otherwise peaceful
coastal populations. These pirates established semi-permanent bases throughout the ­Mediterranean and main-

tained control over maritime routes by engaging in a medley of raiding and commercial exchanges (see more in
Dawson and Rauh, this volume).
Conversely, individuals from lower social strata also participated in piracy, though typically through
­different avenues. Many served as crew members or engaged in raiding on a temporary or ad hoc basis, having
been drawn into pirate activity through economic hardship, displacement resulting from conflict or the c­ ollapse
of traditional subsistence lifeways. For example, one plausible scenario –previously proposed by the present
author (Samaras 2015, 193)– is that, following the disintegration of the Mycenaean palatial system in the
­Postpalatial Aegean, “the unemployed mercenaries of the Palatial period” continued to deploy their martial
­expertise ­independently, turning to, among other activities, piracy as a means of survival and wealth acquisition.
An important aspect of pirate identity –potentially relevant for archaeological interpretation– is the social
and ethnic heterogeneity of pirate crews. Although direct evidence is often limited, textual sources attest to
the fact that these groups often comprised individuals from diverse geographic origins and socio-economic
backgrounds, reflecting the translocal, interwoven nature of seaborne raiding parties and the flexible structures
that supported them. For example, Appian reports that the Cilician pirate fleets of the late Hellenistic period
comprised not merely Cilicians, but also “men of Syrian, Cyprian, Pamphylian, and Pontic origin and those of
almost all the Eastern nations” (Mith. 14.92, trans. H. White, New York, 1899). It is safe to assume, therefore,
that the collective designation Cilicians most probably referred to pirate bands whose origins were ethnically
heterogeneous.
The social origin of individuals engaged in piracy also most likely shaped the motivation of those who
­ ursued such activity. For people originating from marginal, resource-scarce environments –such as arid isp
lands, mountainous coasts or depopulated rural zones– piracy plausibly represents one of the only available
means of subsistence or economic advancement. In contexts of pronounced social inequality, where wealth and
status were as a rule inherited and beyond the reach of impoverished elements, piracy offered an alternative
route to power, prestige and sometimes even to formal authority. For those of elite status, piracy served different, though complementary, functions: it enabled the accumulation of wealth, the demonstration of martial
skill and the reinforcement or expansion of social influence. In this regard, piracy functioned not only as an
economic activity but as a socio-political mechanism embedded within local and regional dynamics of power,
status and survival.

findings.evidence_excerpt:
Piracy and trade: rethinking an apparent paradox
Very often, scholars or commentators assert that interruptions in maritime trade during a given period were
likely attributable to piracy or, conversely, that periods of flourishing commercial activity demonstrated an
absence of piracy. Underlying such views is the self-evident assumption that piracy worked as a disincentive to maritime trade. However, the historical reality is far more complex. Longitudinal studies of piracy
clearly demonstrate that maritime trade not only persisted but often thrived during periods of intense pirate
­activity. This apparent paradox challenges linear models of economic disruption and invites a more nuanced
­interpretation of the historical relationship between piracy and trade.
Vincent Gabrielsen, a scholar who has studied the significant upsurge in piracy during the Hellenistic p
­ eriod,
emphasizes that commercial centers prospered during this upsurge throughout the Aegean (Gabrielsen 2001,
220–23; 2013, 147–53; see also Gabrielsen 2003, which focuses in particular on the relationship between piracy
and a distinct form of commercial activity, namely, the slave-trade). His analysis discredits the simplistic duality
of trade versus piracy and instead proposes a model of functional coexistence, wherein pirate enterprise was
structurally integrated into broader patterns of economic exchange. As Fernand Braudel has observed (1973,
887), this positive correlation between piracy and trade is not unique to antiquity, but extends into more recent
periods as well. The reasons for this seem clear: maritime trade provided the necessary structural conditions
–the targets, the sea-lanes and the maritime markets– for piracy to thrive and to prevail. Typically, following

findings.evidence_excerpt:
a successful pirate venture pirates would engage in forms of exchange to realize the value of their plunder,
for example, to exchange whatever goods they had plundered for those they actually needed. Contrary to the
­romanticized portrayals in literature and film, pirates did not hoard treasure in caves or bury it beneath the
sand. Rather, they raided ships and settlements, seized portable goods and subsequently entered the ­commercial
orbit themselves –licitly or illicitly– to convert their booty into profit. As Philip de Souza aptly observed (de
Souza 1999, 56), “piracy itself could be considered as a form of trade”. As such, it was extremely commonplace
for some individuals to alternate between piracy and mercantile activity, depending on the circumstances and
the calculated prospects of financial gain. This fluidity between roles reflects not merely opportunism, but a
socio-economic continuum within which violence, commerce and illegality frequently overlapped.
The Odyssey offers several illustrations of this dynamic. In the Cretan tale that Odysseus relates to E
­ umaeus,
a Phoenician merchant decides to sell the “son of Castor” into slavery (Od. 14.287–298). The scenario is then
repeated by a group of Thesprotian traders (Od. 14.334–359). Likewise, Eumaeus recounts that he himself was
­abducted by Phoenician merchants after they had stayed in his homeland “for a whole year [...] and traded for
much substance” (Od. 15.455–456, trans. J.E. Huddleston, https://topostext.org/work/3). These episodes are not
so much narrative ­embellishments as they are culturally grounded reflections of a world in which the boundaries between trade and raiding were permeable, and where seafaring groups could assume multiple identities
depending on ­context and objectives.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
Official responses to piracy: suppression, toleration and collaboration
Another issue that merits critical attention is the relationship between legitimate authority and piracy – a
­relationship that ranges from overt hostility to open collaboration. While the antagonistic stance of states or
local powers toward piracy may appear natural or even inevitable, it must be emphasized that this hostility was
by no means hypothetical. Throughout antiquity, a number of political and military authorities actively ­pursued
large-scale campaigns to suppress piracy. Occasionally, ancient literary sources attributed the eradication of seaborne piracy to a particular figure, such as Minos (Thuc. 1.4.1, 1.8.1–2) or Jason (Plut. Thes. 19.4). Historical figures, like Themistocles (Nep. Them. 2.1–4) and Cimon (Plut. Cim. 8.5), were likewise credited with clearing the
seas of pirates. Naval powers, including Corinth (Thuc. 1.13.5), Athens (Aristid. Or. 13.113), Rhodes (Diod. Sic.
20.81.3; Strabo 14.2.5; Aristid. Or. 44.570), and Rome (Cic. Leg. Man. 33; Strabo 14.3.3; App. B Civ. 2.1.1; Mith.
14.95), earned widespread reputations for policing the seas and keeping them safe from pirates. Nevertheless,
despite these confident assertions by ancient sources, the actual effectiveness of anti-­piracy operations appears
to have been limited, especially with regard to any long-term impact. Even in the case of the most renowned
anti-piracy campaign, that of Pompey in 67 BCE, modern scholars (e.g., de Souza 1999, 179–85; Tröster 2009,
esp. 28–31; Lampinen 2022, 52–3) have significantly questioned ancient testimony that Pompey eradicated
piracy once and for all (e.g., Cic. Leg. Man. 33; App. B Civ. 2.1.1; Mith. 14.95; Flor. 3.6.13–15; Oros. 6.4.1).
Such assertions appear to have been shaped or amplified by Roman political propaganda intended to glorify
Pompey’s extraordinary efficiency and military competence as a commander. Scholars have expressed similar
concerns regarding the success of Rhodian anti-piracy efforts, the actual effectiveness and long-term consequences of which appear to warrant closer scrutiny, despite the assertions of ancient sources (see K
­ almpourtzi,
this volume).
Alongside these repressive strategies, there is substantial evidence of cooperation and complicity between
official powers and pirate actors. Pirates frequently depended on the collaboration of or toleration by authorities, frequently by offering a share in their stolen gain in exchange for strategic advantages. These might include
access to safe harbors during storms or while attempting to evade pursuit, as well as access to marketplaces,
where they could dispose of their plunder and procure essential supplies. Conversely, political and military
leaders often collaborated openly with pirates by actively recruiting their naval expertise, local knowledge and
combat skills to further strategic goals or to undermine rivals.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
This symbiotic dynamic between piracy and political authority is attested in various periods of ­antiquity with
abundant examples of blurred boundaries, where piracy overlapped with state-sanctioned raiding. In C
­ lassical
Athens, for instance, the state occasionally collaborated with pirates on military expeditions and o
­ therwise
disguised quasi-pirate campaigns under the guise of official military operations – particularly in periods of resource scarcity (e.g., Thuc. 4.9.1; Xen. Hell. 4.8.35). During the Hellenistic period, several ­poleis –most n
­ otably
Aitolian and Cretan poleis– were notorious for harboring and collaborating with pirates. A
­ itolian leaders frequently employed pirate tactics for territorial expansion and population control (e.g., Polyb. 4.3.1–4.1, 4.9.9).
Cretan poleis often served as pirate bases, offering infrastructure, markets and even political ­protection. As
Philip de Souza observes (de Souza 1999, 98), “it is clear that many Hellenistic rulers and communities preferred to ­benefit from piracy rather than attempt its suppression”. Indeed, during this particular era, state
­authorities exhibited such extraordinary tolerance of piracy, if not outright cooperation therewith, that the
pattern of state-­sponsored ­piracy corresponded to that of a widening intensification of piracy across the eastern
­Mediterranean. One striking example is provided by Demetrius I Poliorcetes’ use of pirates as auxiliary forces
to disrupt m
­ aritime communication and support naval operations during his famous siege of Rhodes in 305/4
BCE (e.g., Diod. Sic. 20.82.5–83.1, 20.97.5; see also de Souza 1999, 43–6). Equally illustrative is the response
of Queen Teuta of Illyria to the Roman ambassadors who protested against the repeated attacks on Roman
shipping by Illyrian pirates in the Adriatic: “[…] it was contrary to the custom of the Illyrian kings to hinder
their subjects from gaining booty from the sea” (Polyb. 2.8.8, trans. W.R. Paton, London and New York, 1922).
This declaration epitomizes a mode of governance, where piracy was not only tolerated by a royal authority but
effectively sanctioned as legitimate customary practice. In other instances, piracy was not merely tolerated but
directly financed, organized and politically instrumentalized. Numerous examples attest to the use of pirates as
instruments of state power or as formally employed mercenaries. In short, there is ample historical evidence of
authorities who shielded and supported pirate activity – be that through passive toleration, covert cooperation
or active sponsorship. As Vincent Gabrielsen rightly noted (Gabrielsen 2013, 135), “piracy and statehood are
intimately connected.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
Whose side are you on? Moral relativity and the perception of piracy in antiquity
Referring to the “early times”, namely, the period prior to the 5th century BCE, in which he himself lived,
­Thucydides remarked that “this occupation [piracy] did not yet involve disgrace, but rather conferred something even of glory” (Thuc. 1.5.1, trans. C.F. Smith, Cambridge, Mass., 1920). This observation is corroborated
by a typical greeting of the Homeric poems, according to which locals, upon the arrival of an unknown ship,
would ask whether the newcomers are traders or pirates:
“Who are you, strangers? From where did you sail the watery ways?
On some business, or did you roam at random,
even as pirates over the sea, who roam
and risk their lives and bring evil to foreigners?”
(Hom. Od. 3.71–74, 9.252–255, trans. J.E. Huddleston, https://topostext.org/work/3; see also Hymn.
Hom. Ap. 452–455).

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
On the strength of this passage, and especially the authority of the great Athenian historian, it is often
­asserted (e.g., Ormerod 1924a, 97; Garlan 1978; van Wees 1992, 257–58; Cavazzuti 2004, 46; Lewis 2019, 82)
that, prior to the 5th century BCE, piracy was not only tolerated but viewed as a legitimate path to prestige
and honor within one’s community, whereas, following the rise of polis society, it was morally condemned and
­socially rejected (for piracy in the EIA Aegean see Samaras 2015; Gounelas, this volume).
The evidence of the Homeric poems points, however, to a more complex moral landscape than Thucydides’
concise remark implies. A telling example is furnished by the persona that Odysseus invents in his c­ onversation

findings.evidence_excerpt:
with Eumaeus, where he impersonates the son of Castor from Crete (Hom. Od. 14.199–359). Here piracy
­appears as a legitimate form of livelihood: raiding, pillaging and warfare are presented as established and even
admirable ways of acquiring wealth, enhancing status and gaining respect:
“For before the sons of the Achaeans set foot on Troy,
I’d led men and swift-sailing ships nine times
against foreign men, and very many things fell to me,
from which I picked out many choice ones, and many later
came to me by lot. My house soon prospered, and thereafter
I became feared and revered among the Cretans.”
(Hom. Od. 14.229–234, trans. J.E. Huddleston, https://topostext.org/work/3).

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
Yet, when the pseudo-Cretan’s fortunes change and he himself falls prey to pirates, his tone shifts and
he condemns the very practices he formerly embraced (for detailed discussion see Samaras and Gounelas
­forthcoming):
“a Phoenician came then, a man expert in lying tales,
a gnawer, who’d done many evils to men,
[…] he put me on a seafaring ship to Libya,
falsely advising me that I’d be bringing back cargo with him,
but so he could sell me there and get an untold price for me.”
“an evil plan about me pleased their minds,
so that I’d still be brought completely to a calamity of woe.”
(Hom. Od. 14.288–297, 337–338, trans. J.E. Huddleston, https://topostext.org/work/3).

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
Such ambivalence was not confined to the Homeric society; comparable attitudes can be traced across
­antiquity and beyond. Perceptions of piracy were often shaped by one’s point of view: those who participated
in or benefited from it could depict it as normal, even heroic, whereas, victims of piracy and communities
excluded from its gains viewed it as illicit, reprehensible and unjust. For the researcher of ancient piracy this
twofold perspective seems crucial: moral judgement was not necessarily fixed, but rather contingent upon one’s
position vis-à-vis the practice.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
THE ARCHAEOLOGY OF PIRACY: FROM MARGINAL NOTES TO EMERGING
FIELD
Until the early 21st century, archaeological investigations linked to piracy remained sparse and largely ­incidental.
Since the 2000s, however, scholarly interest in the archaeology of piracy has increased significantly, with a
growing number of studies exploring the phenomenon through material remains. Among the most systematic
contributions are the edited volumes by Russell Skowronek and Charles Ewen (2006, 2016, 2023), Jean Soulat
(2019) and Lynn Brenda Harris and Valerie Ann Johnson (2022), which collectively represent key milestones
in the development of the field (see also Hartnett and Dawdy 2013). Unsurprisingly, these works concentrate
on the so-called “Golden Age of Piracy” (late 17th to early 18th century), focusing primarily on the Caribbean
Sea and, to a lesser extent, the Indian Ocean. In contrast, the Eastern Mediterranean, and particularly the

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
Greek seas, has yet to see comparable systematic archaeological engagement, despite evidence of sustained
pirate and privateer activity throughout the early modern period (e.g., Krantonelli 1985, 1991, 1998; Harlaftis
et al. 2016). Recent studies by George Koutzakiotis (2023, this volume) demonstrate the potential of integrating
­archaeological research with the rich documentary evidence of the period, revealing promising avenues for the
study of piracy in this region.
A similar paucity of archaeological studies is evident for piracy in classical antiquity. A pioneering example
linking specific archaeological finds to the phenomenon of piracy was advanced by Antonios Keramopoullos
(1923, 42–3), who argued that the seventeen shackled individuals uncovered during Konstantinos Kourouniotis
and Stratis Pelekidis’ excavations at Phaleron were probably pirates executed for their deeds (see also Bosnakis
2020, 159–69). Otherwise, references to piracy in the archaeological literature have been few and, when they do
appear, they are typically brief and interpreted from a victims’ perspective. Some have pointed to the numerous
Late Classical and Hellenistic towers situated on islands and along the eastern Mediterranean mainland coast,
to suggest that these functioned as bastions to protect coastal communities and private landowners from pirate
raids (e.g., Ormerod 1924a, 41–3; 1924b, 31–2; Young 1956, 132–33; Osborne 1986, 173–74; Pritchett 1991,
352–58; Seifried and Parkinson 2014, 310). Likewise, the intense piracy that plagued the Aegean in the first half
of the 1st century BCE has led many scholars to attribute the contemporaneous evidence of violent d
­ estruction
at Delos to pirate raids that are reported to have occurred there in 88 and 69 BCE (e.g., Mattingly 1980; Rauh
1993, 68; Hatzidakis 1997, 293, 307; Siebert 2001, 93; Rotroff 2014). Vassilis Lambrinoudakis (1981, 161; 1987–
1988, 299) has suggested that a destruction layer dated to the early 1st century BCE at the sanctuary of Apollo
Maleatas in Epidaurus is likewise attributable to a pirate assault.
In addition to studies that rely on archaeological data to address the likely impact of piracy on the wider
public, some researchers have attempted to utilize archaeological remains to identify the likely habitats and
operational bases of pirates themselves. Probably the most systematic archaeological research of ancient ­piracy
to date is the Rough Cilicia Archaeological Survey Project, directed by Nicholas Rauh (1997, 2003, 2004, 2019;
see also Rauh et al. 2000, 2009, 2013, Kaye and Rauh 2020, Hoff et al. 2024, as well as Dawson and Rauh, this
volume), which, from 1996 to 2014, attempted to identify the settlements and hideouts of the notorious ­Cilician
pirates along the coast of modern day Gazipasha, Turkey (for the Cilician pirates see also Avidov 2008; Zoroğlu
2009; Tomaschitz 2013). Beginning in the mid-1980s, Elpida Hadjidaki (2001, 2015, 2020) has been directing the
systematic excavation of ancient Phalasarna, a polis in western Crete closely associated with ­Hellenistic piracy.
Since 2000, Aris Tsaravopoulos (2015, 2023; see also Johnston et al. 2012; Kozatsas et al. 2014; T
­ saravopoulos
and Kroustalis, this volume) has been excavating the site of Antikythera, a colony of Phalasarna, that is likewise
presumed to have functioned as a pirate base. Meanwhile, Adonis Kyrou (1990, 137–41; 1996–1997; see also
Lolos 2006) has persuasively argued that the fortified hill of Choriza on the island of Hydra served as a base
for Samian pirates, who were active around 530 BCE. Yet another category of remains plausibly linked to piracy, those of ancient shipsheds, straddles the boundary between terrestrial and underwater archaeology (Baika
2007–2008; Blackman et al. 2013, 238–41; see also Tsaravopoulos and Kroustalis, this volume on the shipshed
at Antikythera).
This last-mentioned category (shipsheds) shifts attention to the main stage of pirate operations, namely the
sea, and to the material evidence recovered by underwater archaeology. The methodological challenges confronting underwater archaeologists who attempt to associate underwater remains with piracy notwithstanding
(see Gianfrotta 1981, 2001, 2013, and Koutsouflakis, this volume), several finds recovered through marine
­archaeology have gained credence in the discussion. These include a helmet containing part of a human skull
that was recovered from the early 1st-century BCE at Spargi in the Madalena Archipelago (Gianfrotta 1981,
2001, 2013; Cavazzuti 1997, 2004; Bruni 2013).
Perhaps the most significant underwater discovery to date to conjure the prospect of piracy is undoubtedly
the wreck of the ancient merchant ship found near Kyrenia, in northern Cyprus. The Kyrenia shipwreck is dated
quite precisely due to its closed context of cargoes to 294–290 BCΕ. Scholars have raised compelling arguments

findings.evidence_excerpt:
to suggest that this vessel was attacked by pirates and deliberately scuttled (Schmitt and Kieburg 2016; Berlin
2019; Katzev and Swiny 2023, esp. 41–2). A similar explanation has been proposed for the charred remains
of a late 5th-century BCE shipwreck at Peristera in the Northern Sporades: that it may have sunk as a result
of fire (Hadjidaki 1996, 590–91; see also Mantzouka 2004, 6, 111). Such an explanation has been disputed by
the ­excavator, who argued that piracy did not become a serious problem in the Northern Sporades until the
mid-4th century BCE (e.g., Dem. 12.12–13; for piracy in the Northern Sporades during early modern times,
see also the contributions by G. Koutzakiotis and K. Pantzouris in this volume). However, this argument is
open to question, since the assumption that piracy posed a lesser problem during the 5th century BCE is not
sufficiently substantiated by the available evidence. According to ancient sources, the practice of scuttling or
setting fire to prizes to avoid detection was commonplace among pirates, so much so that the 5th century CE
bishop and grammarian Isidore of Seville (Etym. 10.220) erroneously asserted that the term πειρατής (pirate)
derives from πυρά, the ancient Greek word for fire. Accordingly, one cannot rule out the possibility that both the
Peristera and the Spargi shipwrecks, the latter of which likewise displayed evidence of firing (Gianfrotta 2013,
54), ­resulted from pirate ambuscades.
Although the archaeology of piracy in classical antiquity is relatively underexplored, the study of piracy in
prehistoric periods remains even more neglected.
Initial attempts to address Bronze Age piracy were vague, generalized and devoid of any systematic or
i­ n-depth investigation (e.g., Renfrew 1972, 440, 763; Basch 1986, 429–33; Doumas 1988, 27–9; Agouridis 1997,
20; Nowicki 2001, 36–7). Most recently, a few scholars have attempted to treat the evidence of piracy during
the Early Bronze Age (EBA) (e.g., Tzovaras 2020, 17; Yeagley 2022). Significant progress has been made regarding the likely impact of piracy during the transitional period from the Late Bronze Age (LBA) to the EIA,
a period of major socio-political transformation, with several recent studies employing fresh, methodologically rigorous, data-driven approaches (e.g., Artzy 1997; Lurangi 2006; Jung 2009, 2018; Kramer-Hajos 2009;
Gilan 2013; ­Samaras 2015;

findings.evidence_excerpt:
either to the preference for more conventional explanations –for
instance, ­imported objects are typically interpreted as evidence of trade or elite gift exchange– or to an implicit a­ ssumption that piracy, as a historically elusive and mobile practice, leaves no imperceptible trace in the
­archaeological record.
The methodological difficulty of identifying the archaeological remains of piracy has been emphasized by
numerous scholars (e.g., Cavazzuti 2004, 51; Baika 2007–2008, 56, 61, 68; Bruni 2013, 766; Gianfrotta 2013, 53;
Hartnett and Dawdy 2013, 40; Rauh 2019, 49). The problem stems primarily from the fact that the material remains of pirates are often indistinguishable from those of wider, “law-abiding”, society. For example, structures
and ships employed by pirates frequently resembled those employed by the general public, in the same manner
that the destruction inflicted on an ancient settlement by a pirate raid might resemble that of a military assault.
What seems crucial is that archaeologists assess the question within an interpretive framework, one that considers piracy as a fluid, dynamic phenomenon with the potential to shape local and regional economies and, at
times, to catalyze political and social transformations in any given era. This interpretive framework is precisely
what the A.P.Pir.A. project has intended to create.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
THE A.P.Pir.A. PROJECT: INVESTIGATING THE ARCHAEOLOGY OF
ANCIENT PIRACY
Scope and objectives
Hosted by the Department of History and Archaeology at the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens, the
A.P.Pir.A. project transpired between January 2021 and June 2024, with funding from the H
­ ellenic F
­ oundation
for Research and Innovation. The research team consisted of seven archaeologists, led by the present author
as principal investigator, alongside Nadia Giagkoudaki, Orestis Goulakos, Panagiotis Gounelas, Alexandra
­Malliou, Konstantinos Pantzouris and Dimitris N. Sakkas. Throughout the duration of the project, this small
group of early-career researchers attempted to construct a spatially diachronic approach to the archaeology of
piracy. Our aim was to develop a framework through which piracy could be meaningfully integrated into the
archaeological discourse, a framework sufficiently broad to incorporate evidence of piracy across the breadth
of the eastern Mediterranean Sea and across a timeframe extending from the Final Neolithic to the Roman era
(ca. 4000 BCE – 330 CE).

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
Methodology and research implementation
The project unfolded in four distinct stages. The initial phase focused on piracy in classical antiquity, specifically
from the Archaic to the Roman period. This decision has the obvious advantage of drawing on the information
provided by literary sources about piracy to allow for more comprehensive analysis. Textual references provide the added value of furnishing detailed information about piracy that can be cross-referenced against the
­extensive archaeological record of the same era.
To facilitate systematic documentation and analysis, the team developed a digital database using the opensource online platform Heurist. Design by the author of this paper, the database is intended to record, manage
and analyze material drawn from a wide range of ancient Greek and Latin sources (e.g., historical narratives,
oratory and inscriptions) that contain either explicit or implicit allusions to pirate activity in the Greek maritime
world during the period in question. The entries –compiled primarily by A.P.Pir.A. research team members
Orestis Goulakos and Konstantinos Pantzouris– amount to nearly 500 records and have yielded tremendous
insights into the historical evolution of piracy in classical antiquity, the operational strategies of pirates and
the manner in which they were perceived by their contemporaries. This database constitutes a comprehensive
repository that will facilitate the systematic study of ancient piracy through textual evidence.
For example, the analysis of the statistical data derived from the database reveals that, while piracy ­appears
to have been a continually recurring phenomenon throughout classical antiquity, the Hellenistic period (323–27
BCE) stands out as a peak moment of pirate activity, particularly in the eastern Mediterranean basin. These
­findings validate two fundamental conclusions: first, that piracy constituted an endemic feature of the maritime
landscape of classical antiquity; and second, that sustained efforts to suppress piracy by naval powers, such as
Athens, Rhodes and Rome, achieved limited and temporary success at best (on this issue see de Souza 1999,
38–41, 48–53, 83–4, 161–78, 184, 204–10; Lampinen 2022, 52–3; also, on Rhodes and Rome’s campaigns against
piracy, see respectively Kalmpourtzi, and Dawson and Rauh, this volume).
Following the study of the written sources, a systematic correlation was undertaken between the
a­ rchaeological evidence and the data extracted from the database. This process facilitated the formulation of
specific archaeological criteria and attributes derived from the material record that may under certain conditions be applicable to the phenomenon of piracy. For example, a list of representative features emerged that
appear to characterize an archaeologically identifiable pirate base, that is, a settlement where a portion of the
population, however large or small, engaged occasionally or habitually in piracy. The scale of such bases ranges
widely from small encampments to full-fledged cities. Importantly, the material remains of these sites often
do not diverge significantly from those of conventional settlements, thereby making their identification all the

their recognition. These can be grouped into four broad thematic categories:
1. Chronological context

in the vicinity. Establishing the habitational time frame of a settlement within the context of known

Site selection: Pirate bases are frequently situated in coastal areas that offer concealment or limited
visibility from the sea and/or mainland. These sites exploit natural topographical advantages, yet are
strategically positioned in proximity to important maritime routes.

Suitability for pirate operations: Pirate suitability is typically linked to topographical features, such
as bays, coves or natural harbors, that facilitate ambushes, provide shelter and enable eavesdropping
on passing sea traffic. In certain instances, the suitability of a location is further corroborated by the
chronological reuse of the exact same site or an adjacent location as pirate bases, most likely because
the physical and strategic advantages of the site lent themselves to recurring use by pirates over time.

Martial character: The presence of weaponry, martial iconography or other artifacts associated with the
use of violence may point to a community familiar with or habituated to armed conflict. While such
indicators are not exclusive to piracy, their co-occurrence with other characteristics described above
strengthens the argument for pirate occupation.

findings.evidence_excerpt:
It should be emphasized that the presence of one or even several of these traits does not by itself confirm the
identification of a given site as a pirate base. Nor is the combination of all these features required to justify such
an interpretation. Obviously, the greater the number and consistency of such indicators at a given site, the more
compelling the need to include pirate activity within a range of archaeological interpretations. For instance,
the application of the above criteria, in conjunction with the analysis of literary sources on ancient piracy, led
Konstantinos Pantzouris to propose that the fortified site at Kastraki on Agathonisi may not have served solely
as a defensive outpost safeguarding Miletus and its maritime trade against the pirates, who were particularly
active in the region during the Hellenistic period. Rather, the site itself may have participated in pirate activity
–likely targeting non-Milesian interests– thereby functioning both as a protective and a predatory node within
the complex maritime landscape of the time (see Pantzouris, this volume).
The establishment of archaeological criteria for the identification of piracy enabled the team to proceed to
the second phase of the project, namely the investigation of piracy during periods, when archaeological data

findings.evidence_excerpt:
constitute the primary, or even sole, source of information due to a lack of literary sources, for example the
periods extending from the Final Neolithic to the EIA (ca. 4000–700 BCE), mentioned above. The team divided
this broad timeframe into four chronological segments: Nadia Giagkoudaki examined the Final Neolithic to
EBA, Dimitris N. Sakkas focused on the Middle Bronze Age (MBA) to LBA I–II, the present author studied the
LBA III, while the EIA was investigated jointly by Panagiotis Gounelas and the present author.
The results of this study are particularly promising and highlight the potential for advancing our
­understanding of piracy through archaeological inquiry. As demonstrated in the contributions to this volume
by members of the A.P.Pir.A. project, secure correlations between specific archaeological sites or assemblages
and evidence for piracy are both limited and problematic. This is demonstrated by the paper of Dimitris N.
Sakkas in this volume, who tackles the challenging task of examining piracy during the MBA and early LBA.
Nonetheless, as both Nadia Giagkoudaki’s study on the origins of piracy in the EBA Aegean and Panagiotis
Gounelas’ examination of those during the EIA in this volume indicate, this difficulty stems primarily from our
limited understanding of the phenomenon. They each propose ways to show how pirate activity conceivably
provides a distinct archaeological signature, even in these early periods.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
Dissemination and public engagement
As part of the A.P.Pir.A. project, the Museum of Cycladic Art (MCA) participated as a collaborating institution,
for the purpose of undertaking both the design and the production of an educational program featuring piracy
in antiquity. Upon completion of the research phase, the A.P.Pir.A. research team submitted a detailed report to
the MCA’s Department of Educational and Social Programs. This report marked the beginning of the project’s
third phase, which was intended to develop the educational component. The report included extensive data
on ancient piracy, descriptions of relevant archaeological sites and finds, as well as suggestions for the educational program’s structure and activities. Drawing on this material, the MCA’s team of dedicated museologists
proceeded to generate the educational program, entitled “Piracy in the Cyclades”. Directed toward an audience
of students age eight and above, the program comprises teaching resources, suggested activities and an educational board game. As Eleni Markou elaborates in her contribution to this volume, the program was designed
for flexible use both within the MCA and in school settings, ensuring nation-wide accessibility for teachers and
students alike.
The final phase of the A.P.Pir.A. project focused on the dissemination of its research outcomes. The
­international hybrid conference “The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity”, held under the auspices of the
­Department of History and Archaeology of the NKUA on October 5–6, 2023, along with the publication of its
proceedings in the present volume, represent key elements of this effort. The decision to organize an international hybrid conference stemmed from the research team’s intent not only to present the results of our work,
but also to engage with scholars working on related aspects of ancient piracy in order to generate a productive
academic dialog.
Beyond the international conference, the A.P.Pir.A. team undertook a variety of additional activities ­intended
to promote communication and dissemination. Among them was the participation of Panagiotis Gounelas and
the present author in the international hybrid conference “Nostoi II: Traveling in the Eastern Mediterranean Sea
and Inland Routes from the Early Bronze Age to the End of the Early Iron Ages”, held at the Acropolis Museum
from 11 to 13 November 2022. The conference proceedings, soon to be published under the editorship of Konstantinos Kopanias, Çiğdem Maner, Nikolaos Stampolidis and Ioannis Fappas, will include our paper entitled
“‘Who Are You, Strangers?’ The Contribution of the Homeric Epics to the Study of Ancient Piracy”. This study
explores the phenomenon of piracy as it appears in the Homeric epics and examines the usefulness of these
literary sources to the investigation of piracy in antiquity (Samaras and Gounelas forthcoming).
Additionally, the present author has prepared a study entitled “Fortifications in the Middle and Late Bronze
Age Aegean: When, Where and Why?”, which is forthcoming in the edited volume Polemika: Perceptions of
Warfare in the Bronze Age Aegean, to be published under the direction of Kyriakos Grigoropoulos, Angelos
