2000, 135–36).
The population decline was one of the most serious problems faced by EC communities, which, among
other causes, could have been attributed to infertility and the unequal ratio between men and women. To
address this, the movement of people (especially women) between communities or even between islands was
crucial, as healthy descendants were ensured by exogamy. It is reasonable to assume that exogamy was generally
consensual, by mutual agreement between families or communities. However, the forcible abduction of women
also seems possible, especially given the “heroic” context in which such actions are carried out by societies that
often accept and undertake robbery and piracy. Thus, the abduction of women may have increased significantly
in times of crisis, when the population was dramatically reduced (e.g., due to a shipwreck or disease), so that
the forcible transportation of women from another region or island for procreation was one of the few available
options for community survival.
The potentially important role of the abduction of women and animals in the ΕΒΑ Cyclades is further
strengthened by ethnographic parallels from societies with weak or absent major state organizations and high
mortality due to wars or ways of life, in which such practices were commonplace. For example, at least in the
13th century CE, in the Chaco Canyon region of the United States, raiding for women for reproductive or labor
reasons was a well-established practice, and successful warriors were associated with polygyny (Kohler and

findings.evidence_excerpt:
Relationships between sea voyages, trade, and women, as well as manifestations of violence, may be
­suggested by the deliberate breakage of folded-arms female figurines in the Kavos “special deposit” on Keros
­(Androutsopoulou 2013, 47). Because of the large number of figurines found in the deposit and the deliberate
breakage, most scholars attribute this breakage to ritual practices that took place in a funerary or religious
context (e.g., Doumas 1972, 163; Davis 1984, 16; Renfrew 1984, 27–8; Barber 1987, 132; Sotirakopoulou 2005,
329–30). If this is the case, the quantity of the figurines, the way they were handled, and the fact that only fragments of the abdomen, vulva and legs have been found in the depository may shed light on the way women were
treated in religion and, by extension, in EBA society.
The role of men and women in the ΕΒΑ society and economy, as reflected in the aforementioned aspects of
material culture, namely in the anthropomorphic figurines, the frying pans, the general presence of weapons,
and the way of using the above objects, as well as the importance and the “heroic” character of sea voyages for
island communities, suggest that exogamy and the acquisition of objects, raw materials, and animals were of
vital importance and that in order for community survival and growth everything was legitimate. In the context
of raids, therefore, woman and animal abductions were probably a common practice, and constituted a major
source of social power and prestige for the warriors-pirates who provided them to the community.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
SETTLEMENT PATTERN
Major changes in the settlement patterns and the ways of living are usually considered to be a result of the
­emergence of new needs and demands. In this regard, the abandonment of coastal sites and the move to fortified
sites away from the sea are often attributed to threats and invasions from the sea. Therefore, a brief synopsis of
the settlement patterns of the EΒΑ Cyclades and the identification of such changes may be able to contribute
to the debate on the phenomenon of piracy during this period (see Angelopoulou, this volume for a more
­comprehensive discussion on the EC settlement patterns).
The EC I settlements appear to be scattered and short-lived (Broodbank 2000, 150–51, 154–56; ­Angelopoulou
2016–2017, 134). They were small settlements, based mainly on the agricultural economy, while their external
contacts were limited. The settlements of the EC IIA period were also small in size and duration, with a few
­exceptions of larger and more organized settlements, such as Ayia Irini on Kea (Caskey 1971, 368–72; B
­ roodbank
2000, 216–18; see also Wilson 1999, 2013), Dhaskalio on Keros (Boyd 2013, Renfrew 2013), and Skarkos on Ios
(Marthari 1997, 2008a, 2018). The settlements of this period were mainly coastal or near the sea and at nodal
points of sea routes, indicating the interest of their inhabitants in sea voyages. There seems to have been some
concern for protection from sea raids, by choosing either defensible sites, as in the case of Dhaskalio, or sites
at a short distance from the sea, as at Skarkos (Broodbank 2000, 212–21; Angelopoulou 2016–2017, 134–35).
An even stronger concern for protection from the sea emerged in the following EC IIB period. Several
­settlements were now situated on defensible hilltops, and many of them were reinforced by strong fortification
walls. For example, settlements like Kastri on Syros (Marthari 1998, 2017), Panormos on Naxos (Angelopoulou
2014, 67–88), Kynthos on Delos (MacGillivray 1980) and Markiani on Amorgos (Marangou 2006, 81–93)
­indicate feelings of danger and insecurity. Kastri and Panormos were indeed destroyed and then abandoned,
probably after a maritime raid. This change in the settlement pattern from sites near the sea to defensible sites on
high and steep hills and with strong fortification walls, combined with the evidence of attack, destruction and
abandonment observed in at least two settlements, are indications of the fear during this period and the violent
raids that seem to have come from the sea.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
SETTLEMENTS WITH POSSIBLE PIRATE ACTIVITY
In order to be able to recognize that a small or large part of the community of a settlement was involved (­ either
occasionally or systematically) in pirate activity, this settlement should present some or all the features identified
by the A.P.Pir.A. project: coastal and defensible sites, not easily visible but close to at least one safe harbor, nodal
point for the nearby sea routes, fortification walls, etc. (see in more detail Samaras, this volume). ­Moreover, in
settlements of this type, valuable and exotic objects are often found, the presence of which is sometimes not
adequately explained by other “legal” activities (see also Samaras 2015, 191–92).
Settlements in naturally defensible sites, close to the sea, and with strong fortification walls have already
been witnessed in the FN period and the EBA I, as can be seen at Strophilas on Andros (Televantou 2006, 2008,
2018a) and Vathy on Astypalaia (Vlachopoulos and Angelopoulou 2019; Vlachopoulos 2021). As mentioned
above, ship rock-engravings have been found at both these sites, some of which even decorate the main gates
of the fortified settlements. It is noteworthy that in Strophilas there are over a hundred rock-engravings with
this theme, making the ship a symbol of the community and revealing its naval orientation. Several metal
objects have also been found in the same settlement, including a metal spearhead, while in Vathy there are
rock-­engravings of a unique theme with daggers, symbols of bravery and heroism indicating violent actions.
Considering that material culture is a powerful means of social display, it may be possible to accept the view that
ships transmitted messages of collective power and weapons that of individual power.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:

voyages brought wealth to the communities, but at the same time there was fear from the sea. After all, island
communities were systematically engaged in trade and sea voyages as early as the FN–EBA I period (Papadatos
and Tomkins 2013, 355, 374); therefore, it is not unlikely that banditry was practiced in the context of these
voyages, even if during this period these phenomena seem to have been sporadic and opportunistic.
As mentioned above, the intensification of maritime contacts during EBA II may have motivated the ­increase
in pirate raids, a fact that seems to be documented by the presence of more fortified settlements. The possible
outbreak of piracy may even suggest the existence of pirate settlements, without this necessarily implying that
there were communities exclusively engaged in pirate activities.
Kastri on Syros (Marthari 2006, 2007, 2008b) displays several characteristics usually found in pirate bases
(see also Yeagley 2022, esp. 95–7). It is a short-lived settlement, since it was inhabited only during the EC IIB
period, and is located on a high and steep hill above the sea, in a position that is extremely difficult to access.
The natural defense of the site was further reinforced by the construction of a complex fortification system, in
which the main wall had horseshoe-shaped bastions. At the same time, the site provided visual control of the sea
routes to Tenos, Andros and southern Euboea towards the north, and to Rheneia, Delos, Mykonos and Naxos
towards the south (Broodbank 2000, 243–44). In addition, bronze objects made of tin bronze have been found
at the site, which are prestige objects because of the raw material used in their manufacture, especially tin, which
is imported from the east. A metalworking workshop has also been found within the fortified settlement.

and increased when these contacts intensified and valuable goods were concentrated in the Aegean. Moreover,
the same people who took defensive measures, possessed valuable objects that could be obtained either by
participating in maritime trade or by raiding. Taking into account that during the period under consideration,
activities such as robbery and piracy probably did not have the negative connotation that is given to them today,
and that in the face of survival such activities were not only legitimate but could even constitute “heroic” acts,
it seems very likely that the same people who participated in trade would have carried out pirate raids in times
of crisis or when the opportunity arose. Besides, according to Agouridis (1997, 20), “trading and raiding are
often the two sides of the same coin”, which means that no distinction can be drawn between them, and consequently between their archaeological footprints. It is true that the boundaries between trade and piracy are
blurred, especially in such early periods, but at the same time this assumption concludes that the same people
were engaged in both activities.

findings.evidence_excerpt:
Also, in periods of intensive large-scale contacts and without the existence of a strong central power, as is the
case of the EBA Aegean (see also Driessen, this volume), it is almost unlikely that raids for quick and immediate
profit would not take place. More generally, most island communities were able to practice piracy, some more
and some less, and probably did so alongside other activities.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
CONCLUSIONS
In summary, it seems quite likely that in the context of the EBA sea voyages, not only trade was practiced, but
also piracy. The frequency of this phenomenon cannot be determined, but there are other aspects that can be
understood with greater certainty. During the period under discussion, and especially in EBA II, there were
both the appropriate means (i.e., ships suitable for raiding) and strong motives, sometimes even linked to survival. At the same time, the absence of a central power created ideal conditions for piracy to flourish. Indeed,
it seems that in prehistory such acts did not carry the negative connotations that are attached to it today, as the
legality or the illegality of an action was not perceived in the same way. On the contrary, a daring and dangerous
action may have been considered an act of bravery and glory.
Therefore, the motivation for piracy was not only driven by material factors, which would ensure survival
and/or the acquisition of wealth. Participation in risky activities, such as sea voyages and piracy, increased
the reputation and power of those who took part in them. It proved their martial and naval prowess and thus
gained the respect of the whole community. Through the possession of valuable objects and people it ensured
the ­perpetuation of future generations and the community, the warrior-pirates also demonstrated their power
and thus strengthened their social status and legitimized their authority.
The evidence in the material culture may be indirect but, complementary to the possible perceptions of
the period, seems to suggest that piracy may have been practiced in the EBA Aegean by the same people who
­participated in maritime trade. It is very likely that the traders of the EBA were at the same time warriors, pirates
and hunters, charged with the duty of providing their community with essential goods, animals and women,
either through exchanges or through raids. In general, the trap of interpreting all relevant finds as the result
of trading activities should be avoided, especially in periods with no written sources, such as the EBA. On the
contrary, the strong possibility that a greater or lesser part of the maritime traffic of people and goods is due to
piracy should always remain open.

findings.evidence_excerpt:
ABSTRACT
The development of habitation in the Cyclades during the Early Bronze Age (3rd millennium BCΕ) is little known,
as a result of the limited number of investigated Early Cycladic settlements. The proliferation of fortified sites and the
development of weaponry imply an increased interest in defense during the Early Cycladic II period (middle of the 3rd
millennium BCΕ). The establishment and the violent abandonment, following war-like conflict, of the fortified citadels at
Kastri on Syros and Korphari ton Amygdalion on Naxos (2500–2300/2200 BCΕ), are considered signs of the arrival of
new populations that marked an era of crisis and intense competition in the islands.
The aim of this paper is to evaluate the significance of both fortifications and weaponry for the evolution of the Cycladic
civilization. The war conflicts associated with the phenomenon of piracy are not a symptom of an era of cultural decline
and regression. Hostility intensified in a period of prosperity as this is reflected in settlement patterns, demography,
economy, society, and last but not least in the expanded cultural contacts in the Aegean during the Early Bronze Age. The
Early Cycladic fortified citadels are outstanding examples of collective work – a milestone in the evolution from small
farming communities to large “urban” ones.

Erkanal 1996, 78–80; 1999, 240–41; 2008, 182–83; Düring 2011, 284, 287).
The identity of the intruders who destroyed the citadels at Panormos and Kastri is and will remain unknown.
However, it appears that the nature of the attacks was that of predatory raids, as both sites are abandoned after
their destruction. The latter implies that the main aim of the attackers was to acquire the wealth that was kept
inside the fortified areas. Thus, the destruction of the acropoleis could be interpreted as the result of a pirate
attack (Angelopoulou 2008, 159; 2014, 512–13). Thucydides (1.4.1–8.3) states that piracy was a serious problem
in the Cyclades until Minos, the mythical king of Crete, restored safe navigation by expelling the pirates and
colonizing the islands. He also relates the rise of piracy to advances in maritime expertise and notes that early
settlements on the coast were most vulnerable to pirate attacks and plundering. For that reason, people living
on the islands and on the mainland preferred to settle at a distance from the sea.
Thucydides’ comments are of vital importance for understanding the differences in settlement and growth
patterns during the Middle and Late Bronze Age in the Aegean. Nevertheless, it cannot be excluded that piracy,
closely connected with the intensification of maritime activities and the use of the longboats, had already be­
come an acute problem for the islanders as early as the EBA. For example, it is probably no coincidence that the
inhabitants of the fortified sites of the Kastri group period were prepared for an attack from the sea, as is implied
by the location of the settlement sites close to but at a safe distance from the shores and on hills that command
the sea routes leading to the islands. The fortified acropoleis of the second half of the 3rd millennium BCE are
closely related to an era of increased threats and conflict, as implied by the developed war tactics, fortification
systems and weaponry used. The root cause for the occurrence of predatory raids is a question to be answered.
Nevertheless, an interesting scientific inquiry is whether the ascertained aggressiveness was related to climate
factors such as aridity that might have affected agriculture and other aspects of social life in the Aegean during
the last centuries of the 3rd millennium BCE (Jarriel 2020, 3–5, 10–1).
Creations of prosperous communities with an advanced social organization and an extensive network
of ­external contacts, the Kastri group acropoleis are the continuation of the cultural tradition of the large
­unfortified settlements of early EC II, such as Skarkos, Dhaskalio, Ayia Irini and Chalandriani. At the same time,
they ­probably foreshadow the developments at the end of the 3rd and the beginning of the 2nd millennium
BCE, when the residential model in the Cyclades changes with the concentration of the population in fewer in
number but larger in size settlements, which can be characterized as small towns, as, for example, Phylakopi
on Melos, Akrotiri on Thera, Paroikia on Paros (Renfrew 1982, 38; Barber 1983, 77; Broodbank 2000, 326–
31). Perhaps this change was necessary to deal more effectively with the dangers and instability in the Aegean
­(Angelopoulou 2016, 66–7; 2016–2017, 145), gradually entering a new era of cultural growth.

findings.evidence_excerpt:
ABSTRACT
The investigation of piracy in the Middle and early Late Bronze Age Aegean is closely linked to contemporary maritime
activity. In that context, the active incorporation of Crete, in the ­beginning, and then of the Greek mainland in the
­international eastern Mediterranean system established maritime networks and intensified communications and the
circulation of goods among the aforementioned areas. In addition, the architecture of some contemporary coastal settlements, and particularly the presence of fortifications together with iconographic evidence indicate other-than-peaceful
contacts as well. From this point up to the identification of piratical activity, however, lies a considerable distance. This
paper examines this distance through different types of archaeological evidence. After outlining the major maritime networks in the Aegean of the Middle and early Late Bronze Age, the present work discusses material evidence and several
case studies that have been interpreted as indicative for piratical activity, and which thus afford the evaluation of the
phenomenon of piracy in the area and era under consideration.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
INTRODUCTION
According to the definition that was introduced and adopted by the A.P.Pir.A. project, the term piracy refers
to the seaborne robbery through some sort of ship, and also to the looting of a sunk ship even if this activity
is taking place directly from the coast, both motivated by personal profit (Samaras, this volume). This paper
is a brief review of the case studies associated with piracy in the Aegean of the Middle Bronze Age (MBA)
and the early Late Bronze Age (LBA), the Old and the New Palace period, and, also, the Final Palatial period,
in Cretan or Minoan terminology. The challenge of exploring a series of case studies with the corresponding
evidence is developed in three parts. The former roughly presents the context of maritime communications,
the major sea routes and the dominant networks in the area and era under study. The second part reviews the
actual case studies that have been interpreted as indicative for piratical activity by previous research – each one
is established on a different sort of evidence, so that they provide the opportunity not only for an up-to-date
consideration, but also for an evaluation. This is the subject of the final part, which explores in detail the best
documented case study for identifying piracy, in order to conclude with a reassessment on piracy in the MBA
and early LBA Aegean.

THE EVIDENCE: TIME UNITS AND CASE STUDIES
In the earlier and the middle part of the MBA, which roughly correspond to the period of the Old Palaces on
Crete, the settlement at Kolonna on Aegina stands apart, first of all due to “the most impressive fortifications
in the Aegean world after those of Troy” (Rutter 2001, 126; see also Gauss 2018, 52–6, figs. 5.4–5.6; 2019, 60–1,
figs. 8–9, 66, figs. 13–15; Samaras forthcoming). The fortifications of Kolonna IX and a contemporary series
of ship representations on matt-painted jars were considered indicative for the identification of the site with a
“nest of pirates” (Basch 1986, 429). Although an earlier hoard of the Early Helladic III period with finds from
different origins (Felten 2007, 15, fig. 5) is not opposed to that interpretation, and this is further the case for
the also coming from Kolonna, later and possibly contemporary to Town X, “Aegina Treasure” (Higgins 1987;
­Simantoni-Bournia 2003; Fitton et al. 2009), Kolonna is currently understood as an outstanding residential
center with an early elite. ­Minoan and Minoanizing pottery and a potter’s wheel, as also additional evidence,
including among other a ceremonial stone hammer and a mason’s mark (Hiller 1993; Kilian-Dirlmeier 1997;
Gauss 2006), ­document the relations between the Kolonna and the Old Palatial Crete and even led to the hypothesis that the site might represent the earlier state outside Crete (Niemeier 1995).
The outstanding role of Kolonna in the MBA is also evidenced by the elite burial in the earlier so far shaft
grave

vases for drinking, pouring and transportation, an assemblage that is elaborated in the later shaft graves (Rutter
2001, 140). Furthermore, it is documented by the recent excavation of a monumental building with possible
­administrative character (Gauss et al. 2011; Tartaron 2013, 220). This evidence, along with the unprecedented
distribution of Aeginetan pottery in the coast of Thessaly and central Greece, and also in the Saronic and the
­Argolic Gulfs, the Cyclades and Crete (Gauss and Knodell 2020), question the identification of Kolonna as
a pirate nest. Instead, Kolonna, which is currently regarded as the core of the “small world” of the Saronic
gulf (Tartaron 2013, 213), developed maritime activity that brought the latter closer to other, not-so-small

the emerging elites.

Regarding that Aegean “siege” iconography and particularly the Mycenae rhyton, however, which is

Grave IV at Mycenae have ordered a precious item to be made for him showing nothing more than a ­piratical
raid”, so that seaborne raids were rather interpreted in the context of the acquisition of goods and supplies
(Papadopoulos 2006, 134–35; 2019, 409). In that direction, albeit through a more complicated course, also
points the hegemonic strategy of violence that was mentioned above, which could generate genuine representations for reproduction in the period and the area under consideration. After all, the linkage between the
­aforementioned ­iconography and the Aegean elites is evidenced through both the specialized production centers and the ­consumption ­patterns of the finds themselves.
Therefore, the surviving iconography of the New Palatial period in the Aegean documents seaborne raids
and the consideration of the nature of this assignment by the current research brings the discussion in the
essence of the topic for identifying piratical activities. If piracy was an enterprise for the direct acquisition of
personal profit, then it stands apart from the hegemonic strategy of violence, which, even without exercising,
intended to control an area in order to secure regular flows; this conceptual distinction raises the question of
whether it is possible to distinguish between these incidents and how the latter can be documented in the MBA
and the early LBA Aegean.
Actual evidence for addressing this issue derives from the next time unit, that is the period after the

demarcates the chronological limits of the present consideration as well. In that period, at the end of the Late

THE REASSESSMENT: PIRACY IN THE MBA AND EARLY LBA AEGEAN
Attarissiya’s involvement in the raid against Alashiya is therefore considered a piratical action (Cesarano 2008,
41–5, 93) and deserves further exploration, even if its identification required the spatial expansion of the r­ esearch
area, in order to include Cyprus, and it further occurs in the expiration of the period under ­consideration.
­However, it is argued below that the main significance of the text for the assessing piracy in the early LBA
­Aegean lies not that much in Attarissiya’s involvement to the raid that caused the indictment of Madduwatta, as
to that of the latter person. Moreover, that the evidence that derives from the reviewed text should be considered
rather as analogical instead of direct.
First of all, it is safe to argue that the accusation by the Hittite king against Madduwatta for raiding Alashiya
is established on two arguments. The former considers the claim that Alashiya was under Hittite control –
­although this was possibly not the actual case according to Beckman (et al. 2011, 99); the latter that Madduwatta
was a client ruler and thus a vassal to the Hittite king. The very combination of these aspects renders the raid

view of the Hittite king Arnuwanda. This, however, is not the case for the remaining two participants to the
raid, the Mycenaean Attarissiya and the unnamed ruler of Piggaya, at least according to the existing evidence. In
other words, this politically unacceptable action, which was meant to be signified as piratical in a later context,
considers exclusively the client ruler to the Hittite king, and is not evidenced for Madduwatta’s independent
allies. In these terms, it can be assumed that this same event, the raid against Alashiya, likely represents piratical
activity for one of the participants and an act of war for the remaining two.
The difficulty of distinguishing between war and piracy has already been noted and previous considerations
on piracy in the Bronze Age Mediterranean in general and the Aegean specifically did not proven particularly
fruitful. Baruffi (1998, 10) argued that, although “coastal raiding and piracy were also significant factors during
the Bronze Age, as they have been during sporadic periods in the Mediterranean ever since. […] war and piracy
were so closely linked that it was not always clear when an enemy action was to be treated as one or the other”.
In the same vein, for the Aegean and for the periods before the composition of the Homeric poems and that of
the poems themselves, de Souza (1999, 18) argued that “piracy is so closely related to warfare in both aims and
methods that they are virtually undistinguishable” (see also de Souza 1999, 16, 21). This argum

Although the archaeological record of the MBA and the early LBA Aegean lacks such solid evidence
and in order to retrieve it we had to turn eastwards, the field of the relationships is at least promising for the
­consideration of piracy. Here too, one or more dominant powers established special relations with a series of
settlements, including nearly all the sites which yielded the evidence that supported the case studies previously
discussed. It is therefore argued that the secure identification of piratical activity can be attempted through the
reconstruction of relations among sites and, if possible, among individuals as well, while, if this consideration
demonstrates the limitations of the archaeological record, then the sequel of the A.P.Pir.A. project might be
developed as an interdisciplinary one.

CONCLUSIONS
In the previous parts of this paper and following a brief presentation of the context of maritime contacts and
networks in the MBA and early LBA Aegean, a series of case studies for piratical activity was critically discussed.
It was argued that archaeological evidence previously interpreted as indicating piratical activity in the study area
and era should be reconsidered. In the case of architecture, that the fortifications of Kolonna, even if combined
with early ship representations, are currently understood in association to the site’s outstanding role in the
Aegean of the Old Palace period, where evidently the maritime element is for the first time in the period under

consideration associated with the martial one. In the case of the iconography of the period of the New Palaces, it
was argued that, although it reproduces seaborne raiding events, the latter possibly indicate activities other than
piracy. On the other hand, the textual case study of the Hittite record known as the “Indictment of Madduwatta”,
not only produced evidence for the secure identification of a piratical event, but also demonstrated what was
perceived as piracy by the LBA hierarchical societies and its close affinities with warfare. On the basis of this
evidence, it was argued that particularly promising for the identification of case studies for piracy in the MBA
and early LBA Aegean might similarly require the consideration and the reconstruction of relationships among
sites and even among individuals, especially macro actors.

findings.evidence_excerpt:
ABSTRACT
The 13th/12th centuries BCE saw the appearance of large walled sites on Crete – a major change for an island p­ reviously
distinguished by the scarcity of fortifications. The use of these sites was brief; therefore, they were the outcome of particular circumstances – those prevailing around the 1200 BCE collapse. This paper examines three fortified sites that are
distinguished by their proximity to the coast, in order to determine if they aimed at countering ­seaborne raids or were
established by groups that carried out such acts. Regarding Kato Kastellas, a site near the bay of Zakros, the topography
is not suggestive of a pirate base. Kato Kastellas probably provided refuge to the inhabitants of the s­ urrounding area – or
to settlers that came from the sea. The fortified promontory of Elias to Nisi is near the d
­ efensible settlement of Vrokastro
but does not seem to have served as its port. Instead, it was probably established earlier, p­ ossibly by people involved in
sea raiding. The fortification on the island of Dia was hitherto dated to the Early Bronze Age; however, it should rather
be placed in the 13th century BCE. Given the importance of Dia for seafaring and the concurrent decline of Knossos, the
enceinte may tentatively be ascribed to bands of sea raiders who attempted to turn that island into a pirate base.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
the respective regions – which did not eventually occur. However, others probably served as temporary refuges
for the surrounding populations – or they eventually came to be used as such. Accordingly, the fortifications
may have been commissioned by the authorities of the neighboring centers or by agents who only came into
prominence in the course of this troubled transitional period – such as local functionaries, fallen nobles and
their followers, former mercenaries and sea-raiders, or wandering groups of displaced people.
This paper will discuss three fortified sites that are distinguished by their proximity to the coast in order
to determine the implications regarding the insecure conditions that apparently prevailed at seas – namely,
their potential relation to pirate activities or intrusions from the sea. Accordingly, this study will examine if the
­fortifications aimed at countering these phenomena, or were erected by the perpetrators of such deeds.

CRETE, PIRACY AND THE FORTIFIED SITES OF THE 13TH/12TH CENTURIES
BCE
Piracy is a varied and adaptable phenomenon, which according to the circumstances appears in different forms
regarding its intensity and range, or the motives, organization and origin of those actively involved (see e.g.,
Bevan and Conolly 2013, 187–89). Geography defines the coastal zones and islandscapes best suited to piracy (Hitchcock and Maeir 2018, 4–5), but does not predetermine the role(s) of their inhabitants (Bevan and
Conolly 2013, 193–95). Thus, the same regions may alternately constitute pirate nurseries or the preferential
targets of sea-raids. For example, the flourishing of the small and rocky island of Antikythera in the Hellenistic
period was largely because it became a pirate base (Bevan and Conolly 2013, 189–92). Conversely, this strategically placed island witnessed successive episodes of abandonment from the 7th century CE onwards; these
coincide with periods of insecurity at seas, which suggests that the inhabitants became the victims of pirate

findings.evidence_excerpt:
attacks instead of being the perpetrators of such acts (see Bevan and Conolly 2013, 192). Regarding Crete,
in the ­Hellenistic period piracy may have contributed significantly to the economy and wider importance of
many of its ­poleis. ­Accordingly, after the Arab conquest in the early 9th century CE, the fleets setting sail from
Crete ­devastated the coastal regions and islands of the East Roman Empire (Christides 1981; 1984, 162–63,
165–67, 192; ­Yannopoulos 2011, 163), so much so that it was called θεόλεστος Κρήτη (“goddamned Crete”)
by ­Constantinus P
­ orphyrogenitus (1830, 651.15). In the 13th/12th centuries BCE, though, Crete was in the
­opposite position.
The progressive decline of the main ports and the abandonment of the coastal areas in LM IIIB suggest that
Crete became the target of systematic attacks from the sea – a situation that apparently continued in LM IIIC.
The causes of these developments, all the more so their precocious appearance in relation to the rest of the Aegean, may lie in the lack of strong polities on the island during the later part of the 13th century BCE – if not
much earlier at certain regions. The geographical position of Crete at the crossroads of the sea routes that joined
the Aegean with the central and eastern Mediterranean would have also contributed to the frequency and scale
of the depredations; if nothing else, these routes were also used by the mercenaries who offered their services to
the states of both the Aegean and the east Mediterranean – groups that would have been prone to turn to piracy
and freebooting when in need or enabled by the circumstances (Samaras 2015, 192; Jung 2018, 285–86; Maran
2022, 240–41). Having frequented Crete and being aware of its riches and internal political situation, such bands
may have chosen the island as a target of their raids and a base for further attacks – and this may have occurred
on an even larger scale in the context of the displacements caused by the 1200 BCE collapse. In this regard, if
the hypothesis of a pirate base on Dia, right in front of the port of Knossos, is indeed true, this would signify a
reality radically different from that of the “Minoan Thalassocracy” of the Neopalatial period: instead of dominating the seas, the inhabitants of once mighty Knossos were under the threat of a θεόλεστος Δία.

ABSTRACT
The heyday of the Mycenaean palaces coincides with a period when international trade and overseas voyages increased,
due to the complex and centralized administrations that encouraged such actions. The Mycenaean palaces were part of an
international network linking Mediterranean elites, although there are lacunae concerning the agents who e­ ngaged in those
actions, their social identity, and the variety of seafaring activities that they could accomplish with their ­contemporary
technological means. The social background of the Mycenaean seafarer seemingly matches that of the palatial elite as the
prime agent of such actions, since the latter had the resources but also the motivation, which was the acquisition of exotic
goods, a common practice for the rulers of the Late Bronze Age. The need to obtain valuable resources may not have been
limited to peaceful means, like trade and gift exchange, but it could have involved violence, warfare, pillaging and piracy.
The main purpose of this paper is to try to approach seafarers and their affiliations, i.e., the palatial and non-palatial
agents. The difficulty in distinguishing between the last two intensifies even more when the line between warfare (which
would have been characteristic of the Mycenaean administration center) and actions related to piracy is blurred.

findings.evidence_excerpt:

sectors could have overlapped (de Fidio 2001, 22–3).
To study and understand the characteristics of the Mycenaean seafarers, we would need to utilize every piece
of evidence we have at our disposal. Detailed analyses have been conducted regarding maritime affairs by the
examination of contemporary iconography and written sources (Wachsmann 1981, 1995, 1998; Wedde 1999,
2001, 2005, 2006; Emanuel 2014, 2017, 2021), which we can utilize to investigate the people behind them. The
aim of this paper would not be to categorize certain groups rigidly as traders, mercenaries, pirates or military
personnel, but to assess the “fluidity” of their positions, as they could have been able to attain a variety of roles
(either overlapping or not mutually exclusive), depending on the circumstances and their needs.

De Souza (1999, 16–7) rejects the term piracy without the proper legislative framework, thus identifying
them all as acts of warfare by default during the LBA. However, Emanuel (2018, 73–4) argues that even without
proper definition, we can still distinguish the two of them by several distinct characteristics; for example, the
involvement of a state in such actions would make it an act of warfare. Furthermore, the operational scale is
essential, since pirates would usually utilize speed and avoid conflict, then war actions would have been conducted on larger scales. For example, the famous relief of the battle with the Sea Peoples from Medinet Habu
implies the organizational level of a state-like authority (Wiener 1999, 411–12) and would not have had such
impact, at least as the one described by the Egyptian sources, if it was a minor pirate raid. Therefore, identifying agents as palatial or non-palatial can be difficult given our current evidence. In this regard, a tablet from
­Amarna (EA 38) seems to suggest that participation of a state authority in raids was not impossible; in this letter,
the king of Alashiya, referring to the Pharaoh, denied his involvement in raiding the coasts of Egypt, while also

southwestern Anatolia) (Emanuel 2021, 94–5).
Returning to the people amenable to such actions, we can look again at Wiener’s view (Wiener 1999, 411–
12) that large-scale raids required good organization. Without discounting the ability of independent agents in
the Aegean, the Mycenaean palaces were probably the only entities capable of conducting significant enough
raids that were able to damage other centers of similar or larger size. Conversely, less influential agents could
only operate on a more limited scale, without causing significant disruption at a broader level (Knapp and Manning 2016, 122–23, 135; Knapp 2020, 155–56; contra Hitchcock and Maeir 2016, 256–60).
The obscurity that veils the perpetrators of those hostile actions, either if those were considered piracy
or ­warfare, seems to be related to two significant factors. The first one is that the resources gained from
­accomplishing such deeds were essential in administration as much as in maintaining and improving social
status. The second factor is the “flexibility” that a seafarer could have had. Those specific groups could utilize
their skills and assume different roles depending on each situation. Mycenaean elite groups constantly needed
valuable r­ esources (e.g., copper) and were also capable of launching naval expeditions (in consideration of PY
An 610, see Tartaron 2013, 125–26). Consequently, actions like raiding and piracy, which could have provided
the ­necessary materials, should not be excluded from the agendas of the palatial agents (Samaras 2015, 200).

For trade and transportation, they would have chosen their vessel by cargo capacity; for warfare or piratical

Considering the characteristics of those ships and the general picture of the LBA in the Mediterranean,
­ ycenaean seafaring groups could have taken up

findings.evidence_excerpt:
CONCLUSIONS
The purpose of this paper has been to discuss some critical aspects of the identity and status of the people who
were crossing the Aegean during the LBA. Nevertheless, as shown by the discussion above, the evidence does
not point to a unique direction. On the contrary, the more we focus on these activities, the more we understand that the sea was not only a place where ships sailed and goods moved through. Groups originating from
different backgrounds were able to sail the seas, each one of them bearing different agendas. The lack of total
control of the sea routes allowed those groups to accomplish various feats and assume multiple roles, potentially
interchangeably. Traders, mercenaries, warriors and pirates were able to interact with palatial and non-palatial
agents depending on the circumstances and the needs of each group.
Detailed archaeological research and analytical studies of various categories of evidence (e.g., textual,
­iconographical) may enable us to identify certain factors, activities and networks that did affect or were affected
by long-distance sea travel. The LBA seafarers were not necessarily representatives of their cultures, but they
inevitably connected them through their own mobility, ideas and objects that moved with those groups.

findings.evidence_excerpt:
ABSTRACT
The Egyptians used cedar wood for the construction of both the sacred barks and the ships sailing in the ­Mediterranean
and the Red Sea. However, the lack of cedar and timber suitable for shipbuilding in general led Egypt to seek various ways
of securing the required quantity of wood. This is precisely the reason for the journey of the Egyptian priest Wenamun,
who was sent by the High Priest of Amun at Thebes to the Phoenician city of Byblos to procure the ­necessary cedar wood to
build the sacred bark of the god. During this journey, Wenamun was led into an action that could be described as piracy.
The present paper attempts to show whether the text with Wenamun’s adventures is a historical narrative, which offers
valuable information about the political, social and economic developments that took place in the eastern Mediterranean
during the end of the Late Bronze Age and the beginning of the Early Iron Age. It also attempts to identify the political,
economic and even psychological factors that contributed to Wenamun’s action of attacking a ship on the high seas and
stealing its silver. The main aim of examining this evidence is to determine whether Wenamun became, even temporarily,
a pirate.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
INTRODUCTION
At the end of the Late Bronze Age (LBA) in the Levant, powerful empires, such as those of the Egyptians and
Hittites, coexisted with small kingdoms, which were mostly subordinate to some of the powers of the time.
Egypt succeeded in consolidating its position in the region. The construction of Egyptian temples in Byblos
and Egyptian-style fortresses in the Levant area, as well as the installation of an Egyptian governor in Byblos,
confirm that Egypt tried in every way to secure its interests and procure the necessary supplies (Stein 2017, 17).
This situation was maintained until the 19th Dynasty (Sherratt 2003, 49–51), but changed significantly after
the fall of the Hittite empire and the gradual weakening of Egypt in the early 12th century BCE. The new situation in the Levant is reflected in an 11th century BCE text, the story of Wenamun. The eponymous hero of
the story, whose name is transcribed as WN-Imn, traveled to Byblos to obtain the necessary timber to build the
sacred bark of Amun. This paper discusses the historicity of Wenamun’s narrative and examines the depiction
of piracy as per this text. To approach these issues, it is necessary to re-examine the text in direct relation to the
social and political conditions developed in the eastern Mediterranean during the period of its composition, i.e.,
at the beginning of the 11th century BCE.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
EGYPTIAN OFFICIAL OR PIRATE?
Wenamun’s decision to rob a Tjeker ship reminds many of an act of piracy. The term piracy first appears in an
Attic inscription of the mid-3rd century BCE from Rhamnous (de Souza 1999, 3–4). However, it can be argued
that the concept of piracy predates the appearance of the term. For example, the term bandits was used by
Homer (ληϊστῆρες, e.g., Od. 3.73, 17.425) and Thucydides (λῃσταὶ, e.g., 1.8.1, 6.4.5) to refer to robbers of the
sea, i.e., pirates (LSJ, s.v. λῃστεία). In the eastern Mediterranean texts, there are several references to acts that
could be characterized as piratical (e.g., Ormerod 1924, 81–8; Sandars 1985; Derks 2016, 17–9; Hitchcock and
Maeir 2016; Kopanias 2019; contra de Souza 1999, 16–17). The Amarna letters reflect the insecurity existing at
sea and the danger faced by coastal areas, which were often attacked by groups, whose main objective was to
secure loot (EA 38; Μoran 1992, 111–12). At the same time, many inscriptions that accompany the reliefs with
the achievements of the Pharaohs point out the naval battles they fought to repel enemies attacking Egypt by
sea, with a typical example being the naval battle of Ramses III at Medinet Habu (Emanuel 2017, 63–70; Kopanias 2021, 257–58; Fig. 2).
Before proceeding with the characterization of Wenamun as a pirate or not, it is necessary to clearly d
­ efine
the context within which an act can be considered as piracy. The general observation that in war armies meet
and face each other on land or sea seems rather simplistic (Emanuel 2017, 33). Shelley Wachsmann (1998,
317–21), on the other hand, considers that in war there is involvement of the participating state with its troops
and vessels, which does not happen in the case of piracy (see also Emanuel 2017, 33–5). Philip de Souza (1999,
1), referring to the piracy of Graeco-Roman times, has characterized the pirates as “armed robbers whose
­activities normally involve the use of ships”. In the story of Wenamun, there is no involvement of any state
power. Wenamun acted alone, made a decision by himself and put it into effect immediately, without waiting
for approval of an official state authority. In Egypt, no one knew anything about the unexpected turn of events
that took place at Dor and then off Tyre. Wenamun neither reported anything back to his superiors, nor asked
for their guidance about what course of action he should follow. His action was financially motivated and done
for personal gain; he had to complete his mission and return to Egypt with the required amount of cedar.
The question inevitably arises, whether Wenamun could be classified as a pirate. It is a fact that, based on the
modern perception of pirates, as it began to take shape in recent times, i.e., after the so-called “Golden Age of
piracy” (late 17th – early 18th century CE), pirates are described as dangerous, marginalized groups, who plied
the seas with the aim of plundering territories, killing, capturing inhabitants in order to sell them as slaves or
to receive ransom for their release. For example, such an image of pirates is captured in The Travels of Reverend
Ólafur Egilsson, a 17th-century text describing the raid of pirates from Salé and Algiers on Iceland (Hreinsson
and Nichols 2008).
At the end of the LBA and the beginning of the Early Iron Age (EIA), however, the identity of the pirate does
not seem to correspond to the one of a marginalized person, as it emerges from history and literature of the Early
Modern and Modern periods. The environment in which the sailor, the merchant, the seafarer moves is fluid
and full of multiple and unexpected risks. This element of the variability of conditions in the marine environment influenced and ultimately shaped trade relations and exchanges (Monroe 2011, 95). In this ever-changing

ite, which sought to establish itself, among other ways, through sea raids.
This new elite, members of which participated in the commercial networks controlled by the palaces in the
previous period, was now actively involved in trade but for their own benefit. Their involvement was achieved
either through trade (by controlling the already existing trade routes and markets) or through piracy. Therefore,
piracy should be understood as an “irregular, typically hostile, ongoing economic activity carried out for personal benefit and involving the use of ships, maritime mobility and plundering, at sea and along coastal areas”
(Knapp 2018, 36). The pirate was not necessarily an adventurer, a bandit, but could be a ship owner, a merchant
or even a government official, like Wenamun, who plundered when that was deemed necessary (Knapp 2020,
155).
Therefore, what needs to be taken into consideration is under which circumstances a person can become a
pirate. In the Odyssey (14.191–359), the king of Ithaca, transformed into a beggar by Athena, tells Eumaeus a
fake story, as he presents himself as the son of Castor from Crete. He recounts that, just a month after his return
from the ten-year war in Troy, he sought new adventures; thus he and his companions went to Egypt for raiding.
However, this expedition did not have a positive outcome, because of a factor pointed out by the narrator
himself, which is directly related to human nature: “But my comrades, yielding to wantonness, and led on by
their own might” (Od. 14.262, trans. A. T. Murray, Cambridge, Mass., 1919). Namely, arrogance led O
­ dysseus’
companions to raid the fields, to enslave young children and women, and to kill unsuspecting farmers and
­fishermen, until Pharaoh sent an army to confront the invaders.
Wenamun’s transformation from the Elder of the Portal of the Temple of Amun to a pirate cannot be
­attributed to arrogance but to necessity that prompts him to such an act. The purpose of his journey was to
secure the timber needed to build god’s great noble bark. His mission was going smoothly until he himself became the victim of a robbery. Wenamun’s decision to take a piratical action was not chosen from the beginning.
At first, he appealed to the commander of Dor to help him find the amount that had been stolen from him,
but Beder (or Bederi) refused to get involved, as the robbery had not been committed by any of his citizens.
Without the help of any official authority, he decided to solve his problem by himself resorting to piracy, which
was financially motivated and done for Wenamun’s own benefit. A possible failure would damage his prestige
and it was highly likely he would be accused of very significant crimes. On the contrary, successful completion
of his mission would further consolidate his position.
For a better understanding of his act, some other factors must be taken into account. The text of
Wenamun dates to the 11th century BCE and captures the new political situation that has been formed in the
­Mediterranean. Cyprian Broodbank (2013, 394) has characterized the Mediterranean as “an anarchic, f

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
CONCLUSIONS
The text of Wenamun’s adventures has caused several disputes among scholars as to its historicity. There were
many who questioned the historical basis of the text, considering it to be a literary narrative with elements of
verisimilitude. However, the re-examination of the text that was attempted showed that the evidence presented
is confirmed by both the archaeological findings and the written sources from the eastern Mediterranean at the
end of the LBA and at the beginning of the EIA. The purpose of Wenamun’s journey, namely to procure cedar
from Byblos, is not a product of fiction, but seems to correspond to historical reality as Egypt did not have cedar
wood, which was necessary for shipbuilding. Also, the course followed by the Egyptian official is as expected as
the sea currents that sail in the area favor navigation. Furthermore, the mention of specific coastal cities, such
as Dor, Tyre and Byblos, confirms the historical core of the text, since they have been proven to have had a port
and port facilities and participated in the international trade network that had been formed at the beginning of
the 11th century BCE.
At the same time, the narrative seems to reflect the political and social situation that had developed on the
shores of the Levant after the fall of the Hittite empire and the weakening of Egypt. The autonomy and power
the coastal cities in the aforementioned region had gained, affected the way that trade was as of then conducted
for Egypt, and more specifically the cedar trade. Byblos was no longer a vassal to Egypt; instead it was its ruler
who managed the cedar trade. This new reality turned Wenamun from a Priest of god Amun to a pirate in order
to complete his mission. The hero’s decision to attack and rob the Tjeker ship was a conscious action on his
part. It constituted a solution, undoubtedly unorthodox, but acceptable, which could be applied whenever the
circumstances dictated.

findings.evidence_excerpt:
Sailing through the “Unresting Sea”
The Archaeology of Piracy in the Early Iron Age Aegean

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
ABSTRACT
This paper investigates piracy in the Aegean during the Early Iron Age (late 11th–late 8th/early 7th century BCE), a
phenomenon that remains difficult to trace archaeologically due to the absence of clear diagnostic indicators. It argues
that the ­conditions emerging after the collapse of the Mycenaean palatial system, conditions that continued to shape the
ensuing ­centuries, created an exceptionally favorable environment for the development of piracy. Small, autonomous
communities o­ perated within expanding networks of maritime mobility and exchange, at a time when strong, centralized
mechanisms of ­control were largely absent. The analysis brings together five strands of evidence: maritime connectivity,
fortified island ­settlements, depictions of sea-borne conflict in Geometric pottery, warrior burials and the Homeric epics.
Considered in combination, these elements suggest that piracy was a plausible and often pronounced aspect of Aegean
seafaring during the Early Iron Age.
The paper then re-examines selected categories of evidence, from fortified sites and potential pirate havens to the ­pictorial
pottery of the 8th century BCE, highlighting particularly revealing cases such as the New York krater MMA 34.11.2
and Tomb 79 at Lefkandi. These examples underscore the fluidity of maritime roles in this period: individuals and
­communities could act simultaneously, or alternately, as traders, warriors, sailors or raiders, depending on ­circumstances
and ­opportunity. Moreover, both Geometric iconography and the Homeric epics appear to draw on contemporary
­practices and lived experiences, reflecting forms of maritime violence and raiding that were far from exceptional. Overall,
the study proposes that piracy should not be viewed as a marginal or occasional occurrence, but as a critical component
for understanding the social and maritime dynamics of the Early Iron Age Aegean.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
INTRODUCTION
The principal challenge in the study of piracy in antiquity lies in developing an interpretive framework capable
of addressing the theoretical and practical problems associated with the phenomenon, while at the same time
foregrounding its significance as a substantive analytical component for understanding the past. Scholars have
long grappled with issues that pose considerable interpretive difficulties, such as the definition of piracy (e.g.,
Ormerod 1924, 60; de Souza 1999, 1; Samaras 2015, 191; Skowronek 2016, 4) or its distinction from warfare
(Samaras 2015, 191; Emanuel 2017, 33–7; 2018, 73–7). Even more demanding (and arguably more intriguing)
is the question of how piracy can be identified and meaningfully interpreted within the archaeological record.
It is common, not only for antiquity but also for later periods, that the relationship piracy bears to other
activities, as reflected in its material traces, evokes the notion of equifinality, namely “the principle that the past
could have unfolded in a multitude of ways, each of which could have resulted in the same evidence we are

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
presented with today” (Graham and Weingarτ 2015, 249). Indeed, several activities could generate outcomes
identical to those produced by piracy, such as trade, elite gift exchange or warfare.
When the circulation of goods in the Aegean during the Early Iron Age (EIA; that is, from the late 11th to the
late 8th/early 7th century BCE) is taken as an example, trade is typically privileged by researchers over alternative interpretations. And although the possibility of aristocratic gift exchange is frequently acknowledged (e.g.,
Morris 1986, 7–14; Wagner-Hasel 2006; Arrington 2016, 3, 5–6), the prospect of theft or piracy is almost never
considered, despite the fact that, as will be discussed in greater detail below, the acquisition of wealth through
raiding, whether on land or at sea, was both acceptable and commonplace in the Homeric epics.
In the case of piracy, the notion of equifinality extends to a range of issues beyond the circulation of goods.
Some of these issues enter the sphere of agency and social identity, such as, for example, the deliberate projection
of identities like those of the warrior, the seafarer or the trader. These identities are closely connected to the
figure of the pirate and may, in certain circumstances, be expressed in the funerary record.
Regarding the EIA Aegean, which forms the focus of this paper, the well-known difficulties inherent in any
archaeological approach to piracy (see Samaras, this volume) are compounded by the particular challenges of
the period itself. These include the limited number of written sources, the generally reduced archaeological
visibility and the absence of final publications for many sites, all of which restrict the interpretive possibilities
even further. In short, piracy fails to receive adequate attention in the interpretive frameworks applied to the
archaeology of the Aegean during the early historical period, not because the phenomenon was absent, but
because clear answers to the issues outlined above, together with other questions that cannot be addressed here
in detail, remain difficult to obtain.
Nevertheless, since the closing years of the twentieth century a number of scholars, including David Tandy
(1997), Reinhard Jung (2009, 2018), Louise Hitchcock and Aren Maeir (2014, 2016, 2017, 2018a, 2018b),
­Vangelis Samaras (2015), Jeffrey Emanuel (2017, 2018, 2021) and Bernard Knapp (2018, 2020), have sought,
each from a distinct perspective, to shed light on the phenomenon of piracy in the Late Bronze Age (LBA) and
the EIA. The A.P.Pir.A. project, which since 2021 has examined the archaeological study of piracy in antiquity
and includes the EIA within its scope, forms part of this broader scholarly current.
The present contribution aims to offer a modest addition to this line of inquiry by investigating piracy in
the EIA Aegean through a reassessment of selected well-known archaeological sites and finds. Three working
assumptions, discussed in greater detail in the introduction to this volume, are essential for this undertaking:
•
