Trade and the Elimination of Piracy
The Case of Hellenistic Rhodes

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
ABSTRACT
Throughout classical antiquity, several naval powers attempted to eliminate piracy, as this activity represented a constant
threat to human safety and the efficient conduct of maritime trade. Among these powers, Hellenistic Rhodes holds an
exceptional place, due to its systematic efforts for the elimination of pirate activity, which was at its peak during this
period. This paper examines the relationship between Rhodes and the pirates, and in particular the causes behind the
Rhodian anti-piracy policy and the ways in which this policy was pursued. The design of the trihemiolia –a type of light
and extremely fast ship, capable of pursuing the pirate hemioliai that stormed the Hellenistic Aegean– undoubtedly had
a crucial part to play in the Rhodians’ anti-piracy actions, the highlight of which was the victory of Rhodes in the First
Cretan War at the end of the 3rd century BCE. The analysis of the relevant historical and archaeological data attempted
in this paper reveals that piracy was a decisive factor in both the establishment of Rhodes as a leading naval power in the
Hellenistic Aegean and its decline.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
INTRODUCTION
Throughout classical antiquity, Rhodes was an important trading center of the Aegean and the eastern
­Mediterranean, but it rose to prominence during the Hellenistic period. As discussed in detail below, the Rhodians are praised by ancient authors as “masters of the sea”, mainly due to their systematic efforts to ­eliminate
piracy. This paper examines the relationship between the Rhodians and pirates, as Hellenistic Rhodes is an
excellent case study of how the naval powers were dealing with the phenomenon of piracy. It opens with a brief
discussion of the relationship between trade and piracy, as it was this relationship that determined the attitude
of each naval power towards pirates. Subsequently, the various aspects of Rhodes’ anti-piracy policy and the
ways in which it sought to enforce this policy are examined. Finally, the conflict between the Rhodians and the
Cretan pirates is examined, which had a decisive impact on both the prosperity and the decline of Hellenistic
Rhodes.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
TRADE AND PIRACY
The prevailing view among early and mid-20th century scholars was that piracy represented one of the most
important factors damaging trade and, consequently, the economy of cities (e.g., Ormerod 1924, 113, 128, 155.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
ed
by more recent scholars, arguing that the economic growth of trade in the Mediterranean area during the
1st and 2nd centuries CE was thanks to suppression of piracy by the Romans (e.g., Hopkins 1983, xviii–xix).
­Besides, the contrasting relationship between trade and piracy seems to be confirmed by ancient authors, such
as ­Thucydides (1.5.1, 1.13.5) and Strabo (e.g., 3.2.5, 10.4.9).
Recent research has offered a different perspective on this previously held belief. Shipwrecks, as well as
amphorae distributed in large ­quantities and in various places, prove that trade in the Aegean continued uninterrupted, even during periods of intense pirate activity (Parker 1992, 31–5; Davies 2001, 27–9; Gabrielsen
2013a, 149, with further bibliography). Interestingly, during the second half of the 3rd century BCE –a period of
economic prosperity in the C
­ yclades and the flourishing of important commercial ports, such as Thasos, Delos,
Kos and Rhodes itself– there was a significant increase in pirate attacks (Gabrielsen 2001, 221).
Contrary to what was generally accepted in the past, scholars now perceive trade and piracy as two closely
related forms of economic activity (e.g., Gabrielsen 2001, 221; Samaras 2015, 191). Goods and people stolen
by pirates gradually began to reach the markets of the Aegean and neighboring regions (Rauh 1997; 1999, 171;
de Souza 1999, 22, 56, 201–2). Pirates seem to have been the main supplier of slaves, as they served various
trading centers, the most famous being Delos (cf. Strabo 14.5.2). Some scholars have claimed that the pirates’
main aim was the enslavement of people (e.g., Marόti 1969–1970, 70; Brulé 1978, 18, 159, 161, 183), while de
Souza (1999, 60–3) later considered statements about the piratical contribution to the Hellenistic slave trade to
be highly exaggerated. However, the fact that Hellenistic cities protected their citizens from being snatched and
enslaved suggests the gravity and frequency of the risk (Lewis 2019, 93–9). Regardless of the actual size of the
pirates’ contribution to the slave trade, it is plausible that it was vital for them to find markets to sell their prey,
and more than a few cities were willing to provide them with port bases and markets for their ill-gotten goods
(de Souza 1999, 188).
It can therefore be concluded that trade and piracy have more in common than might have been expected.
These are activities with a similar motive (i.e., the economic gain of the participants), which fulfill their purpose
only when their products reach the markets to be sold. On the other hand, it should not be forgotten that trade
was a non-violent practice and that merchants were in direct danger from pirates, as they risked being enslaved
or even dying and losing their goods if they were confronted with a pirate ship. Pirates, for their part, sought to
keep maritime trade going uninterrupted and even chose to operate in new places from time to time so as not
to exhaust the merchants of a single region (de Souza 1995, 187–88). Finally, for the markets it was immaterial
whether the cargo came from stolen goods or not (Gabrielsen 2013a, 148–49).
As far as Rostovzeef ’s statement (Rostovzeef 1941, 1242–243) that the economic development of cities was
harmed by piracy is concerned, it is obviously only partially true. Τhe cities targeted and plundered by the pirates were indeed damaged, both economically and materially. But other cities, those that provided a market for
piratical goods, prospered as a result. The cities that cooperated with the pirates for their economic growth were
not few. In fact, piracy was a solution for the poor habitants of a region, since it was probably a conscious choice
that was linked to socio-economic and political dimensions (Davies 1984, 290; Gabrielsen 2001, 221–22).
Several ancient authors confirm that it was common practice for the Hellenistic cities to recruit pirates as
mercenaries, when there was a need for sea or infantry forces (e.g., Dem. 23.148–149, 162, 166–167; Strabo
10.4.10). During this period, the distinction between pirates and mercenaries is often quite blurred, as the same
people could engage in both activities (Ormerod 1924, 143). The fact that the cities recruited pirates as mercenaries suggests acceptance of the practice of piracy, but the trust they placed in these people often turned out
to be misplaced, since pirates did not hesitate to betray their commanders if a better economic deal was offered
(Pacheco 2020, 102).
Perhaps the prime example of the use of pirates as mercenaries in the period under discussion comes from
Demetrius I Poliorcetes, who cooperated with the pirate Timocles in the unsuccessful siege of Rhodes in 305–
304 BCE (Diod. Sic. 20.97.5). He also recruited to his army merchant ship captains, who followed them appar-

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
ently to benefit from the spoils they would secure in the plundering of rich Rhodes. This example illustrates the
fluid context between pirates, merchants and mercenaries. Merchants could turn into mercenaries just as easily
as pirates if a profitable opportunity arose (Gabbert 1986, esp. 156; Pacheco 2020, 102).
For the Rhodian side, on the other hand, there are no reports of the use of pirates as mercenaries in their
military conflicts, nor of the granting of markets or harbor bases to pirates. Even during the troubled ­Hellenistic
times, pirates and their prey were not welcome in all commercial ports, as Rostovtzeff had argued (1941, 196; for
arguments against Rostovtzeff ’s view, see Lewis 2019, 100–1). However, as discussed in more detailed below, this
did not prevent Rhodians from overlooking piracy, when it worked in their interests. It is therefore e­ xtremely
interesting to study the perspective of a city economically dependent on maritime trade and how it dealt with
the long-standing problem of piracy to preserve its economic vitality.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
THE RHODIANS AS “MASTERS OF THE SEA”
During the Hellenistic period, Rhodes based its economic prosperity on maritime trade, especially long-­
distance trade. The island’s most important trading partner was Egypt, “for it happened that most of their
revenues were due to the merchants who sailed to Egypt, and that in general the city drew its food supply
from that kingdom” (Diod. Sic. 20.81.4, trans. R.M. Geer, Cambridge, Mass., 1954). The city was provided
with five harbors, which were naturally fortified thanks to the topography of the island (Gabrielsen 1997, 37–9;
­Filimonos-Tsopotou 2004, 46–70, with further bibliography). The Rhodians, however, did not content with this,
but proceeded to build fortifications and walls to strengthen the protection of the bog and the harbors (for the
impressive ­fortification system of Hellenistic Rhodes see Filimonos-Tsopotou 2004; Manoussou-Ntella 2016).
According to several ancient authors, the Rhodians constantly tried to suppress piracy during the Hellenistic
period. Among the naval power of classical antiquity, few seem to have made such intense and systematic efforts
to control this phenomenon as Rhodes. Strabo praises the Rhodians for the care “with which they administered
affairs of state generally, and particularly those relative to their marine” and thanks to which they became “for
a long period masters of the sea” and “they put an end to piracy” (Strabo 14.2.5, trans. W. Falconer, London,
1903). Similarly, Diodorus refers that “the city of the Rhodians […] was strong in sea power” and that “she
advanced to such strength that in behalf of the Greeks she by herself undertook her war against the pirates and
purged the seas of these evil-doers” (Diod. Sic. 20.82.1, trans. R.M. Geer, Cambridge, Mass., 1954). Even in
the 2nd century CE, Aelius Aristides mentions with admiration the enormous booty the Rhodians had seized
from the Tyrrhenian pirates and points out that they once “ruled the seas” (Aristid. Or. 24.53, trans. C.A. Behr,
Leiden, 1981). In addition, thanks to Rhodes, merchant ships were often escorted by warships or with armed
men on board, to ensure the safety of the crew and the cargo during the voyage (e.g., Diod. Sic. 20.82.2; Lycurg.
Leoc. 18). But how far are these statements true? Can the Rhodians really be described as “masters of the sea”
in the Hellenistic period?
There is little but significant evidence for Rhodian anti-piracy actions. In 220 BCE they drove off Demetrius
of Pharos from the Cyclades, which he was plundering (Polyb. 4.19.8; see also Davies 2004). Also, in 200 BCE
they acted against pirates from Chalkis raiding Attica, and in 190 BCE they protected the strait of Kephalonia
from pirates, in both cases with the help of the Romans and their allies (Livy 31.22.5–7, 37.13.11–12; see also
de Souza 1999, 86, 88; Gabrielsen 2001, 228, 230). The Rhodians even played an important role in the great
campaign against piracy with the measures of the “Lex de provinciis praetoriis”. This law appears to date from
around 100 BCE and survives in two versions, one found at Delphi and one from Knidos (Crawford 1996,
231–70; de Souza 1999, 108–14). Additionally, the involvement of the Rhodian navy in anti-piracy actions is
further ­confirmed by certain inscriptions, which are discussed in more detail below.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
Gabrielsen rightly argues that these are just a few examples of the great effort of the Rhodians to protect the
seas from pirates, as the inscriptions record actions against piracy as a common phenomenon. Furthermore,
in the peace treaty between Rhodes and the Cretan city of Hierapytna about the end of the 3rd century BCE,
the former show a keen interest in pirates and those accepting them in their ports (see in more detail below,
“Rhodes and the Cretan pirates”). Finally, by the last quarter of the 3rd century BCE Rhodes could boast of
both the resilience of its maritime infrastructure and the good use of it (Gabrielsen 2001, 229). It is indicative
that in that period Rhodes had managed to control many offshore naval bases from present-day Kastellorizo to
Antikythera (ancient Aigilia) and from eastern Crete to as far away as Delos (Gabrielsen 1997, 41–2).
The Rhodian navy included ships distinguished for their speed and agility, the phylakidai nees (φυλακίδαι
νῆες), which means guardships in ancient Greek (Diod. Sic. 20.93.2; see also Gabrielsen 1997, 108–9; 2013b, 74).
The name of these ships clearly refers to their use, as they were designed in such a way as to provide protection
against raiders. Rhodian phylakidai were mainly intended for special missions, perhaps against pirate attacks,
even giving them this name in order to advertise their effectiveness (Gabrielsen 2001, 230).
The use of phylakidai is revealed by a series of inscriptions referring to this type of ship. By way of example,
the inscription IG XI.4 596 from Delos, dating after 250 BCE, mentions that a Rhodian navarch and his three
trierarchs received honors for ensuring “the protection [φυλακῆς] of the islands and the safety [σωτηρίαι] of
the Greeks”, presumably against pirates (Holleaux 1907, 359 n. 4; de Souza 1999, 81; Gabrielsen 2001, 230;
Constantakopoulou 2017, 150–51). In another Delian inscription, of the early 2nd century BCE, the Rhodian
navarch Epikrates is honored for “the safety [ἀσφαλείας] of the shipping trade and the protection [φυλακῆς]
of the islands”, as well as for the fact that he took care to issue a regulation that no one of his crews should use
Delos as a naval base (ὁρμηθῶσιν) in their piratical raids (πειρατεύοντες) against enemy (IG XI.4 751; de Souza
1999, 87–8; Gabrielsen 2001, 230–31; Constantakopoulou 2017, 151). The same navarch also participated in the
chase of pirates off Kephalonia in 190 BCE, which has already been mentioned (Livy 37.13.11–12). In general,
the Delian inscription corpus includes several cases attesting to the protection provided to the island by the
Rhodians (e.g., IG XI.4 1133 [ca. 300–250 BCE], 1135 [mid-3rd century BCE] and 752–753 [beginning of the
2nd century BCE]).
However, beyond the protection they offered, the Rhodians also acted as a means of securing trade relations
and administering justice among merchants. In 220 BCE, Rhodes declared war against Byzantion, because the
Aegean merchants had turned to them for help, as Polybius recounts:

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
It is therefore clear that, during the Hellenistic period, Rhodes was a dominant naval force. With their navy
the Rhodians chased pirates, protected the islands and merchant ships, while Aegean trading communities
facing serious problems turned to them for help. However, to complete the picture of the Rhodians as “­ masters
of the sea”, three further comments need to be made: firstly, for Rhodian protection and help, the island’s allies
often paid exorbitant sums in return, significantly boosting the economy and, by extension, the naval power of
Rhodes (Gabrielsen 2001, 233–35). Secondly, the effort to suppress pirate activity was not generalized and unconditional, but depended on the political and economic interests of Rhodes (Pacheco 2020, 101). For ­example,
as Strabo comments (14.5.2), the Rhodians did not intervene when Cilician pirates were harassing the ­Seleucids
in the eastern Mediterranean, as they were themselves hostile to this dynasty. Thirdly, when necessary, the
­Rhodians themselves carried out attacks and raids against merchant ships, producing maritime violence for
their own benefit (e.g., Diod. Sic. 20.93.2–5).

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
THE RHODIAN NAVY
It is obvious that the navy of Rhodes played a key role in the island’s effort to eliminate piracy. Even if the claim
that the Rhodian navy “was particularly designed as an antipirate force” (Berthold 1984, 98) seems exaggerated,
there is some direct evidence for its action against the pirates. Diodorus mentions a Rhodian law according to
which “the bodies of those who fell in the war should be given public burial”, while there was also a provision
for support for the families of the dead at public cost (Diod. Sic. 20.84.3, trans. R.M. Geer, Cambridge, Mass.,
1954). This custom is attested by a funerary inscription found on the island that honors three brothers who lost
their lives fighting for the Rhodian navy:
[ἄνδρας τ]ούσδ’ ἀγαθοὺς κεύθει
[τόδε χῶ]μα θανόντας.
[․․․․․ Τ]ιμακράτευς πρωιρατεύων
[εἰς Αἰγι]λίαν ἀγωνιζόμενος ποτὶ
[λαϊστὰς] ἐτελεύτασε.
[․․․․․․]ης Τιμακράτευς πλέων ἐν τᾶι
[ναυαρχίδ]ι ἐν τοῖς παρακαθημένοις ἀγω[νιζόμενος] ποτὶ Τυρρανοὺς ἐτελεύτασε.
[Πολέμαρχο]ς Τιμακράτευς συνταγματάρ[χας ταχθεὶς] ποτὶ τοὺς λαϊστὰς ἀγωνιζό[μενος ἐτελε]ύτασε.
[Κα]σαρεῖς. (Segre 1932, 457–61 [= Syll.3 1225])

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
The most probably date for this inscription is about the middle of the 3rd century BCE (Sekunda 2014;
see also Gabrielsen 2001, 229, n. 43). For the third brother, Polemarchos, it is clearly mentioned that he died
fighting against the pirates (τοὺς λαϊστὰς), but most scholars accept that the other two brothers were killed in a
similar way (e.g., Ormerod 1924, 130 n. 3; de Souza 1999, 50–1). The Tyrrhenians mentioned in relation to the
two brothers may represent any pirates of the Adriatic Sea or the Italian peninsula (on the Tyrrhenian pirates
see Bakhuizen 1988; Bresson 2007; Fritzilas, this volume). Polemarchos is also mentioned in another inscription
from the island, which is earlier, dating back to the beginning of the 3rd century BCE (Jacopi 1932, 169–70). In
this second inscription, he is honored for his participation in an attack on Aigilia (present-day Antikythera),
once more against pirates (Brulé 1978, 31; de Souza 1999, 51; Bresson 2016, 162–63; see also Tsaravopoulos and
Kroustalis, this volume).
Another inscription offering valuable information about the actions of the Rhodian navy against the pirates
comes from an impressive monument discovered on the acropolis of Lindos: a marble prow of a warship, on
which a statue (probably Nike) once stood (Blinkenberg 1938, 30–7; 1941, 301–13 no. 88; Filimonos-Tsopotou
2013, 269–70; Gabrielsen 2013c, 69–71; Figs. 1–2). The preserved part of the inscription of this monument,
which was dated between 265 and 260 BCE based on the letter forms and prosopographical data ­(Blinkenberg
1941, 308; see also Gabrielsen 2013c, 70 n. 24), testifies that it was dedicated to Lindos’ principal deity, Athena
Lindia, by the commanders and crews of a squadron of trihemioliai as a tithe (ἀπαρχὰν) from the booty
(λαφύρων) they had captured during a successful naval expedition. Blinkenberg argued that this expedition was
against Tyrrhenian pirates, a view accepted by most scholars (e.g., Filimonos-Tsopotou 2013, 269; Gabrielsen
2013c, 71–2; contra Wiemer 2002, 134).
This inscribed monument raises many interesting issues for discussion, but the present paper is limited to
commenting on two specific aspects. Firstly, in this case the booty resulting from the successful expedition
against the Tyrrhenians did not become state property, but was claimed by the crews, which reveals that at
least in Hellenistic Rhodes private anti-pirate campaigns could be organized and conducted (Gabrielsen 2013c,
71–2). Secondly, considering the cost of this impressive monument and the fact that it was dedicated as a tithe
of the booty, it becomes clear that these campaigns could yield a very substantial profit (Wiemer 2002, 134),
which explains the private interest in them. Moreover, of particular importance is that the expedition against
the Tyrrhenians was carried out with trihemioliai, a ship type developed by the Rhodians specifically for their
anti-pirate operations.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
Furthermore, in the battle of Chios in 201 BCE, the existence of trihemioliai (τριημιολίαι) in the allied fleets
of Attalus and Rhodes, which defeated the fleet of Philip V of Macedonia, is mentioned by Polybius (16.2.10).
Apart from the references of the ancient writers, there is a series of inscriptions attesting to the Rhodian origin
of the trihemiolia (for an overview of this inscription corpus see Blinkenberg 1938, 14–19).
But why did the Rhodians design the trihemiolia and incorporate it in their fleet? During the 4th century
BCE, pirate hemioliai were very successful, as they were light and extremely fast, making the traditional ships
of the Greek fleets up to that time unsuitable for their pursuit (for hemioliai see Casson 1958, 14–16; Morrison
1980, 121–24; Nakas, this volume, with further bibliography). It is illustrative that Theophrastus, who lived at
that time, mentions ships as a synonym for the pirate threat (Theophr. Char. 25.2). The Rhodians sought a solution to the difficulty of pursuing pirate hemioliai by adapting to the traditional model of the trireme elements of
the hemiolia (Casson 1958, 17). The result was the trihemiolia, a ship type heavier and faster than the hemiolia,
suitable for both pursuit and combat.
The trihemiolia was used exclusively as part of the organized navy and not as a pirate ship (Casson 1958,
16, n. 16). Its ­effectiveness in the pursuit of pirate ships contributed significantly to the establishment of the
reputation of the Rhodians as “masters of the sea”. So strong is the connection between the Rhodian navy and
the ­trihemioliai, that the ships both in the aforementioned monument of 265–250 BCE, dedicated to Athena
Lindia, and in other well-known monuments (e.g., the relief prow below the entrance to the acropolis of Lindos
and the ­famous Nike of Samothrace; Figs. 3–4) were long considered to be trihemioliai (e.g., Blinkenberg 1938,
22–40; ­Morrison 1980, 124–25; Rice 1996, 214; Mark 1998, 157–58), a view now seriously disputed (Casson
1971, 102–3; ­Gabrielsen 1997, 88–9; Stewart 2016, 404, 407–8; Clinton et al. 2020, 565–67; Palagia 2021, 155).

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
RHODES AND THE CRETAN PIRATES
As already mentioned, during the Hellenistic period Rhodes made systematic efforts to eliminate piracy. These
efforts lasted until about the end of the Second Cretan War (153 BCE), which found Rhodes extremely ­weakened
and Rome gaining the role that Rhodes had occupied until then. The primary objective of the Rhodians was to
patrol the seas and ensure the safety of trade, as this served their economic interests (Brulé 1978, 29–30). In the
Rhodians’ anti-piracy operations, the main targets seem to have been the Cretans, who had developed intense
pirate activity, especially towards the end of the 3rd century BCE, when Philip V of Macedonia encouraged this
activity in order to harm Rhodes economically and militarily, aiming to make his kingdom the leading Aegean
power (for the Cretan piracy see Brulé 1978; de Souza 1999, esp. 80–4; Perlman 1999).

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
As a result of the increasing Cretan piracy and its impact on the commercial activities and economic ­interests
of Rhodes and its allies, the First Cretan War broke out in 206/5 BCE (for a brief outline of this war see de Souza
1999, 80–4; Perlman 1999, 134–37, and in more detail Brulé 1978, 29–56). The Rhodians’ main opponents
were Gortyn, Hierapytna and Eleutherna. The treaty between Rhodes and Hierapytna (IC III iii 3), which is
preserved in full and its dating has been controversial (see Dmitriev 2011, 433–34), reveals that the war ended
with Rhodes prevailing.
According to the treaty’s terms, Rhodes could recruit Cretans as mercenaries, use Hierapytna as a military
and naval base and, in the event of an attack against the island, demand that the Hierapytnians assist in its defense (de Souza 1999, 82–3; Perlman 1999, 136). On the other hand, the Rhodians promised that they would
help with all their forces if Hierapytna was attacked. It is clear that, despite the apparent alliance, the Cretan city
was in a subordinate position, conceding part of its independence to Rhodes. Nevertheless, although Rhodian
ships could enter the ports of Hierapytna at any time, there is no evidence suggesting the permanent presence
of a Rhodian garrison in the city.
Furthermore, according to the treaty, Hierapytna was obliged to assist Rhodes in its fight against the pirates
(Brulé 1978, 52–4; de Souza 1999, 83):

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
“[…] And if pirates [λᾳστήρια] establish bases in Crete and the Rhodians wage war at sea against
the pirates [λᾳστὰς] or those who provide shelter or assistance to them, the Hierapytnians shall take
part in the operations by land and by sea with all possible strength at their own expense. The pirates
[λᾳσταὶ] who are captured shall be handed over to the Rhodians together with their ships, while
each of the allies shall take half of the rest (of the booty). […] And if during a campaign which the
Hierapytnians are waging with the Rhodians to destroy a pirate base [λαιστηρίου], any of those who
provide shelter or assistance to the pirates [λαιστὰς] wage war on the Hierapytnians because of this
campaign, the Rhodians shall come to the help of the Hierapytnians with all possible strength, and
anyone who acts in this way shall be an enemy of the Rhodians” (IC III iii 3, lines 52–59, 80–83,
translation in Austin 2006, 214–15).

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
These terms reveal Rhodes’ anticipation of continued anti-piracy campaigns and the strong possibility that
these campaigns would be conducted against Cretan pirates. For that reason, although in a superior position,
Rhodes did not order the disarmament of the Hierapytna fleet, as this fleet could assist them in their “war at sea
against the pirates”.
The Rhodians’ victory in the First Cretan War meant the regaining of their power in the Aegean, which
is reflected in the revival of the Islander’s League (κοινὸν τῶν νησιωτῶν) (otherwise known as the Nesiotic
League), a league “headquarted at Tenos and serving as the instrument of Rhodian hegemony” (Reger 1994, 35;
for the Second Islanders’ League see also Étienne 1990, 101–24; Sheedy 1996; Gabrielsen 1997, 56–63). During
the first third of the 1st century BCE, Rhodes continued its efforts to eliminate piracy, and de Souza (1999, 84)
is probably right in arguing that “the reputation of the Rhodians as the suppressors of piracy for the common
good, which Diodorus mentions dates to this period (Diod. Sic. 20.81.3)”.
The hegemony of Rhodes in the Aegean lasted until 167 BCE, when Rome made Delos a free port and
­proclaimed the freedom of Lycia and Caria, severely damaging the two main poles of the Rhodian economy
(Diod. Sic. 31.43.1–45.1; Polyb. 30.31.4–12; see also de Souza 1999, 90–1). The gradual weakening of Rhodes
­allowed the Cretan pirates to intensify their activities. Gabrielsen (1997, 55–6) is probably right in arguing that
the revival of Cretan piracy was not the real principal motive for the Second Cretan War (155–153 BCE), but it
certainly had a significant impact (Brulé 1978, 63–4; Berthold 1984, 223).
The Second Cretan War was a conflict that pitted the Cretan cities against Rhodes once more. Not much
is known about this war; however, it is worth mentioning that Polybius referring to the Rhodian general

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
CONCLUSION
The case of Hellenistic Rhodes is representative of the way a major naval power manages the phenomenon of
­piracy. Such a power is obliged to pursue pirates as they challenge its authority and severely damage its e­ conomic
interests. Nevertheless, despite the systematic effort of the Rhodians to eliminate piracy in the Aegean, and even
though some ancient written sources claim that this effort was successful, the deep-rooted problem of piracy
remained a persistent and adaptive threat beyond full eradication. Pirates always found ways to continue their
activities and sell loot. Perhaps this is due to the nature of piracy, since both pirate bases and the areas where
pirates operated could be easily changed. Furthermore, there have been recorded cases in which a great naval
power, such as Rhodes, chose not to intervene to put an end to the activities of certain pirates, as they served
its interests.
The Rhodians could not only ignore or even encourage pirate activity, but often produced maritime violence
themselves, as they attacked the merchant ships of their rivals. In general, the anti-piracy policy of Rhodes, like
that of the naval power of any period, seems to have been determined primarily by its political and economic
interests. It should not be forgotten that, in pursuing the pirates, the Rhodians were not only defending the
merchant ships of the island and their allies. The protection and security offered by the famous Rhodian navy
and especially by their beloved trihemioliai provided them with considerable revenues. Overall, the analysis of
the historical and archaeological data on the relationship between Rhodes and the pirates during the Hellenistic
period reveals that piracy was an essential factor in both the establishment of Rhodes as a leading naval power
in the Aegean and its decline from this role.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
ABSTRACT
In this paper we summarize the results of the Rough Cilicia Archaeological Survey Project as they pertain to piracy,
by introducing two fresh avenues of investigation: a covert spaces analysis of potential pirate bases in the region and a
presentation of the evidence demonstrating a link between the pirate settlements on the coast and the Isaurian tribal
elements of the Taurus hinterland. GIS analysis of the coastal terrain reveals the potential for pirate infestation based
on the visibility of moorages, lines of sight at sea and the ability to target offshore shipping. It considers the problem
from a topographical perspective and illuminates the extent to which the maritime landscape of the Rough Cilicia
was suitable to piracy. The second avenue attempts to demonstrate how the evidence of an Isaurian cultural horizon in
coastal Rough Cilicia reveals a conjuncture between the warlords of the hinterland and the pirates on the coast. Much
like the GIS analysis of pirate base visibility, the highland connection can be demonstrated both through material
assemblages and GIS least-cost-path analysis.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
HISTORICAL OUTLINE OF THE CILICIAN PIRATES
The Cilician pirates emerged from the dynastic disputes of various pretenders to the Seleucid throne ca. 146–
138 BCE, having been organized by Diodotus Tryphon, a former Seleucid military officer from Apamea, during
his conflicts with Demetrius II and Antiochus VII Sidetes. Before his death in 138 BCE, Tryphon managed
to install his renegade naval forces at a number of impregnable fortresses along the eastern Mediterranean
corridor – most particularly at Coracesium (Korakesion; Fig. 1) in western Rough Cilicia (Cilicia Tracheia or
Aspera). In the aftermath of Tryphon, these naval elements continued to launch naval assaults on Syria and
Cilicia, ­apparently acting of their own volition. In a short time, a number of independent warlords (tyrannoi,
strategoi, ­archipiratae) carved out small domains for themselves, particularly along the remote mountainous
coast of western Cilicia. At first, their marauding activities were tolerated by other powers of the region –the
­Republic of Rhodes, the Attalid kings of Pergamum, the Ptolemies of Egypt and Cyprus, and Roman commercial elements active in the Aegean– since they not only directed the thrust of their assaults against Seleucid
assets, but they also benefited the slave-economy of the region by generating sales of kidnapped prisoners. Their
commerce became welcome at harbors such as Aegean Delos, Lycian Phaselis and Pamphylian Side. However,
the pirates soon grew increasingly indiscriminate and predatory in their selection of prizes. A sufficient quantity
of ­evidence indicates that non-Seleucid shipping likewise fell prey to their ambuscades.

findings.evidence_excerpt:
By 102 BCE, as Roman influence over the Mediterranean grew, the indiscriminate attacks of the Cilician
pirates outweighed the benefits of their trade. This provoked the Romans to act against them through a combined program of diplomatic pressure, legal prohibition and military force. These measures proved minimally
effective. The pirates survived the naval assault of the proconsul Marcus Antonius Orator, who apparently
­campaigned as far as Side, and soon gained new-found support from Rome’s greatest adversary in the region,
King Mithridates VI Eupator of Pontus. By aligning themselves with Mithridates at the outset of his war against
Rome (88–84 BCE), the pirates greatly enhanced their naval capacities and expanded their sway to new territories. For example, they participated in the king’s assaults on Delos, Rhodes and Lycia and harassed the Roman
proquaestor Lucius Licinius Lucullus, as he sailed from Crete to Egypt to recruit naval forces for his commander, Lucius Cornelius Sulla. Unwisely, Sulla resolved to leave these assaults unpunished. His pressing need
to return to Italy to defeat his internal adversaries compelled him to make an imperfect peace with Mithridates,
a peace that left the pirates not only unscathed, but in a better position than before.
Pirate realms now dominated the entire gulf of Pamphylia (Fig. 2). By 78 BCE, a pirate chief named Z
­ enicetes
appears to have carved out an independent territory for himself in eastern Lycia, centered in a castle that dominated the harbors of Olympus, Corycus and Phaselis. Further east, other pirate chiefs constructed impregnable
fortresses at Coracesium and the Cragus mountain allegedly equipped with well stocked harbors, warehouses,
ship sheds, skilled artisans and laborers chained to their stations. Cities along the Pamphylian coast appear to
have cooperated fully.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
From this point onward, the sources describe the pirate menace in highly sensational terms. According
to authors such as Strabo (14.3.3), Plutarch (Pomp. 24.4, 28.2), Appian (Mith. 14.93, 14.96) and Cassius Dio
(36.21.1), the pirates organized themselves into fleets that eventually wielded a combined armament of several
hundred warships and 30,000 combatants. Operating from more than a hundred fortresses, castles and hidden
coves, the pirates engaged in widespread depredations throughout the Mediterranean. Allegedly they stormed
more than four hundred cities and pillaged as many as twelve sanctuaries of the Greek world. They also roved
the western Mediterranean, aiding and abetting Sulla’s recalcitrant enemy, Quintus Sertorius, in Spain and marauding commerce in and around Sicily, Sardinia and Corsica. Cicero (Verr. 2.4.21) claims that the pirates
cruised an annual “pirate round” between Phaselis and Dianium, Sertorius’ base in Spain.
Cognizant of the seriousness of this threat, the Romans dispatched several promagistrates against them.
The most successful prior to Cnaeus Pompeius Magnus was unquestionably Publius Servilius Vatia Isauricus
(cos. 79 BCE), who during a three-year campaign stormed the pirate empire of Zenicetes and restored Roman
rule in Pamphylia (Ormerod 1922, 25–56). He then led his forces over the Taurus Mountains into the Isaurian
hinterland, to sack the stronghold of Isaura Vetus and to compel its twin fortress Isaura Nova into submission.
The reasons given for this overland campaign remain unsatisfying, particularly since Isauricus failed to assault
the pirate bases of Rough Cilicia, Coracesium and the Cragus. Nonetheless, the effectiveness of his campaign
and the prospect of further Roman incursions appears to have convinced the pirates to refocus their raids toward the western Mediterranean, hoping in this manner to draw Roman attention as far from their hideouts
as possible. As a component of this strategy, they established close diplomatic relations with Mithridates and
Sertorius, an arrangement culminating in the “Unholy Alliance” that converged on Rome from all points of the
Mediterranean in 75–74 BCE. Piratical assaults on Italy proper were highlighted by inland raids and scorched
earth campaigns in southern Italy, firings of fleets (military and commercial) in Ostia and Caieta, and by a series
of sensational kidnappings of Roman dignitaries and very important persons (Rauh 1997, 267).

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
Roman counter offensives remained desultory until 67 BCE, when the Roman popular assembly
c­ ommissioned a proven young general, Cnaeus Pompeius Magnus, with an extraordinary command to eradicate
the pirates once and for all. With some twenty-four legates, 270 ships and the authority to draw upon a potential
complement of 120,000 infantry, 4000 cavalry and 8000 talents of revenue, Pompeius swept the Mediterranean
from west to east in a three-month campaign, cornering the last holdouts in their bases in Cilicia and defeating
them, ultimately, in the waters off Coracesium (Broughton 1952, 146; de Souza 1999, 166–72). Through lenient
terms, Pompeius was able to persuade the majority of the pirates to surrender, and after dismantling the walls
of the dreaded pirate bases, he resettled his former adversaries as colonists in Cilicia Pedia and elsewhere (Plut.
Pomp. 28.1–4). With that, Mediterranean piracy subsided for at least a generation, or until Pompeius’ son,
Sextus Pompeius, renewed the pirate wars in his rivalry with the triumvirs, Antony, Octavian and Lepidus. But
that is another story. With Pompeius’ settlement of the Cilician pirates in 67 BCE, their menace largely subsided.
The above summary is compiled from ancient literary testimony, much of which tends to address the
­Cilician pirate menace with a considerable degree of hyperbole. It is worth noting, however, that surviving
public records likewise acknowledge the gravity of the pirate menace. For example, the SC de piratiis of 102
BCE, the preserved texts for which survived at Delphi and Knidos, records the Roman Senate’s decision to
declare the waters of Cilicia a provincia, that is a sphere of military influence where Roman forces intended
to engage the pirates, as well as the expectation that neighboring states would cooperate fully (Hassall et al.
1974; de Souza 1999, 108–15). Votive offerings, oracular responses and civic decrees recorded at Delos, Klaros,
Epidaurus and Megara similarly attest to the menace of piracy (IG IV.22 750; Sokolowski 1968; Rauh 2003,
64). The French excavations at Delos have demonstrated that this once affluent trading community underwent
irreversible decline through repeated pirate assaults, including a devastating raid in 69 BCE (Rauh 1993, 68).
Publius Servilius V
­ atia’s victory over the pirates is not only preserved in the Fasti Triumphales at Rome, but his
sack of Isaura Vetus is confirmed by the discovery of his ritual evocatio of the city’s patron deity, inscribed in
Latin on a block found in Bozkır, Turkey (Strabo 12.6.2; Hall 1973). Several sources, meanwhile, claim to quote
directly from preserved records of Pompeius’ triumph in 61 BCE. According to Pliny the Elder, in the “senatus
consultum” that officially sanctioned Pompeius’ triumph, the Senate proclaimed that he had “rescued the seacoast from pirates and restored to the Roman People the command of the sea” (HN 7.98, trans. H. Rackham,
Cambridge, Mass., 1942; cf. 37.6.12–13; Palmer 1990, 3). As stated by Plutarch, bronze tablets borne at the head
of Pompeius’ triumphal procession displayed a list of the adversaries he conquered, including “all the power of
the pirates by sea and land which had been overthrown” (Plut. Pomp. 45.1–3, trans. B. Perrin, Cambridge, Mass.,
1917; cf. Diod. Sic. 40.4.1; Vogel-Wiedemann 1985). Referring to the same tablets, Appian adds Pompeius’
claim to have captured some 800 warships with brazen beaks (Mith. 17.117). These records lend considerable
credence to the argument that the Roman hierarchy viewed the Cilician pirate threat and the events culminating
in its defeat as significant milestones.
The significance, the breadth and the scale of the pirate wars remains contradicted, nonetheless, by the
seeming absence of an archaeological footprint in Rough Cilicia. Participants in the Rough Cilicia ­Archaeological
Survey Project (RCSP), conducted between 1996 and 2011 in the region of the pirate bases of Coracesium and
the Cragus, have addressed this matter in several publications (e.g., Rauh 1997; 2003, 169–202; 2019, 45–50;
Rauh et al. 2000; 2013). As we will demonstrate below, the evidence for piracy in this region is meager and all
but indistinguishable from an otherwise nondescript pattern of Hellenistic settlement along this coast. Scholars
legitimately question the existence of pirate enclaves along this shore (de Souza 1999, 128–30, 136–41; 2013;
Tomaschitz 2013, 57–8). Philip de Souza (2013, esp. 46-53) challenges the categorization of indigenous navies
as pirates altogether, arguing that dominant maritime powers, such as Rhodes or Rome, were all too inclined
to brand as pirates any lesser polity that attempted to control its neighboring sea lanes. De Souza’s argument
has the advantage of associating the pirate enclaves on the coast with local populations, including those of
the Taurus interior. As we noted above, not only did Publius Servilius Isauricus extend his campaign to the
­Isaurian interior, but Plutarch and Appian recount that the “mountain Cilicians” (ὄρειοι Κίλικες) likewise opposed ­Pompeius, only to see their tyrants paraded in his triumph (Plut. Pomp. 45.2–4; App. Mith. 14.96; cf.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
Strabo 14.5.10). More recently, Rauh (2019, 49) has conceded that piracy of this magnitude could only have
occurred through collaboration between indigenous Cilician populations and renegade maritime elements. In
many respects, the Cilician pirate menace represented a Mediterranean-wide response to rising political instability provoked by the severity of Roman imperialism. Especially during the wars against Mithridates VI, the
harshness of Roman exactions and reprisals reportedly drove provincial elites into the fold of the pirates (Plut.
Pomp. 24.2; App. Mith. 14.92; Cass. Dio 36.20.2–4). In essence, disturbances catalyzed by Roman expansion
created both a power vacuum for piracy to thrive in and a recruiting ground for disaffected warriors, sailors,
profiteers and sympathizers.
These musings return us to the question of ancient historical hyperbole. Conceivably, the ancient sources
i­ nterpreted as a sustained menace something resembling a series of sporadic, geographically shifting outbreaks
of piracy over a seventy-year interval. We have attempted to argue, for example, that the original core region
of the Cilician pirate phenomenon was possibly Pamphylia and eastern Lycia (Rauh et al. 2000, 152). Several
sources draw attention to the fact that urban centers, like Phaselis, Attaleia, Side and Aspendos, openly colluded with pirates, such as Zenicetes, prior to their suppression by Publius Servilius Isauricus (CIL I2 2662;
Cic. Leg. agr. 1.5; Verr. 2.1.53). With the suppression of this Lycian-Pamphylian-Isaurian network in 75 BCE,
retreating pirate elements conceivably relocated eastward to bases at Coracesium and the Cragus. Christoph
Konrad (1994, 217) has proposed a similar pattern of relocation in the western Mediterranean, where, following
the ­demise of Quintus Sertorius in 72 BCE, renegade supporters coalesced at Sertorius’ pirate base in Dianium
before abandoning the Spanish peninsula altogether for Sicily. As Konrad notes, these holdouts would have
included warriors, merchants, pirates and citizens that were, for whatever reason, incapable of making peace
with Rome. As such, the pirate menace may have posed not so much a through line of violence, as it did an undulating series of crises, with contingents repeatedly coalescing, relocating, and recombining, only to reemerge
with renewed vigor. A better perspective requires, accordingly, a balance between what is recorded with what
seems geographically feasible, chronologically coherent, and archaeologically demonstrable. In this respect, our
summary highlights several issues that return us to the relationship between maritime topography and social
dissidence.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
SURVEY EVIDENCE IN WESTERN ROUGH CILICIA
What the evidence of the RCSP survey has revealed is that a Hellenistic horizon of ceramic remains is ­consistent
throughout the region, but the numbers are minimal in quantity and indicate a shallow pattern of small, d
­ ispersed
settlements. As the published context ceramics of the survey indicate (Autret et al. 2019), counts of H
­ ellenistic
ceramics in the survey region were limited (6%, or 339 out of some 5418 dated sherds). It is not so much their
numbers as it is their distribution that seems significant. Hellenistic ceramics were encountered in every region
that has been investigated, including the coastal sites and ridges investigated in 1996–1999, the Adanda Canyon
in the mesogeia investigated in 2000–2003 and the highland sites in the upper Bickici river basin investigated in
2003–2011. One highland site, Sugözü Yayla (RC 1102), seems particularly noteworthy, because it sits at 1600 m
elevation, overlooking the pass that connects the Bickici River on the coast to the southern branch of the Göksu
or Calycadnus River on the interior. Moreover, Hellenistic ceramics were encountered at every categorized
locus, regardless of scale, from the large urban sites such as Iotape and Selinus, to village scale settlements, to
isolated farmsteads, kiln sites and press complexes, to random rural survey units. As we have noted previously,
the presence of pre-Roman ceramics at Iotape and Antiochia ad Cragum (Fig. 3) seems particularly important,
because both communities were established in the mid-1st century CE by the Roman client king Antiochus
IV of Commagene. What the pre-Roman pottery indicates, therefore, is that local settlements preceded these
foundations, settlements that may possibly have served as pirate bases.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
Any attempt to contextualize these remains with the era of the pirates is easily frustrated, however, by the
limited value of the data itself. Take, for example, our occasional finds of Italian transport amphoras that date
precisely to the early 1st century BCE and were found in large quantities at the Roman trading community at
Delos, where the pirates supposedly fenced their stolen prisoners (Strabo 14.5.2; Rauh 2003, 60). The upper
portion of a Lamboglia 2 amphora from Italy was recovered by the RCSP dive team in the harbor of Antiochia
ad Cragum in 2003 and fragments of the same form were found at a fortified rural site in the Adanda Canyon,
Tomak Asarı (RC 0019; Rauh et al. 2009, 272–75; Fig. 3). These finds demonstrate that the two sites were occupied at the time of the Cilician pirates. However, the question remains whether or not this is sufficient in and of
itself to demonstrate the presence of pirates, particularly when it is offset by the rising numbers of Lamboglia 2
and other Italian forms of the Republican era that are emerging throughout the wider eastern Mediterranean,
including examples published at the nearby Alanya, Anamur and Taşucu Archaeological Museums (Sibella
2002, fig. 10; Şenol 2009, 216; Autret et al. 2021). These finds demonstrate that Italian amphoras were far more
widely distributed in the eastern Mediterranean that previously understood. It is fair to ask, therefore, whether
the presence of these forms indicates the transactions of pirates, or whether they are merely indicative of an
eastern Mediterranean distribution pattern for Roman trading commodities?
Turning to the evidence for economic activity, the pottery recovered at the Bickici kiln site indicate that
this site was utilized during the Hellenistic era. The Koan type amphora that was manufactured at this site
conceivably came into production in the 1st century BCE. The freshwater caves with rich clay deposits that
loom directly above the site, and timber brought down from the mountains via the river, undoubtedly attracted
artisans and passing maritime shippers at that time. In the same coastal plain the RCSP survey identified an extensive press complex at nearby Kale Tepe (RC 0201), a fortified village (RC 2201) and another nearby site (RC

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
9605), all of which yielded Hellenistic ceramics. In other words, a cluster of small Hellenistic sites were situated
at the mouths of two perennial rivers (the Delice and the Bickici) that descend precipitously from the Taurus
highlands, where additional sites, such as Kenetepe (RC 0304) and Sugözü Yayla (RC 1102), likewise yielded
Hellenistic remains. This will become important to the hinterland discussion that follows.
From an architectural standpoint, the evidence for Hellenistic settlement in Rough Cilicia is equally meager,
the one exception being the presence of numerous Hellenistic fortification systems. Fortifications exhibiting
unbonded courses of large limestone blocks (ashlar, polygonal, pseudo-isodomic) represent the earliest stone
monuments of any significance throughout the region. Surviving remains range from the impressive fortresses
at Hamaxia, Alanya (Coracesium), Meydancık Kale (Kiršu) and the Ovacık peninsula (Aphrodisias), to small
acropolis citadels at Selinus, Kahyalar (RC 2201), Anemurium and Kelenderis, to the isolated towers at Lamos
and Antiochia ad Cragum, and the roughly hewn vernacular defenses recorded at Iotape, Guda Tepe (RC 9712),
Güzelce Harman Tepe (RC 9716) and Tomak Asarı (RC 0019) (Rauh et al. 2013, 66–78; Kaye and Rauh 2020,
156–62). Memorializing as they do the scarred landscape of the Macedonian Wars of Succession, these defensive
remains mark the incipient phase of monumental architecture throughout Rough Cilicia. Livy (33.20.4–5) refers, for example, to the existence of “fortified places” (castella) at several coastal settlements that were seized by
Antiochus III in 197 BCE, including Aphrodisias, Anemurium, Selinus and Coracesium. As such, the remnant
fortifications at these sites predate the rise of Cilician piracy. Fortifications constructed with a “­ vernacular” masonry technique are more difficult to date and could be indicative of pirate activity, were it not for the possibility
that they were indigenous constructions. None of this eliminates the possibility, moreover, that pirate e­ lements
simply seized and utilized preexisting defenses as they infiltrated the region. From a practical standpoint, it
needs to be added that, apart from Alanya-Coracesium, none of these sites (including A
­ ntiochia ad Cragum;
Figs. 1 and 3) exhibit harbor remains or topographical features capable of accommodating large, decked warships; whereas, several of the sites could easily have accommodated smaller, open hulled pirate ships that were
more typically employed by pirates. In this respect, the emphasis placed on Coracesium as the center of the
pirate menace in 67 BCE grows in importance, as does our awareness of the capacity of the region to harbor
small clusters of pirate war craft along its intimidating coast.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
COVERT SPACES OF THE PIRATE BASES
Although the material evidence for the Cilician pirates may be scant, it can be contextualized to gain a firmer
understanding of the archaeology of piracy. By contemplating the affordances of the Cilicians, we can evaluate
the use of settlements during the “pirate period” and how they differ from other sites. Devised by the ecological
psychologist James J. Gibson (1977, 1979), affordance theory states that our perception to the world is not only
built on the physical characteristics of a space, but that a large amount of an actor’s perception derives from the
possibilities an actor can conceive for that space. In short, affordance is determined by an actor’s relation to the
environment as opposed to the environment alone. For example, a tree may have a high affordance for climbing
(climb-able) for a monkey, whereas it would have a low affordance for a dog. Or a knife may be “cut-with-able”
for a person, but impossible to use for a creature without fingers or thumbs. By identifying what is pirate-able, it
is possible to use geo-spatial analysis to reconsider the archaeological material in Rough Cilicia and understand
how pirates would have made use of the landscape at the time.
Much can be gleaned of the affordances of Cilician pirates, both from ancient history and maritime
e­ thnography. Appian (Mith. 14.92) mentions that Cilicians favored light swift craft, naming specifically the
myoparo and hemoilia (a one-half decked ship). To this list could logically be added the lembos, an older Illyrian
pirate vessel, which later became a mainstay of the Hellenistic navies the Cilicians would associate with. These
­navies would use lemboi for reconnaissance and small raids, which are operationally very similar to piracy. In
­
practical terms, it appears it was common for pirates of this era to lurk behind juts in the landscape, hidden

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
que landscapes. Cilicia, Crete and the Balearic Islands all
contain rocky jagged coastlines, ideal for hiding small fast ships.
Cilicia in particular had the ideal environment for piracy to prosper. The impoverished land was, c­ ompared
to the rest of Anatolia, devoid of natural resources apart from cedar timber ideal for ship building. In addition, recent studies by Gal et al. (2023, 424), which focus on modeling sailing mobility in antiquity, suggest
the straight between Cilicia and Cyprus was one of the most challenging sections of the Mediterranean to sail,
making it more likely that ships would be driven off course and into the hands of pirates. Plutarch states that
the main Cilician stronghold was Coracesium (Pomp. 28.1), whilst Appian suggests it was Cragus (Mith. 14.92).
They further say that pirates did not wholly contain themselves to the coastline. Plutarch mentions that during
Pompeius’ campaign the pirates placed their families and treasures in “strong citadels near the Taurus Mountains” (Pomp. 28.1, trans. B. Perrin, Cambridge, Mass., 1917). Similarly, Appian mentions Cilicia was a useful
region to the pirates because of its high mountains (Mith. 14.92). Wandsnider and Nelson’s (2015, 55–69) work
demonstrates how cities in Asia Minor signaled group identity through monumental architecture broadcast
throughout the landscape. This could be expanded to suggest that settlements communicated via signals to pass
messages from the coast up to the mountains, and vice versa.
This grants a blueprint of how pirates in Cilicia could have operated at this time. Small swift ships hiding in
inlets and behind promontories would attack unsuspected vessels struggling in difficult waters. Raiders were
likely aided by agents at inland sites observing passing ships and signaling to those on the coast. They would
therefore have required locations to harbor their ships, protect their goods and areas offering expansive views
to survey potential targets. Despite offering expansive views, the sites would still need to be hidden from the
sea. In this manner, signaling could occur undetected by passing sailors, otherwise alerting them to an attack.
Therefore, we have our required affordances for Cilician piracy. Just because Coracesium and the Cragus are
the only sites with sufficient harbors to store ships, does not automatically make them suitable for piracy. What
seems required are sites that simultaneously offer expansive views of the sea whilst also being hidden. The best
way of measuring this is through a form of visibility analysis known as covert spaces.
Covert spaces is a form of visibility analysis that not only maps invisibility, but also areas “that are hard to
see but afford expansive views” (covert spaces) and in particular areas that “see little but are overseen” (ambush
zones) (Gillings 2015, 5). This is doubly beneficial for piracy, as covert spaces would indicate the optimum
location for pirate settlements, whereas ambush zones would indicate areas where ships are most likely to be
attacked by pirates. A basic viewshed analysis works as a simple binary; you have a single point and a pixelized
map known as a raster. Viewshed analysis shows whether a pixel is visible from your stated point (1) or not
visible (0). Multiple points on the same map can be combined to show the most visible areas on that map. Here,
the scores of individual pixels in every viewshed are totaled and displayed on a new raster. The pixels most commonly visible have the highest scores, whilst the least visible have the lowest. Covert spaces analysis works by
creating two separate cumulative visibility rasters of the same region, one which shows how many views can be
seen from a given location, views-from (Vf ), and another which shows how many times a viewpoint was visible
from the surrounding landscape, views-to (Vt) (Gillings 2015, 3–5). Vf and Vt rasters are then normalized to
scale values, after which Vf are subtracted from Vt to create an index for covert sp

THE ISAURIAN CULTURAL HORIZON ABOVE GAZIPASHA
To understand the likely connection between the pirates of coastal Rough Cilicia and the unruly tribal e­ lements
of the Taurus interior, we need to contextualize the latter. Rauh has previously referred to the Taurus ridge
as an ancient “Green Line” that separated the semi-periphery of the Cilician coast from the periphery of the
­Isaurian hinterland (Rauh et al. 2009, 296, 299). In some respects, this serves as a useful line of demarcation. The
­hinterland was inhabited by dispersed populations of rural agro-pastoralists identified according to four tribal
entities: the Isaurians to the northwest (directly south of Konya), the Homonadenses to the southwest (bordering Pisidia and Lycaonia), the Lalasseis directly north of western Rough Cilicia and the Cennetae slightly
east (Fig. 5). The matter is confused somewhat by references to an additional tribal element known as the
Ceitae. However, this term appears to apply generally to highlanders throughout eastern Rough Cilicia, in the
same manner that Isaurians referred to those in the west (Hild and Hellenkemper 1990, 301; Casabonne 2004,
85; ­etymologically, Qedi, Kitti, Ketis, Ceitae). Two things need to be stressed at the outset: social organization
among these tribes was segmentary, lineage based and dominated by tribal chieftains, and their cultural heritage
was Luwian (Hopwood 1983; 1989; 1991; Shaw 1990; Lenski 1999a; 1999b; Casabonne 2004, 22–5; Grünewald
2004, 105, 119–23). One characteristic of segmentary societies is their tendency toward r­ ecombination over
time. By late antiquity, the inhabitants of the interior were known generally as Isaurians, which entitles us to
refer to them collectively as such. Each tribal element consisted of separate chiefdoms, which were o
­ ccasionally
galvanized by particularly powerful warlords into larger realms. These chieftains are referred to by several
terms, such as tyrannoi or basileis in Greek and dux in Latin (Strabo 14.5.10; App. Mith. 17.117; Tac. Ann.
12.55). Rarely are they named as individuals; more typically, they are bunched together as warlords. Pliny the
Elder (HN 5.94) comments that, in 52 CE, some 44 castella existed in the Isaurian hinterland, from which one

a likely descendant being Epyaxa, the wife of the Persian satrap Syennesis of Tarsus, in 401 BCE (Casabonne
2004, 148). Another dynasty, the Teucrid priest kings of Olba, dominated eastern Rough Cilicia as client kings
to the Seleucids, at one point claiming authority over the koinon of the Lalasseis and Cennetae (Syme 1986, 16;
Durugönül 1998, 85–9). However, according to Strabo, their ascendancy was overturned by unruly tyrants at
the time of the pirates (Strabo 14.5.10; Trampedach 1999). A pattern of violent competition among highland
warlords generally prevailed (Strabo 12.6.2; Syme 1939; 1986; Grünewald 2004, 119–23). On occasion, leadership was wrested from the hands of the hereditary elite by charismatic leaders who emerged from the impoverished herders of the highlands; for example, the 3rd century CE warlord Lydius, who “had been brought up in
the brigandage customary to his nation, and surrounding himself with a band of similar men, pillaged the whole
of Pamphylia and Lycia” (Zos. 1.69, trans. R.T. Ridley, Canberra, 1982).
In other words, even among the tribal elements, sharp cleavages existed between dynasts and renegades,
landowners and pastoralists, rich men and poor. These potential sources of conflict were offset by a collective
sense of cultural identity. This is demonstrated by the Luwian names of regional cults and deities, by the iconographic displays of funeral relief

LEAST COST PATH ANALYSIS
Least-cost-pathways (LCPs) are a useful means to analyze the evolving interconnection between the Cilician
coast and Isaurian highlands. This form of geographical analysis is designed to show the easiest route through
a given landscape. Relying on a list of 70 sites in Rough Cilicia and 16 in Isauria furnished by the RCSP (Rauh
and Pejša 2021a, 2021b), we employ an iterative model to reconstruct all potential routes from any given site
in Rough Cilicia to one in Isauria. To accurately simulate the cost of traveling, Tobler’s hiking function (THF)
was used. Devised in 1993 by avid hiker and geographer Waldo Tobler, it estimates walking velocity relative to
slope (Tobler 1993). The equation, as described by Goodchild (2020, 558), is as follows, v=6e-3.5|g+0.05|, “where v
is walking velocity in Km/h, and g is the gradient of the slope expressed as tangent of the slope angle and e the
constant 2.71818” (Goodchild 2020, 559).
If Isaurian warlords supported piracy as a seasonal activity, it would be worthwhile investigating the coastal
bases from which they could undertake these activities. Early Roman campaigns focused on regions west of
Cilicia. Marcus Antonius Orator’s much derided campaign involved him capturing Side in Pamphylia. Philip
de Souza (1999, 137–40) characterizes Servilius Vatia’s campaign against Lycian pirates as pacifying the pro-­
Mithridatic eastern Lycians to the benefit of the pro-Roman western Lycians. After the expulsion of anti-Lycian
League forces from the region, Vatia continued his campaign into Isaurian territory, suppressing the fortified
communities of Isaura Vetus and Isaura Nova. The fact that Vatia earned the agnomen Isauricus indicates that,
together with Lycia and Pamphylia, Isauria enjoyed an important place in the pirate hegemony. The suppression
of Pamphylia and Isauria may have quieted things for a while, as resistance coalesced to new centers of gravity.
In 67 BCE, the pirate bases at Coracesium and the Cragus were perceived as the largest pirate threat and across
the Taurus directly north of them resided neighboring tribes of the Ceitae, including the Lalasseis and the
­Cennetae. Still turbulent in 6, 36 and 52 CE, these elements were clearly unaffected by the suppression of Isauria
in the previous century (Syme 1934, 1986). To what degree were these the “mountain Cilicians” who opposed
Pompeius and who, according to Tacitus, “had already broken the peace on many occasions” (Ann. 12.55, trans.
J. Jackson, Cambridge. Mass., 1937)?
LCPs can be used to evaluate the links between the Isaurians based in Nova and Vetus and the coastal
r­ egions of Pamphylia. These LCPs show not only the shortest distance between the locations, but also the total
pathcost, or the difficulty of a given path. If warlords from these regions were dominating the coast, this analysis
would be useful for identifying the ideal naval centers for these groups, as well as suggesting how they may have
traveled to them. The major coastal centers in this region are Attaleia, Aspendos, Coracesium, Perga and Side.
Table 2 includes distance and pathcost between these coastal sites and Isaurian strongholds, while the map in
Figure 7 shows the LCPs between them.

LCPs suggest that the two coastal settlements closest to the Isaurian strongholds were Coracesium and Side.
Coracesium has the shortest route in terms of distance. However, the steep journey which skirts around some
of the higher parts of the Taurus, means the pathcost is high. The northeasterly journey from Side has a lower
pathcost and would have been more efficient. Both Coracesium and Side are mentioned as important centers for
early Cilician pirates. Coracesium’s value has already been discussed. As far as Side is concerned, according to
Strabo (14.3.2), pirates were permitted to trade in its harbor, giving them a convenient market center to fence
their goods. These two ports nearest to the Isaurian strongholds provided ideal centers to connect Isaurians
to the coast. This may explain why Marcus Antonius Orator captured Side and why Servilius Vatia used it as
a staging ground to assault Isaura Vetus. Initial Roman intelligence possibly indicated that an elimination of
the Isaurian hinterland threat would cause Cilician piracy to wither. Instead, it appears that a coalescence and
relocation of forces in the highlands led to a resurgence elsewhere.
Following the suppression of the Isaurians, tribal disturbances appear to have shifted to the region of the
Lalasseis, or more specifically to a cluster of settlements in the interior mesogeia near the modern Ermenek
reservoir along the southern branch of the Göksu (Calycadnus) River. In the Roman era, this area would
emerge as the seat of the Decapolis of the Lalasseis and the Cennetae. As the names of several settlements (e.g.,
­Germanicopolis, Domitiopolis, Eirenopolis, Titiopolis and Philadelphia) indicate, Roman veteran’s colonies
were installed throughout this region to secure the peace following decades of military intervention. Since the
Ermenek mesogeia emerged as a hotbed of resistance in the Early Roman period, for purposes of LCP analysis
we will utilize Germanicopolis as the symbolic location of the “mountain Cilicians” who opposed Pompeius
(Fig. 8).
From the settlements near Ermenek, the “mountain Cilicians” had excellent accesses to Rough Cilicia, being
uniquely situated at the confluence of the two major routes between the coast and highlands. One of these runs

CONCLUSION
If, as suggested, piracy in Cilicia was catalyzed by a diaspora of Hellenistic maritime actors into the region,
then connections between the Isaurian hinterlands and coastal Cilicia would have been mutually beneficial. As
already discussed, the Isaurians had a penchant for raiding. Where wealth is measured in terms of livestock,
rustling can become a prominent practice. This form of raid mentality lends itself well to a transition into
piracy. Mohamed Ingiriis (2013, 241) states his belief that the origins of contemporary Somali piracy transcend the more obvious explanations of poverty and illegal fishing that results from local political instability.
Instead, he posits that Somali piracy has its origin in camel rustling practices employed by Somali pastoralists.
In this way, Somali piracy was not simply a new phenomenon brought on by changing conditions, but instead
a long-standing Somali cultural tradition that pivoted to the seas. As maritime activity began to increase on the
Cilician coast, Isaurian pastoralists conceivably acquired additional means of employment alongside herding,
muleteering, timbering, mining and itinerant farm laboring. This complements Appian’s comment that “having
lost both livelihood and country by reason of the war and fallen into extreme destitution, [the pirates] harvested
the sea instead of the land” (Mith. 14.92, trans. H. White, New York, 1899), not to mention Plutarch’s comment
that the pirates drew their recruits from “men whose wealth gave them power, and those whose lineage was
illustrious” (Pomp. 24.2, trans. B. Perrin, Cambridge, Mass., 1917). Not only would sailors and merchants new
to the region have acquired local recruits and collaborators for their maritime ventures, but Cilicians and Isaurians would have benefitted from the process of settling sailors in opportune locations and furnishing them with
foodstuffs, supplies and the knowledge of local pathways.
At times when collaboration between pirates operating on the coast and Isaurian highlanders was great,
the shorter, less costly routes to the coast demonstrate an overlay of Hellenistic activity and Isaurian cultural
attributes. For example, a LCPs analysis would suggest that from the Ermenek mesogeia of the Lalasseis, the
easiest coastal region of Cilicia would have been the Bickici river basin from its headwaters at Sugözü Yayla
to its settlements, press complexes and kiln site on the shore. The hypothesis that Isaurians used this route to
exert control over Cilicia is supported by the fact that these routes pass by sites that existed at the time of the
pirates, were rich in Isaurian material culture and were ideal for surveying the wider region. Later, Roman settlements that remained hostile towards Isaurian tribes appear further removed and devoid of intersecting routes
with hinterland Isaurian settlements. What this discussion has demonstrated is that the combined historical
and ­archaeological evidence for the Cilician pirates conforms very well to empirical analyses of the chosen
­landscape.

findings.evidence_excerpt:
Piratical Ships of the Aegean
A Comparative and Diachronic Approach of the Ships Used by the Pirates of the
Aegean during the Classical and Hellenistic Period

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
ABSTRACT
The ship has always been the primary weapon and asset of every form of piracy. The ability of pirates to build, maintain
and man their ships would condition the success of any piratical endeavor, while the size and the type of these ships was,
in turn, determined by their owners’ needs and abilities. In the Aegean Sea, from the beginning of the history of piracy,
lighter and faster oared vessels were preferred, which were able to take advantage of their speed, as well as the r­ egion’s
geomorphology, moving swiftly between friendly and hostile coasts and islands, and offering the possibility of efficient
maneuvering and stealth. At the same time, their size was dependent on the ability of the piratical ­communities to support
their construction and manning. This paper explores the typology of the Classical and Hellenistic-era piratical ships in
the Aegean, as these are known through written sources and iconography, giving a comparative image of these ships and
connecting their use with practical issues, such as cost, manning and seaworthiness.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
INTRODUCTION
Piracy has been one of the main features of the maritime cultural landscape in the Aegean Sea already since
Prehistory, as iconography, textual evidence and verbal tradition has documented, and has remained one of the
most important (and quite troublesome for many) occupations of the locals until the 19th century (Ormerod
1924, 13–4; Krantonelli 1985, 1991, 1998). The ramifications of piratical activity were numerous (political, financial, social, symbolic), affecting nearly all aspects of life on the islands and coasts of the archipelago. Nevertheless, the practice of piracy required one essential tool and/or weapon, and that was the ship. The availability
of ships, their numbers, sizes, crews and seaworthiness dictated to a great extent the possibility of practicing
piracy in a successful way, as well as its impact on the communities that employed it (or suffered by it). It is
thus essential to have a clear view of the types of ships used by pirates throughout the ages, in order to fully
­understand and study the extent, form and impact of piracy both to perpetrators and victims.
This paper deals with the ships that were used by pirates in the Aegean Sea during the Classical and H
­ ellenistic
period based on written sources, which form the bulk of evidence concerning piracy for this period, but also on
iconography, archaeology, experimental archaeology and ethnographical parallels. The period under study was
very important in the history of the Aegean and the Mediterranean in general, witnessing the development of
great naval powers, such as Athens or Rome, as well as an increase and better organization of piracy, especially
towards the end of the period (Tarn 1930, 129–41; Morrison and Coates 1996, 1–93). This study seeks to give
