findings.evidence_excerpt:
a diachronic approach of the development of piratical ships and the practicalities related with their use, such
as their seaworthiness, fighting power and logistics. This is an aspect of piracy that has not yet been sufficiently
explored in such a manner.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
METHODOLOGY: POTENTIAL, PROBLEMS AND MAIN QUESTIONS
Piracy in the ancient world is a rather elusive subject of study (de Souza 1999, 2). The reason is simple: it was
predominantly (as has remained until today) an activity practiced in the margins of organized society and usually by small maritime communities, who had little interest or means in leaving proper documentation of their
activities. Piracy was, also, often interweaved with other, legal, activities, such as trade and warfare, r­ esulting in
the limits between the predatory/piratical economies and domination spaces or thalassocracies being obscure
and difficult to establish with precision in historiography (Bresson 2008, 214–19; for a discussion on the various
approaches on the issue, see Deramaix 2013, 359–87). Things become worse by the fact that the oared vessels
commonly employed for piratical activities in antiquity do not survive as shipwrecks in the region, due to their
light construction and lack of cargo to protect their wooden hulls (Wilson 2011, 33–9; Boetto 2012), and by the
fact that when galley images survive, there is no evidence to connect them to any piratical activity whatsoever.
And this is true also in the Aegean Sea, despite the richness in finds, both in the sea and on land, and iconography.
The only direct (to a certain degree) source of information concerning the ships used by the pirates of the
Classical and Hellenistic Aegean is, therefore, written evidence. The period studied here is, most probably, the
richest in terms of written documentation of nearly all aspects of contemporary life, with sources ranging from
historical texts to inscriptions and from poetry to graffiti. The methodology employed by this study is based
on the thorough examination of all written evidence available and their correlation with archaeological data,
iconography and historical parallels, in order not only to merely document the types of ships used by pirates,
but also to explore the practicalities and logistics of their employment and the ramifications these could have in
the practice of contemporary piracy. The basic questions this paper tries to answer concern the types of ships
used by pirates of the period studied, whether these were specially-built vessels or whether they were the same
as ships used in other types of maritime conflicts, whether these ships had a dual use for trade too, and, finally,
why did pirates choose specific types of vessels.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
THE EVIDENCE
The Classical period
Despite the establishment of strong state naval fleets, such as the famous Athenian one, during the Classical
­period, piracy remained a constant threat to ship traffic and coastal communities (Ormerod 1924, 108–9;
de Souza 1999, 43–96). The earliest references to piratical ships in the period come from two passages from
­Thucydides. In the first one, the historian describes how some Megarians, who conspired with the Athenians in
431 BCE, would pretend to be pirates, using a small boat or akation, which they carried on a cart in and out of
the city walls every night:
“Every night for a long time back, under pretense of marauding [ὡς λῃσταί], in order to have a
means of opening the gates, they had been used, with the consent of the officer in command, to carry
by night a sculling boat [ἀκάτιον ἀμφηρικὸν] upon a cart along the ditch to the sea, and so to sail
out” (Thuc. 4.67.3, trans. J.M. Dent, London and New York, 1910).

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
In the second passage, Thucydides describes the events in Sphakteria (425 BCE). He documents how
the Athenian general Demosthenes, preparing the defense of the islet, took weaponry “from a thirty-oared
[τριακοντόρου/triaconter] Messenian privateer [λῃστρικῆς] and a boat [κέλητος/keles] belonging to some
­Messenians who happened to have come to them” (Thuc. 4.9.1, trans. J.M. Dent, London and New York, 1910).
The use of triaconters as raiding and plundering ships is also attested by Polyaenus, who reports that around
378 BCE Iphicrates raided the coasts of Phoenicia with one hundred such ships with great success (Strat. 3.9.63).
Although the reference does not describe Iphicrates’ actions as piratical, the use of these ships for a successful
raid implies that it was ideal for piratical use too (Casson 1971, 125). Around 350 BCE, Aeschines refers to the
ship epaktrokeles as a proverbial pirate ship, in which men with great lust and desire board as pirates to seek
their fortune: “these it is that fill the robbers’ bands [τὰ λῃστήρια], that send men on board the pirates’ boats [τὸν
ἐπακτροκέλητα]” (Aeschin. In Tim. 191, trans. C.D. Adams, London and New York, 1919).
A new type of piratical ship, the hemiolia, which was a light galley that included a second file of oarsmen at
its center, appears in the 4th century BCE and a series of references in written sources underlines its importance.
It is first reported in the Etymologicum Magnum, at a reference roughly dated in the 4th century BCE, where
a Carian hemiolia, most likely belonging to pirates, is mentioned (450.38). Also, Arrian (Anab. 3.2.4) reports
that in 331 BCE Aristonikos, the tyrant of Methymna in Lesvos, sailed into the harbor of Chios with five pirate
hemioliai (ξὺν ἡμιολίαις λῃστρικαῖς πέντε) before being apprehended by Alexander’s troops and put to death
(Morrison and Coates 1996, 262).

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
The Hellenistic period
The conquest of the Aegean and Ionia by Alexander brought a short period of peace and safety in the seas,
which was, however, soon to finish, with the series of wars of the Successors, in which pirates took advantage
of the instability and were also employed by the rulers of the period as corsairs (de Souza 1999, 43–96). The
hemiolia continues to be firmly associated with piracy. Theophrastus, around 300 BCE, mentions the term as
the ­proverbial symbol of piratical threat, seen by cowards lurking behind each cape: “The coward, when he is at
sea, claims that p
­ romontories are pirate ships [ἡμιολίας] (Char. 25.2, trans. J. Diggle, Cambridge, Mass., 2004).
Even in the 2nd century CE, Longus reports Carian pirates raiding the coast with a hemiolia (Daphnis and Chloe
1.28.1). In the early 3rd century BCE, the Rhodians counteract the piratical hemiolia by developing an improved
and larger version of it, the trihemiolia, one of the most successful warships of the period (Casson 1971, 130–31;
Gabrielsen 2001, 224; Pacheco 2020, 101). The trihemiolia was heavier and faster than the hemiolia by being a
full bireme along its whole length, but with a third file of oarsmen added at its center and, interestingly enough,
is never cited as a vessel used by pirates, but solely by official state fleets.
About 200 BCE, another type of ship is reported as a pirate vessel. The lembos (λέμβος) is first mentioned
as the main vessel of the Liburnian pirates in the Adriatic, along with the later liburnae (Polyb. 2.9.1–2; Livy
45.30.12–15; see also Boršić et al. 2021), but is soon introduced in the Aegean too. In 197 BCE, Philip V sailed
to a parley at the Maliac Gulf in central Greece on a pristis (πρίστις, i.e., saw-fish), accompanied by five lemboi
(Polyb. 18.1.1). It is very likely that the lemboi and pristis (possibly a heavier version of the former) were
­similar to the liburna and were used for similar purposes, i.e., for piracy, raids etc. (Casson 1971, 25–6, 126–27;
­Morrison and Coates 1996, 263–64).
The last heyday of piracy in the Aegean during the Hellenistic period was the Mithridatic wars (88–63 BCE),
during which the region became the main theater of a series of conflicts, both on land and in the sea ­(Morrison
and Coates 1996, 115–19). Mithridates employed and supported the Cilician pirates, who thus became p
­ owerful
and numerous, greatly improving their military power and organization (App. Mith. 14.96; Ormerod 1924, 190–
247; de Souza 1999, 97–148). Initially, they employed relatively small ships, such as h
­ emioliai and m
­ yoparones,
but they soon managed to build or acquire larger vessels, such as biremes (δίκροτοι), triremes and even, for the
first time, heavier cataphract vessels (Plut. Pomp. 24.4–5). The final defeat of Mithridates and his allies and the

findings.evidence_excerpt: occupation of Cilicia by the Romans brought practically the end of Hellenistic piracy (de Souza 1999, 149–224).

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
DISCUSSION
Typology of the pirate ships
The Classical and Hellenistic period saw the creation and development of multitude of galley types, each with
different size, crew and purpose (Morrison 1995, 68–77; Morrison and Coates 1996, 255–78). As it has become
clear, however, from the presentation of the evidence, the ships used by the pirates belonged to relatively small
types, fitted best for their uses within piratical activities. In this section, each ship type is presented and discussed according to its size and size of crew, from the smallest to the largest one.
The akation (ἀκάτιον) and the lembos (λέμβος) appear to have been the smallest piratical ships used during
the period studied, since both terms mean boat or skiff in ancient Greek. The akation appears only once in
written sources in relation to piracy and in the peculiar circumstances of the Megarians using a skiff that can
be easily carried on a cart (see above), so it is very likely that it was not a term employed regularly for piratical
­vessels. It is also possible that the vessel was too small to accommodate any important attacking force to be
useful in piratical activities. Lembos, on the other hand, appears much more often as a piratical ship in written
sources. According to these references (as well as to others, which are not related to piracy), the term described various undecked small galleys with 16 to 50 oarsmen and was quite similar to the liburna, with which
it ­operated side-by-side in Hellenistic Illyria (Ormerod 1924, 29; Morrison and Coates 1996, 264; Boršić et al.
2021) and probably appears on the Illyrian coins of the 2nd century BCE (Höckman 1997, fig. 1.2–3, 5–6). It is
possible that the liburna was introduced in the Aegean by the so-called Tyrrhenian pirates, who had expanded
their operations there in the 2nd century BCE (Ormerod 1924, 127). A unique example of a lembos most likely
survives in Pisa (Boat C): the well-preserved vessel was a small undecked galley with six pairs of oars, a single
mast and a cutwater, that could have been used for various activities, such as espionage, raids or simply for
­ferrying passengers within harbors and estuaries (Bonino 2010; Olaberria et al. 2023).
The triakonter (τριακόντορος) was one of the simplest and lightest types of galleys employed in the Aegean
and known already from the Geometric period (Ormerod 1924, 29; Casson 1971, 44–5). It was a light, undecked
monoreme galley with 15 benches of oarsmen, arranged in single files on the sides of the ship. It was most
­probably equipped, like almost all oared vessels of the period, with a cutwater at the bow. It is unknown whether
such a small vessel could also employ a ram in battle, being probably too light to withstand the tensions created
by ramming. It had limited space both for provisions or loot, as well as for extra marines and, as described by
Polyaenus for Iphicrates’ raid in Phoenicia (see above), oarsmen doubled as fighters. Thanks to its small size and
corresponding draft, a triakonter was not only swift, but it could also approach shallow waters and estuaries and
be hauled on beaches and required a smaller crew. There are no known depictions of this type of ship during
the period studied.
The myoparo (μυοπάρων), which means mouse in ancient Greek, is known as one of the ships used by the
Cilician pirates in the early 1st century BCE, but little is known about its size and form. A unique image of it
survives in the 3rd-century CE ship mosaic of Althiburus in Tunisia, where a series of ships are depicted, along
with their names (Gauckler 1905, 134–35, fig. 16; Duval 1949; Redaelli 2014). It appears to have been similar
to the lembos described above: a small, undecked oared vessel (Ormerod 1924, 30; Casson 1971, 132, fig. 137).
As its name suggests (κέλης, i.e., racehorse), the keles (celes in Latin) and its diminutives (κελήτιον) or
­variations (ἐπακτροκέλης) were swift oared ships, ideal for piratical use. Very little is known about this ship,
which appears in the Althiburus mosaic as a small, simple galley. It was most likely very similar to the lembos
and the myoparo, whereas the epaktrokeles must have been a larger version of it (Ormerod 1924, 30; Casson
1971, 161–62, fig. 137).
Probably the pirates’ favorite ship, the hemiolia (ἡμιολία) was a two-banked, undecked variation of a

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
t­ riakonter or a pentekonter (Ormerod 1924, 29; Coates 1995, 139–40; Morrison 1995, 73–4; Morrison and
Coates 1996, 317–18, fig. 73). It had 30 to 50 oarsmen arranged in two superimposed files but, in contrast to
larger vessels such as biremes or triremes, the second file could only be accommodated in the wider central
part of the hull (hence the name that means one-and-a-half). It has also been suggested that a hemiolia had a
slenderer hull compared to the similar liburna, because it used a rowing outrigger (apostis), which allowed more
efficient rowing, without widening the hull itself (Morrison and Coates 1996, 317–18). Thanks to its low lengthto-beam ratio, it was an easily maneuverable ship, especially when compared to the much slimmer triremes or
heavier galleys, and could accommodate marines, whereas a light deck protected the rowing crew. It is estimated
it could reach a speed of 7½ knots, less than a trihemiolia or a trireme but more than a liburna (Morrison and
Coates 1996, Appendix D). It is possible that the hemiolia was developed as a pirate ship in Caria, since it is
related by written sources with Carian pirates (Morrison 1995, 73).
The bireme, the trireme and the cataphract appear only once in relation to piratical fleets, and that is in the
fleets of the Cilician pirates that allied with Mithridates in the early 1st century BCE. All three types were widely
employed by contemporary and earlier naval fleets, and they were relatively heavy vessels, with crews of 100
to 200 people, whereas the cataphracts were even heavier (usually tetreres’/fours or penteres’/fives; Casson 1971,
123, n. 94), with closed superstructures in order to protect their rowing crews (Morrison and Coates 1996,
255–57). Nevertheless, these cannot be considered common pirate ships, since they only appear within this historical framework, when the Cilician pirate cities developed, thanks to the wealth accumulated through raiding
and the support by Mithridates, proper naval fleet.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
Evolution of the pirate ships
According to the written sources discussed above, in the Classical and Hellenistic Aegean there seems to have
been an evolution from simpler and lighter to more elaborate and heavier piratical ships. The earliest ships employed in piracy were the small triakonters and keletes, which were relatively small vessels. The operation of great
naval fleets during the 5th and the early 4th centuries BCE in the Aegean most likely prevented pirates from
building, capturing or buying larger ships and limited them to the simplest galleys they could afford, which also
fitted their purposes better. The rising of piracy within the endemic warfare of the Successors after Alexander
boosted the size of piratical ships and that is when the hemiolia appeared, a larger and heavier ship, which was
no match for the much larger Hellenistic galleys in terms of fighting power, but was much faster and easier to
handle and hide. Smaller vessels, such as myoparones and lemboi, continued to be used, although the hemiolia
became the “trademark” of the pirates of the period. Finally, as Cilician piracy reached its peak –with the organization of a proper “pirate state”, the acquisition of enough resources, but also the need to deploy stronger vessels
to fight the naval fleets of the Romans– we witness a surge both in the number and in the size of vessels employed, and for the first time triremes and cataphracts appear (Morrison 1995, 73; Morrison and Coates 1996,
115–19). This period, however, is unique in the history of ancient piracy and most probably no ship heavier
than a hemiolia was ever properly used for any piratical operations in the area during the ­Graeco-Roman antiquity. It is not surprising that also in much more recent periods, like the 16th–19th centuries, ships of similar
dimensions, such as the fusta, the galliota, the felouka or the mistico, were used in the Aegean by the local pirates
(Ormerod 1924, 26–8; Krantonelli 1985, 341–49; 1991, 425; 1998, 286–88).

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
Fighting techniques and employment
There is little to no evidence in written sources about the techniques used by the piratical vessels during the
­period studied and ancient authors hardly ever describe how pirates employed their vessels in battle. Pirate
ships always belong to oared types, as would be naturally expected, since the ability to move without the help
of wind and to achieve great speed was an essential part of ambushing, raiding and evading pursuing ships.
­Ramming could have also been employed in battle, but it is quite likely that this would have been possible only
by relatively large and sturdier vessels, such as hemioliai or triremes (Coates 1995, 133–34). It should also be

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
noted that capturing an enemy ship would be much more profitable for pirates, who could reuse it or sell it.
There is no reference to the existence of marines (ἐπιβάται) on pirate vessels. In smaller vessels, where there was
also little space for extra troops, the rowing crew could easily double as marines too, but larger ones should have
had a number of marines (hoplites, archers etc.) onboard in order to tackle enemy ships in sea battles, as well as
hostile forces on land. A useful weapon would have also been catapults, which were a common feature of Hellenistic warships, but there is no reference to their use by pirates. The large piratical fleets of the Cilician pirates
were, most likely, organized in the models of other contemporary naval powers, with larger vessels manned by
large numbers of well-armed and trained marines, were equipped with rams and catapults, and were employed
like every other proper naval fleet of the period, particularly when joining forces with rulers like Mithridates,
but there is no direct information about how these fleets were organized and used.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
LOGISTICS OF THE PIRATE SHIPS
A vital element of the operation of piratical fleets or single vessels that often eludes the attention of scholars is the
logistics related with it. Every ship requires certain resources to be constructed, equipped, manned, provisioned
and maintained, especially the oared vessels, which not only needed much larger crews (oarsmen, ­marines
etc.), but also constant maintenance, in order to remain in fighting condition (Coates 1995, 132; Dotson 1995,
217). The ability of a community or state to maintain a fleet (or in the cases of small islands even a single ship)
depended on the availability of resources, monetary or not.
A major issue must have been the provisioning of timber, which was often scarce in the arid Aegean islands
and would have had to be imported or ships to be constructed in areas, where there were natural forests, such
as the coasts of Asia Minor (Morrison and Coates 1996, 354). Although these practices were common in the
naval fleets of the period (e.g., the Athenians would construct triremes in Macedonia; Borza 1987, 39), it is
doubtful whether pirates had the abilities to fund such endeavors, keeping in mind that local timber would also
have to be used for the rest of the regional fleets, consisting of merchant ships, ferries or fishing boats. It is not
surprising that the largest piratical fleets were the ones employed by the Cilicians, who had direct access to an
extended mountainous hinterland that would easily provide material for galley building.
The same logistic problems would have existed for the rest of the shipbuilding material. Metal was employed
for the nails (bronze or copper), although the extent of their use in galley hulls remains unknown (Coates 1995,
131), as well as for anchors (iron, lead or bronze; Kapitän 1984, 36–43; Votruba 2014, 78) and possibly for
seathing (lead; Kahanov and Ashkenazi 2011). Rigging equipment (ropes, sails, pulleys etc.) was also essential
for navigation, since all ancient galleys would regularly hoist sails and avoid rowing when wind was favorable
(Casson 1971, 229–38; Dotson 1995, 220). Finally, special protective primers or other types of paint were important to protect the wooden hull from rotting and from shipworms, but also to decorate them (Galinier and
Nantet 2020, 60–8), whereas in one case it is reported by Philostratus that scout and pirate ships would be
painted blue for camouflage (Imag. 1.19; cf. Casson 1971, 212, n. 48).
The light, undecked galleys of the period, required regular maintenance, especially during the winter months,
to remain seaworthy, as well as specialized personnel to undertake such tasks. It is thus not surprising that pirates preferred relatively small ships, which were easier to build and maintain. Piratical communities, being,
most probably, small and functioning in the margins of society and in remote and poor regions like some of
the small Aegean islands or Cilicia, were unable and unwilling to maintain proper galley fleets (Ormerod 1924,
14–5, 142–43). Furthermore, for communities, where piracy was a “part-time” occupation of poor farmers or
mariners who had turned to it out of necessity, as Aristotle describes (Pol. 1256b; Gabrielsen 2013, 141; Pacheco
2020, 99), the maintenance of oared vessels was an extra burden, since, due to their lack of space that could be
used to transport cargos, these ships could have no dual use as warships and merchantmen and any income
supplied by them would be strictly related to warfare, raids or piracy (merchant galleys were not ­unknown, but
they are not reported in relation to any piratical activity; Casson 1995, 117–23).
The maintenance of galleys in the ancient world was also commonly related to the construction and o
­ peration

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
of shipsheds and slipways, where galleys were hauled and maintained usually during the winter months (on the
ancient shipsheds, see Blackman and Rankov 2013). There have been many simple, single slipways carved on
the shores of various small Aegean islands or of the mainland, which could have been used by pirate communities to shelter and/or hide their vessels (their size corresponds not to triremes or larger vessels, but to smaller
ships such as the ones employed by pirates; Baika 2013, 248–49) and allow for a swift launching when prey was
in sight. Nevertheless, there has been no firm evidence connecting any of these naval installations with piracy
and these could as well have been outpost for squadrons of small, swift coastguard vessels (φυλακίδες νῆες or
navis speculatoria) that are known to have operated along the coasts in antiquity.
Another important issue related with the logistics of piratical ships was provisioning. A hemiolia, with a
crew of 50 oarsmen, plus five other crewmembers, would require considerable daily provisions of water and
food to be able to operate. Each oarsman would consume 2.1 to 6.6 liters of water per day (­ depending on the
temperature and the amount of rowing involved) and 4,000 to 5,000 kilocalories (Dotson 1995, 219–20). It is
doubtful that such a vessel could carry water for more than a couple of days in the sea due to the limited hold
underneath the rowing benches, and thus would require regular stops for provisioning. ­Furthermore, it would
not spend nights in the open sea, seeking instead shelter in protected bays and beaches (Tarn 1930, 124; Casson
1971, 89–90). Piratical ships, therefore, had a rather limited operational radius, unless they were supported by
allies or managed to control their illegal activities and act as regular vessels.
One final, logistical and human resource deficiency of piratical fleets was their manning. Not only they
required an experienced and trained rowing crew, which would also double as fighters, but it was a task that
had to be undertaken by the fittest members of the community and, at the same time, was a rather dangerous
occupation. The loss of a piratical galley at sea would mean the loss of many of the youngest and most dynamic
members of the community. Taking into consideration that the coastal communities of the Aegean (at least the
ones from the smaller islands and coastal settlements that were most likely to harbor piracy) were relatively
small (Reger 1994, 51–5), the operation of piratical ships would have been an activity done with great caution
and care, especially towards the precious tools of piracy, i.e., the ships.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
CONCLUSIONS
This brief examination of the sources concerning piracy in the Classical and Hellenistic Aegean shows that
the ­pirates of these periods tended to use small, light and swift ships for their endeavors. Their favorite ships
appear to have been the triakonter and the hemiolia, which they preferred for their small size, speed and
­maneuverability. Smaller ships, such as the lembos or the keles, were also employed. Larger units, such as triremes or cataphracts, were only used in the occasion of the heyday of Cilician piracy in the early 1st century
BCE, when pirates expanded their sphere of operations, along with their resources and funding, but this was a
unique event. The choice of smaller vessels was not only due to their qualities concerning speed, small draft and
stealthiness (Ormerod 1924, 26–8), but was also imposed by the nature of piracy, which operated in the fringes
of society and states of the period, and considered relatively small communities of limited means, for which
ships were precious as tools and weapons but also difficult to obtain, man and maintain. Finally, there seems to
have been no type of vessel specially designed and built for or by pirates, who would adopt and use the vessels
most ­suitable for their activities and deploy them in accordance with their needs.

­ entions that
the Corinthians with their fleet cleared up piracy and thus their city gained large profit as a hub of land and
sea trade, becoming very powerful. However, depictions of ships in Corinthian vases are very few and appear
mainly in some black-figure pinakes from Penteskoufia (Fig. 2) dedicated to Poseidon (Morrison and Williams
1968, 87–9; Basch 1987, 234–9; Palmieri 2009; Hasaki and Nakas 2017), at a time when the production of
­pictorial pottery at Corinth was beginning to gradually decline under the predominance of Attic painted vases.
Herodotus mentions a lot about the naval power of Samos during the tyranny of Polycrates, and Thucydides
reports that the Ionians followed the development of the navy during the reigns of Cyrus and Cambyses (Hdt.
3.39.3–4, 3.122.2; Thuc. 1.14.2 on Polycrates and Phocaeans who defeated Carthaginians in a naval battle). He
further narrates that, only shortly before the expansion of the Persians, the Sicilian tyrants and the Korkyraeans
acquired triremes (τριήρεις) in large numbers; these were the most powerful fleets in Greece before Xerxes’
campaign (Thuc. 1.14.3). The Aeginetans and the Athenians, and perhaps some other cities-states, had small
fleets, and most of their ships were equipped with fifty oars. Only later, when the Athenians clashed with the

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
The best-known representation with a pirate warship (ἡμιόλια; Casson 1958) and a merchant ship (στρογγύλη
ναῦς, ὁλκάς; Morrison 1980, 51–8) is found on a late black-figure cup (London, British Museum B 436: BAPD
479). It is worth mentioning some interesting details, such as the fact that the sail of one ship is spread out and
the other is furled (Fig. 6), and that the warship has two rows of oars with different number of rowers on one
side and four sailors engaged in unfurling the sail (Basch 1987, 222–24). Also, visible under one handle is the
forward half of another ship with an eye depicted on the bow.
Mythological scenes with ships (Fig. 7), and perhaps a few of daily life, do not appear often on Attic vases
until the late 6th century BCE (Neckamphora, Mannheim, Reiss-Engelhorn Museum CG 343: BAPD 11; Neckamphora Daybreak Painter, London, British Museum B 240: BAPD 5; Oinochoe Keyside Class, London, British
Museum B 508: BAPD 303254), except for the three earlier ones from before the mid-6th century BCE, which
I mentioned above. Another interesting case is the depiction of the prow as shield device (ἐπίσημα) on hoplite
shields, one of the many iconographic motifs chosen for the decoration of round shields on vases.
In Attic vase-painting of the 5th century BCE, scenes from the world of the sea are few and far between.
A few marine creatures are depicted as secondary elements, mainly dolphins and fish (more rarely Tritons,
seahorses), designating the seascape, occasionally accompanied by chariots of astral deities flying over the sea
(BAPD 223, 13479, 206531, 212985, 213417, 213469, 361416, 43179). On red-figure vases, depictions of ships
are very rare and limited to certain mythological scenes. In these cases, usually only the bow or stern of the ship
is depicted as “part taken for the whole” (pars pro toto). The only known representation of a whole ship is on a
Late Archaic red-figure stamnos of the Siren Painter with Odysseus and the Sirens, where the sea is indicated as
a uniform mass with diluted paint (Fig. 8; London, British Museum E 440: BAPD 202628). The same rendering
of the sea is found on the other side, as three Erotes fly over it.
On some red-figure vases the aphlaston is depicted in the hands of Athena or Nike and then it is obvious
that the maritime power and the naval victories of the city are implied. Indeed, all relevant representations
date to the second quarter of the 5th century BCE, in the aftermath of the Persian Wars (Miller 1997, 33,
39). The presence of statuary types of these two deities holding the aphlaston –sometimes also a mast and a
yardarm or Nike on a ship’s prow (Fig. 9)– on late red-figure vases (bell krater Nikias Painter: BAPD 217479)
and late ­Panathenaic ­amphoras (Williams 2007, 148–49; e.g., BAPD 303133, 303151, 303155, 303156, 303159,
303162, 303166, 303167, 9033910) indicates their association in the collective memory with successes at sea
(e.g., against the pirates in the Aegean in the years of Lycurgus’ tenure, 338–326 BCE) that were the hallmark of
Athenian state policy.

Tyrrhenian Pirates and Dionysus
The Iconography of an Ancient Story of Piracy

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
ABSTRACT
The present study examines, through selected monuments from the Archaic to the Roman era, the iconography of the
myth of the abduction of Dionysus by Tyrrhenian pirates. The Homeric Hymn to Dionysus refers to the abduction of
the god by the pirates and their punishment for this lawless act because they tried by force to keep him as their captive.
Tyrrhenian pirates, identified by modern researchers with the Etruscans who lived in Italy or the inhabitants of Lemnos,
considered him the son of a king and captured him to demand a ransom from his parents. Through a series of miracles
based on symbols of his religion, Dionysus completed the circle of his revenge by transforming the impious pirates into
dolphins. The story of the Tyrrhenian pirates allowed Greek and Roman writers and artists to present their version of
this episode. The pirate ship at sea and its crew play a central role in the pictorial renderings of the subject. By studying
this mythological episode, the plausible elements and historical ramifications are sought in relation to the phenomenon
of piracy, as it exerted a timeless effect on ancient art and religion, each time allowing imagination and faith to provide
distinct approaches to oral or visual narratives.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
INTRODUCTION
The Mediterranean Sea was the first broad geographic area, where piracy took on the features of a mass
­phenomenon. As a means to acquiring material wealth and slaves, it was utilized by almost all the peoples
that settled on its shores during antiquity: the Sea Peoples, the Tyrrhenian marauders, but also the Greeks,
who, along with classical civilization, produced some of the most fearsome pirates in the known world. An
­interesting composition of reality and fiction may be observed in the myth of Dionysus and the Tyrrhenian
pirates, which is commonly found both in ancient literature and in the pictorial arts.
The story of Dionysus is full of journeys and peregrinations to spread his cult, and cruel treatment meted
out in irrational fury to those who opposed it, as was the case with Lycurgus, king of Thrace, Pentheus, king
of Thebes, as well as the Tyrrhenian pirates. Notwithstanding the diversity of the modern theories governing
research into myths, there is often a historical reality that triggers each myth, however abstract and fanciful its
plot may be. Therefore, it is often possible to look for chronological limits and geographical boundaries within
the evolution of the myth.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
THE TYRRHENIANS: THE ETHNIC NAME AND THEIR PLACE
The name Tyrrhenian Sea is attributed to that part of the Mediterranean, which is off the southwestern coast of
Italy and all the way to Corsica, Sardinia, and Sicily. The ethnic name Tyrrhenoi (Tyrrhenians) was used by the
ancient Greeks to denote non-Greeks in general and pirate people in particular (LIMC 8:154–5, s.v. Tyrsenoi).
In ancient written sources, the term “Tyrrhenian” is found for the first time in the end of Hesiod’s Theogony:
And Circe the daughter of Helius, Hyperion’s son, loved steadfast Odysseus and bore Agrius and Latinus
who was faultless and strong: also she brought forth Telegonus by the will of golden Aphrodite. And they
ruled over the famous Tyrsenians, very far off in a recess of the holy islands (Hes. Theog. 1011–1016,
trans. H.G. Evely-White, Cambridge, Mass., 1914).

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
PRESENCE OF THE TYRRHENIANS IN THE AEGEAN
According to the Homeric Hymn to Dionysus, which is discussed in more detail below, Tyrrhenians pirates
wanted to take Dionysus away from the Greek world and sell him to barbarians who lived either in the west or
northwest (Hyperboreans), the south (Egypt) or the east (Cyprus). In Euripides’ Cyclops (10–22), Sicily is mentioned as the area of operations of these marauders from Tyrrhenia (γένος Τυρσηνικὸν / λῃστῶν). The presence
of Tyrrhenians in the Aegean is also attested to by several written sources. Thucydides (4.109.4) reports that
in the old days the Tyrrhenians lived in both Athens and Lemnos. Myrsilus of Methymna, a 3rd-century BCE
author, states that the Tyrrhenians were originally from Italy, but they had migrated to the Aegean region, and
ever since that time they became known as Pelasgians (FGrHist 477 F8–9). In the 1st century CE, Dionysius
Halicarnassensis (Ant. Rom. 1.28.1–4) claimed that the Tyrrhenians were not of Pelasgian origin, but lived in
Italy instead (Kobakhidze 2008, 74–7).
The island of Lemnos has become the focus of numerous debates and arguments ever since the discovery
of the famous inscribed stele of Kaminia in 1884, which depicts a warrior holding a spear. The stele has two
long texts incised on the front face (around the figure of the warrior) and on one of its narrower sides, written
in Greek letters but in a non-Greek language, most probably closely related to Etruscan (Lehr 1942–1945;
Di ­Cesare 2024). Herodotus considered the inhabitants of Lemnos to be Pelasgians (e.g., 4.415.2–5, 5.26.1).
The same author informs us that the Pelasgians of Mountain Hymettos, who, driven away by the Achaeans,
­settled on Lemnos, other islands of the Aegean and the shores of Asia Minor (Hdt. 6.136.2–140.2), were called
­Tyrrhenians (Hdt. 1.57.1–3).
The Tyrrhenians of Lemnos, who were directly related to the Pelasgian Tyrrhenians, must have migrated to
the north Aegean region at the beginning of the 1st millennium BCE (De Simone 1996, 39–84). They rapidly
evolved into a great maritime power and are rightly credited with being the first to use the naval ram. Sources
after the 5th century BCE refer to the inhabitants of Lemnos as “Tyrrhenians”. Numerous pieces of evidence,

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
combined with Thucydides’ testimony, lead to the plausible conclusion that the Tyrrhenians mentioned in the
Homeric Hymn may also include the inhabitants of Lemnos (see Greco 2010, 3–180). One cannot, however,
ignore the reputation of the Tyrrhenians of the west, i.e., the Etruscans, as pirates (Sassatelli 2004). It is not
improbable that Etruscan merchants had settled on Lemnos and occasionally engaged in piracy. From the 5th
­century BCE onwards, Lemnos was considered to be a possession of Athens; this might explain the Athenian interest in the myth of the transformation of the Tyrrhenian marauders and, possibly, hint at its Attic ­provenance
(Chudziński 1886, 9).

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
TYRRHENIAN PIRACY
Despite the great civilization of the Tyrrhenians, the ancient Greek written sources refer mainly to their intense
pirate activity (e.g., IG II2 1629, line 223; IG XI.2 148, line 73; Syll.3 1225, line 8; Diod. Sic. 15.14.3; Strabo 5.2.2,
10.4.9; Aristid. Or. 44.570). One of the better-known Tyrrhenian pirates was Postumius, who went raiding at
the head of a flotilla of twelve pirate ships in the 4th century BCE and was captured in Sicily. Timoleon, the
­Corinthian general and politician who was sent to Sicily to rid the local Greeks of tyrants and Carthaginians,
executed Postumius, whose raids had been playing havoc with the local sea lanes of communication:
Timoleon himself seized and put to death Postumius the Etruscan, who had been raiding sea traffic
with twelve corsairs, and had put in at Syracuse as a friendly city (Diod. Sic. 16.82.3, trans. C.H.
­Oldfather, Cambridge, Mass., 1954).

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
However, the Tyrrhenian pirates are mainly associated with the well-known myth of Dionysus, both in ancient
written sources and in the arts (e.g., James 1975; Paleothodoros 2012).

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
ΤHE MYTH OF DIONYSUS AND THE TYRRHENIAN PIRATES IN THE
­A NCIENT WRITTEN SOURCES
The myth of the abduction of Dionysus by the Tyrrhenian pirates is mainly known from three ancient written
sources: the Homeric Hymn to Dionysus, the Metamorphoses of Ovid (3.564–691) and the Dionysiaca of Nonnus
(31.86–91, 44.231–252, 45.105–168). Brief references to the myth may also be found in Euripides (Cyc. 10–22),
Apollodorus (Bibl. 3.5.3), Hyginus (Fab. 134), Seneca (Οed. 449–466) and Philostratus the Elder (Imag. 1.19).
Oppian also mentions the transformation of men into dolphins by Dionysus (Halieutica 1.650).
The earliest hint of the Dionysiac myth with the Tyrrhenian pirates may be traced to the Late Archaic period. The first reference to the appearance of the Tyrrhenian pirates is in the seventh dithyramb of the Homeric
Hymns, which is dedicated to Dionysus, probably dating from the late 6th or early 5th century BCE:
Presently there came swiftly over the sparkling sea Tyrsenian pirates on a well-decked ship — a m
­ iserable
doom led them on. When they saw him, they made signs to one another and sprang out quickly, and
seizing him straightway, put him on board their ship exultingly (Hymn. Hom. Bacch. 6–10, trans. H.G.
Evely-White, Cambridge, Mass., 1914).

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
According to Apollodorus, mythographer of the 2nd century BCE, when Dionysus decided to sail from
Ikaria to Naxos, with the aim of initiating the local inhabitants into his cult, he chartered a Tyrrhenian pirate
ship (Τυρρηνῶν λῃστρικὴν τριήρη) to ferry him to the island (Apollod. Bibl. 3.5.3). The Tyrrhenians accepted,
but their ulterior motive was to sell him into slavery in Asia (Romizzi 2003, 352 n. 1; Emilio-Ioannidou 2017,

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
140). When Dionysus became aware of the plot, he transformed their oars into serpents, filled the ship with ivy,
immobilized it in its wreaths, and made invisible flutes sound. The pirates lost their minds and dove into the sea,
where they were transformed into dolphins:
And wishing to be ferried across from Ikaria to Naxos he hired a pirate ship of Tyrrhenians. But when
they had put him on board, they sailed past Naxos and made for Asia, intending to sell him. Howbeit,
he turned the mast and oars into snakes, and filled the vessel with ivy and the sound of flutes. And the
pirates went mad, and leaped into the sea, and were turned into dolphins (Apollod. Bibl. 3.5.3, trans.
J.G. Frazer, Cambridge, Mass., 1921).

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
ΤHE MYTH OF DIONYSUS AND THE TYRRHENIAN PIRATES IN THE
­A NCIENT ARTS
The most significant depiction of the myth of the Tyrrhenian pirates in south Italian vase-painting appears on
a Late Archaic black-figure Etruscan kalpis, formerly in the Toledo Museum of Art, Ohio (inv. no. 82.134) and
now repatriated to Italy (Fig. 1). It is attributed to The Painter of Vatican 238, a follower of the Μicali Painter

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
(Rassmusen and Spivey 1986, 2–8). The main subject is painted on the body: six pirates are transformed into
dolphins as they dive into the sea, which is rendered with a running counterclockwise spiral. The figure on the
left is human from the waist up, while its lower part is a dolphin’s tail. All other figures of pirates in the process of
transformation have human legs and the torso of a dolphin. This detail may be interpreted more as the depiction
of two different types of metamorphosis, one beginning at the legs, the other at the head. The figure at the far
right has its legs bent and overlapping with those of the figure to its left. All other figures have their human legs
bent at various angles, which, as modern researchers have correctly observed, may be taken as an attempt on
the part of the vase-painter to portray different snapshots of the pirates falling into the sea. An ivy stem is visible
along the left edge of the panel, possibly an indication of the presence of Dionysus. In any event, this kalpis is
the earliest illustration of the myth in Italy depicting the transformation of the Tyrrhenian pirates into dolphins
(Paleothodoros 2012, 459–60).
The myth of the Tyrrhenian pirates, as described in the Homeric Hymn, has been associated by modern
research with the scene painted in the tondo of the kylix of Exekias in Munich, Staatliche Antikensammlungen
(inv. no. 8729), depicting Dionysus sailing the seas (ABV 146.21; BAPD 310403; Isler-Kerényi 2007, figs 104–7;
Paleothodoros 2012, 462–4, fig. 51). The god is lying within the ship, much like a symposiast, holding a cornucopia in his right hand, while dolphins are dancing all around (Fig. 2). Four dolphins follow along the course
of the ship, while three others move in the opposite direction. Research has shown that the Munich cup by
Exekias illustrates the myth of the Tyrrhenian pirates, since the god is clearly associated with the dolphins. This
association is further enhanced by the presence of a small white dolphin in the bow, as well as in the stern of the
ship. Images of Dionysus sailing the seas, whether accompanied by dolphins or not, also appear on other vases
painted in the late black-figure style, some of which have been commented upon in detail by Paleothodoros
(2012, 463–5).

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
The next notable representation of the Tyrrhenians pirates may be found in an Attic monument of the
second half of the 4th century BCE. We refer to the contiguous frieze in the well-known choregic monument
of Lysikrates (334 BCE), above the architrave of which there is a relief sculpture depicting the clash between
Dionysus’ retinue and the pirates who attempted to capture the god, before he turned them into dolphins (Erhard 1993, 10–11, figs. 1–4; Figs. 3a–b). It is the best-preserved choregic monument of antiquity, situated on the

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt: Fig. 4. Young Dionysus transforming Tyrrhenian pirates into dolphins. Mosaic from a Roman villa. Bardo National Museum, Tunis (photo by DrRachT).

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
ancient “Street of the tripods”, and was erected in 335/334 BCE, during the archonship of Euaenetus, in order to
carry on its top the bronze tripod that would have been awarded as a prize for victory in the dramatic contest
(Ridgway 2001, 15–8, figs. 1–3).
It may plausibly be deduced that the subject of the frieze of the choregic monument derives from a dramatic
performance, for which Lysikrates won the tripod. The story is the transformation of the men into dolphins in
the presence of Dionysus and his entourage. The artistic requirements have modified the myth to a significant
degree. The incident takes place not in a ship, but on the shore. To be sure, the vignettes differ from the myth
as presented in the Homeric Hymn to Dionysus. Dionysus is depicted on the frieze in the shape of a man, not in
that of a lion, as in the hymn. He is shown not aboard a ship, but sitting on a rock by the sea, next to a panther.
The satyrs of the thiasos celebrate over a krater of wine, when they are attacked by the unsuspecting pirates,
who expect to collect a ransom in exchange for the god. In other parts of the frieze, the satyrs react to the assault. They hold down the pirates, beating them with thyrsi. A satyr brandishes a thyrsus to strike at a prostrate
marauder. Another satyr raises his arm in supplication, while a third one chases after a terrified pirate. Some
marauders have survived and jump into the sea, where they turn into dolphins, beginning with the head, while
the transformation has not yet reached their torsos and limbs. Other pirates dive into the sea, almost completely
transformed into dolphins (Erhard 1993, 16–37, pls. 1–19).
The frieze records the Dionysiac episode on a monument that was erected on the occasion of a dramatic
contest, possibly a satyr play. The satyrs who chase the pirates punish them in various ways, tying their hands
­behind their backs as captives. They probably represent the chorus of actors sponsored by Lysikrates. Other
landscape features, such as rocks, trees and large craters, are interspersed between the human figures, ­delineating
the conventional boundaries between the land and the sea. Given the limited height of the frieze, one cannot
comment upon the rendering of the Tyrrhenian pirates’ facial features and expressions. Their muscle structure
is conveyed with very little in the way of details, in a somewhat impressionistic fashion. What we have here is a
frieze that belongs to a choregic monument, i.e., not a public project, but an offering by a private citizen on the
occasion of a theatrical play.
Among Roman art works depicting Dionysus on a ship and the transformation of the pirates into dolphins,
we may mention the excellent 3rd-century CE mosaic pavement from Thugga (modern Dougga), Tunisia, preserved in the National Bardo Museum (Yacoub 1995, 173–4; Fig. 4). It is depicted the warship with Dionysus
and ­Tyrrhenian pirates sailing in sea. Portrayed as an adolescent, the god is accompanied by an elderly Silenus.
Two pirates, terrorized by the god, are already in the water, turning into dolphins. One is being snatched by the
foot by a leopard, which appears ready to devour him. Two small boats are on either side of the divine ship. One
of them is carrying three men, probably fishermen, and the other a couple of Cupids.

The mosaic in question recalls a description by Philostratus the Elder (Imag. 1.19) of an ancient Greek
painting at Neapolis (Naples), which depicts a Tyrrhenian pirate vessel attacking a sacred ship of Dionysus
and his Maenads. The transformation has already begun and the god’s ship is covered in ivy and vines. The
­introduction of a naval battle motif is obviously a later invention, when the myth was incorporated into other
tales that recounted Dionysus’ warlike mien.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
ΤHE MYTH OF DIONYSUS AND THE TYRRHENIAN PIRATES IN EARLY
MODERN AND MODERN ARTS
The Dionysiac myth remained popular after the end of antiquity and up to modern times. A bas-relief depicting
Dionysus’ ship and the punishment of the pirates adorns the main bronze door of Saint Peter’s Basilica in Rome
(Suffi 1998, 26–31; Glass 2012, 549; Fig. 5); the subject is based on an episode from Ovid’s Metamorphoses of
Ovid (3.656–691). It was commissioned for the Old Basilica by Pope Eugene IV (1431–1447) and created by the
Florentine sculptor Antonio di Pietro Averlino (ca. 1400 – ca. 1469), better known as “il Filarete”. The Filarete
Door is the oldest one in the basilica. It was preserved and reused in the New Basilica in 1619. The two door
panels are made of bronze and decorated with scenes in bas-relief. The depiction of the ship carrying Dionysus
and the pirates may be found in one of the smaller bas-reliefs carved between the six main panels that are
­decorated with scenes from Ovid’s Metamorphoses, Aesop’s Fables and other subjects pertaining to the life of
Eugene IV.

findings.evidence_excerpt: Fig. 6. Dionysus and the Tyrrhenian pirates. Jacob Matham, after David Vinckboons, 1616. Engraving. Amsterdam, Rijksmuseum, inv. no. RP-P-OB-102.850).

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
Dionysus and the Tyrrhenian pirates form the subject of an engraving from the year 1616, now preserved
in Amsterdam (Rijksmuseum, inv. no. RP-P-OB-102.850; Matham 2007, 279, no. 284; Fig. 6). The Tyrrhenian
­pirates have been transformed into dolphins: when Bacchus turns himself into a lion and a vine stretches around
the ship, the Tyrrhenians, panic-stricken, jump into the sea and are transformed into monstrous dolphins. The
same subject also appears in a medieval edition of Ovid’s Metamorphoses, published by Veuve Langelier in 1619,
which is preserved in the National Library of France in Paris.
The transformation of Dionysus before the Tyrrhenian pirates was a subject that also inspired modern
painters and artists, as evident in the work of London-born painter and sculptor Glyn Warren Philpot, who
later became a representative of the Art Deco style. In the oil painting in question (1924), Philpot portrays the
god Dionysus, an upside-down pirate and some dolphins in the sea in the background (Fig. 7). The foregoing
brief story of the Tyrrhenians and Dionysus has provided artists throughout the ages, from the time of Homer
to the twentieth century, with the opportunity to present their own artistic version.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
CONCLUDING REMARKS
The sources refer to the Tyrrhenians as violent, brutal kidnappers with a rapacious attitude. The marauders
served as the model of an impious and uncivilized nature, given the fact that their cruelty was proverbial.
Aristotle may be the earliest surviving source that refers to the infamous “Tyrrhenian torture”, the practice of
chaining rotting corpses together with live captives, face to face, limb to limb, one by one as precisely as possible
(Beatrice 2001). To those who referred indirectly to Aristotle’s passage in the Roman period, the “Tyrrhenian
torture” was a genuine Etruscan custom (Paleothodoros 2012, 470). Tyrrhenians pirates were infamous for tying
live captives to dead ones (Nonnus, Dion. 45.110). It is possible that their proverbially harsh and rigid character
became the ideal target for bringing to fruition another one of Dionysus’ divine plans, so that he may eventually
have his revenge, as he usually did with the opponents of his cult.

Dionysus’ victims were transformed into dolphins, because these mammals were considered to have a lot in
common with humans. In the first half of the 5th century BCE, a fragment of Pindar refers to the human n
­ ature
of dolphins, that loveable companion of ships, piratical or otherwise, in Mediterranean waters and beyond
(Pind. fr. 234; see also fr. 140b.13–17, 236). In Lucian’s Dialogues of the Sea Gods, intelligent dolphins are shown
conversing with Poseidon, god of the seas, and express remorse for their transgressions as they accompany

Don’t be surprised, Poseidon, that we’re kind to men. We were men ourselves, before we became fishes
(Luc. Dial. mar. 8, trans. M.D. MacLeod, Cambridge, Mass., 1961).

Between Myth, Lore and Historical Reality
Piracy in the Phournoi Archipelago, Eastern Aegean

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
ABSTRACT
The documentation pertaining to a considerable array of ancient, medieval and modern shipwrecks unearthed during
the recent investigations (2015–2020) conducted by the Ephorate of Maritime Antiquities in the Phournoi a­ rchipelago
has rekindled a long-standing public perception, portraying Phournoi as a historical hub for piracy. This paper delves into
the distinctive geomorphological features and coastal formations of Phournoi, elucidating the n
­ avigational ­advantages
it a­ fforded and its association with piracy. It scrutinizes local toponyms, historical accounts and the ­archaeological
­remnants of approximately fifty shipwrecks to explore this narrative. Despite the multitude of archaeological traces left
by the continuous maritime traffic passing Phournoi over an extended temporal span, the convergence of these investigative methodologies reveals persisting gaps. Historical sources, toponymic evidence and archaeological discoveries exhibit
limited chronological overlap. Furthermore, the archaeological record of shipwrecks on Phournoi predominantly suggests
adverse weather conditions as the principal catalyst for maritime ­mishaps, rather than deliberate acts of piracy.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
INTRODUCTION
In 2015, the Hellenic Ephorate of Underwater Antiquities initiated an extensive survey aimed at the
­documentation and cataloging of ancient, medieval and modern shipwrecks within the archipelago of Phournoi.
Comprising a cluster of 20 islands, islets and rocky shoals positioned to the south of the channel separating
Ikaria and Samos (Figs. 1–2), the Phournoi archipelago served as the focal point for this investigative endeavor.
By the culmination of the project in 2020, the Phournoi initiative had successfully identified and documented
over 50 shipwrecks spanning from the Archaic period through the first decades of the 20th century (Campbell
and Koutsouflakis 2017, 2021; Viglaki-Sofianou et al. 2019, 142–225).
Nevertheless, any scholarly assessment of these shipwrecks encounters an initial challenge rooted in a
­pervasive and somewhat stereotypical narrative prevalent among the indigenous inhabitants of Phournoi. This
narrative posits the historical characterization of their island as a haven for pirates. Such a perception permeates
various media channels, including websites, daily press publications, tourist guides and even scholarly articles
and historical textbooks (Hasluck 1910–1911, 169; Melas 1957, 159; Belavilas 1997, 33). Consequently, this
­perception has become widely accepted, ostensibly corroborated by the abundant presence of shipwrecks.
In the ensuing discourse, I endeavor to elucidate the available historical evidence, discern Phournoi’s
­position within broader navigational networks, scrutinize the island’s coastal morphology and expound upon
underwater archaeological discoveries.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
distinctly alternative manner: by temporarily or semi-permanently establishing operational bases on Phournoi
and engaging in the ancient practice of piracy.
The activities of pirates, operating independently for personal gain and devoid of the protection or sanction
of specific political authorities, have been documented across the broader maritime expanse of Phournoi since
the late Hellenistic era. The geomorphological attributes of the landscape, once conducive to navigation and
trade traffic, assumed a divergent purpose. Elevated vantage points transitioned into signaling stations, concealed hinterlands behind promontories became sites for ambush and assault, the deep coves along the coastline
evolved into havens of refuge and concealment, and the open sea surrounding the archipelago transformed
into a theater of pursuit and plunder. These geographic conditions are universally recognized as pivotal factors
conducive to piracy (Semple 1916, 141). Concurrently, the narrow channels within the heart of the complex
served as escape routes in the event of an unforeseen turn of events. A recurring geographical feature was the
proliferation of small harbors and concealed alcoves serving as lairs for pirate fleets, with numerous promontories doubling as lookout posts and bastions. Utilizing swift, nimble rowing vessels, the temporary occupants of
the islands could menace any merchant ship within reach following brief pursuit.
The distinctive topography of Phournoi consistently favored those acquainted with it and adept at ­exploiting
its unique attributes to their advantage (Belavilas 1997, 63). Pursued vessels could seek refuge in the expansive dead-end bay of Chrysomilia or navigate the narrow channels flanking Kisiria island, thereby risking
­entrapment and capture. In instances when large sailing vessels were deployed to safeguard trade routes or
­undertake clearance operations, the shallow-drafted pirate craft could elude pursuit through these narrow
straits. The constrained and shallow passages between the main island of Phournoi, Kisiria and Thymena served
as escape conduits, dissuading larger vessels from navigating through them due to the perils of rocky shoals or
grounding. This afforded pirate factions the essential time needed to evade capture and vanish into the plethora
of blind spots the landscape afforded.

findings.evidence_excerpt:

Bordone, Anonymous of Lucca, Mercator, Piacenza, Blaeu), Cursie (Ortelius) and Cursia (Agnese). These
variations, undoubtedly linked to the ancient name of Phournoi, often coexist with variants of the name
“Phournoi”. ­Conversely, from the 18th century onwards, variants of the name “Phournoi” appear to prevail
among ­cartographers.
The Latin transliteration of the ancient Greek name and its variants closely resemble the byzantine term for the
act of plunder (koursos/kourson), attested as early as the 8th century (Sophocles 1888, s.v. κοῦρσον 687; ­Kriaras
1982, s.v. κούρσο(ν), κούρσος) and correlate with derivatives of the Italian term corsario, loosely ­translated as
“one who has a license to raid” (letter de course), derived from Medieval Latin term cursarius (­“pirate”, from
Latin cursus; Heinz 2007, s.v. cursarius, cursus). The pronounced similarity between the ­numerous versions of
the ancient name of Phournoi and the various terms for loot and corsair in Latin languages and medieval Greek
has fostered a conjectural association in popular consciousness, often leading to the belief that the islands derive
their name from pirate activity. This somewhat arbitrary popular perception, however, does not preclude the
historical possibility that the archipelago of Phournoi was indeed a hub of intense pirate activity in the past.
A series of coastal toponyms documented on maps or utilized in the modern vernacular of Phournoi
are probably the living remnants of pirate activity in the past: Kourniachto (a place for hiding or lurking),
­Kleftolimano (harbor of thieves), Fygou (escape), Fylakio (guard-post), Vardia (shift or guard), Tourkolimnionas
(harbor of the Turks), Pano and Kato Maneta (upper and lower Maneta). Many of these names are commonplace along the Aegean coastline and are also encountered on other islands historically associated with piracy.
However, the two bays designated as Pano and Kato Maneta, situated roughly in the middle of the eastern coast
of the main island of Phournoi, warrant further comment.
It is highly probable that these two bays derived their names from the Zakynthian corsair Eustathios ­(Stathis)
Romanos or Manetas, who, between 1678 and 1684, operated as a pirate in the Aegean Sea while based in Melos,
commanding the only Greek privately owned corsair vessel at the time, most probably handed to him after the
death of its former owner, the Maltese corsair Hugues Creviliers (Krantonelli 1994, 289–91). Early records of
his exploits date back to 1683, when the rector of Tenos reported that Stathis Romanos Manetas had seized the
Venetian consul in Paros, extorting a monopoly over the supply of galette to Venetian fleet vessels. In May 1684,
Admiral Gerolamo Cornaro courted him on behalf of the Venetians, granting him a free pass permit (salvocondotto). Manetas subsequently conducted operations across the Aegean, Ionian and southern Adriatic, either
independently or in collaboration with the Venetians and the Knights of Malta (Krantonelli 1991, 300). At
the onset of the 6th Venetian-Turkish war (1684–1699), Morosini appointed him commander of the V
­ enetian
cruiser flotilla, where he actively participated in the sieges of Lefkada and Preveza (Sathas 1869, 312–19; Donos
2007, 74–85, 101). Subsequently, he assisted the Venetian admiral in levying taxes on Aegean islands and aiding
in the sieg
