findings.evidence_excerpt:
of Chios. However, Aegean folk legends may have preserved aspects of his activities that historical accounts
have overlooked. Manetas is etched into the popular consciousness due to his tumultuous personal life. Legend
has it that he married the beautiful Marioga in Melos, leaving her under the care of the island’s bishop when
he embarked on a pirate expedition. Marioga, steadfastly refusing the bishop’s advances, was falsely accused of
infidelity to Manetas. Subsequently, Manetas captured her and executed her at his place of business. This tragic
episode forms the central theme of “Manetas’ rhyme”, a popular Aegean folk song known in various renditions
today (Legrand 1874, 296–300; Spyridakis and Petropoulos 1962, 375–78; Poulianos 1964, 121–24). While each
version features adaptations of hero names and locales, the Ikarian rendition places Manetas’s attempt “in the
straits of Samos” (stes Samos ta boghazia), with his wife’s murder purportedly occurring there. Accordingly,
local traditions suggest that the murder took place either in Ikaria or Phournoi, specifically in the bays of Pano
and Kato Maneta. Nonetheless, whether Stathis Romanos Manetas utilized Phournoi as a base and secure anchorage during his operations in the Chios area in 1694 and 1695 remains a conjecture. Offspring of Manetas
continued the family tradition, engaging in acts of piracy for the most part of the first half of the 18th century
(Krantonelli 1998, 35–8, 168–69).

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
HISTORICAL EVIDENCE
Ancient and medieval sources provide scant information regarding piracy in the Phournoi archipelago. In
modern historiography, these islands are often depicted as geographical extensions of ancient Miletus initially,
later transitioning to Samos, possibly as part of an effort to establish an island defense enclosure, acquire naval
bases for overseas trade and extend naval dominance (Papalas 2002, 40–5). The “thalassocracy” of Samos’s
tyrant, Polycrates, exhibited characteristics of aggressive expansionism, as described by Diodorus Siculus
(10.16.1), who noted that Polycrates “by sending triremes to the most opportune places, plundered all those who
sailed”. Phournoi likely served as an overseas base for such naval operations, supported by clear evidence of
Samian guards stationed there until the Hellenistic period (Viglaki-Sofianou et al. 2019, 51–7), a fact corroborated for the island of Ikaria as well.
One of the most renowned episodes of piracy in the ancient world occurred a few miles south-east of
Phournoi, in ancient Pharmakoussa (modern Pharmakonissi), involving the capture of Julius Caesar by Lycian
pirates during his voyage to Rhodes in 74 BCE (Ward 1975; Günther 1999; Osgood 2010). This incident is
recounted by various ancient writers, including Suetonius (Iul. 4), Plutarch (Caes. 1.4–2.4), Polyaenus (Strat.
8.23), Velleius Paterculus (2.41.3) and Valerius Maximus (6.9.15), with Velleius Paterculus providing the most
reliable testimony, written around 30 CE. Julius Caesar’s captivity occurred within a complex political context, a
year preceding the outbreak of the third Mithridatic War (73–63 BCE) and Mark Antony’s (Creticus) campaign
in Crete (72 BCE), during which pirates from Cilicia and Pamphylia expanded their activities across the Eastern
and Central Mediterranean. According to Plutarch:
“This [the pirates’] power extended its operations over the whole of our Sea, making it unnavigable and
closed to all commerce. This was what most of all inclined the Romans, who were hard put to it to get
provisions and expected a great scarcity, to send out Pompey with a commission to take the sea away
from the pirates” (Pomp. 25.1, trans. B. Perrin, Cambridge, Mass., 1917).

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
The accounts provided by Suetonius, Plutarch and Velleius suggest that the pirate band responsible for
c­ apturing Julius Caesar were essentially opportunistic brigands with ships, owing no particular allegiance and
driven solely by the prospect of immediate material gain. Such groups of stateless outlaws, acting independently
and lurking in insignificant islands with the hope of a lucrative catch, were likely common during the turbulent
late 2nd and early 1st centuries BCE, or during any period of maritime anarchy. The Phournoi complex, with its
advantageous physical terrain, would likely have been no exception to this phenomenon.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
Rome responded to the piracy threat by enacting the Gabinian Law in 67 BCE, granting extraordinary
powers to the outgoing consul Gnaeus Pompey to eradicate piracy throughout the Mediterranean. Pompey’s
campaign, meticulously planned and brief, relied heavily on diplomacy rather than outright armed conflict and
proved highly effective.
Unlike Pharmakoussa, which gained notoriety due to a prominent incident, Phournoi never attracted
­significant attention from ancient historians. To uncover tangible evidence of pirate activity in Phournoi, one
must turn to the late Byzantine and post-Byzantine periods.
The earliest account mentioning Phournoi as an ambush site for Turkish pirates targeting merchant vessels
comes from the Florentine monk Cristoforo Buondelmonti in the early 15th century, who was shipwrecked
on the island and endured five days without food before being rescued by a passing ship (Buondelmonti 1897,
109–10 no. 55). Buondelmonti also noted the favorable anchorages provided by Phournoi, where ships could
seek shelter at night to avoid strong winds. However, he observed the island as deserted and abandoned by its
inhabitants. Apparently, its use by Turkish pirates was seasonal, a pattern recurring over the centuries.
Historical records indicate that during the latter half of the 15th century, the Genoese administration
­ rchestrated a mass relocation of the population of Samos to Chios, primarily due to piracy thriving in neigho
boring islands and Phournoi (Hasluck 1910–1911, 169; Melas 1957, 158–59). Ottoman admiral Piri Reis also
depicted a similar scene of desolation at the beginning of the 16th century (Bülent 2002, 157). The abandonment described by Buondelmonti and Piri Reis seemingly rendered Phournoi an ideal refuge for various bands
of pirates to regroup and distribute their plunder.
In the summer of 1602, the Spanish pirate Alonso de Contreras sought refuge on the deserted islands
of Phournoi with his Maltese frigate and companions, following a series of successful operations in Serifos,
­Astypalaia, Amorgos and Patmos, intending to regroup and divide their spoils. However, they were compelled
to abandon the islands when two galleys under Suleiman of Catania, then Bey of Chios, appeared, forcing de
Contreras to flee via Ikaria and Mykonos (Durant 1975, 146–56; Krantonelli 1991, 107–9, 333; de Contreras
1994, 97–102).
The involvement of corsairs from the Order of the Knights of St. John of Malta and other Christian forces in
the Archipelago of Phournoi is corroborated by the description of Ikaria by Joseph Georgirenes, the archbishop
of Samos and Ikaria, published in London in 1677, reflecting his experiences in the early 1670s (Georgirenes
1677, 3–4, 55; Papalas 2002, 258–67). Georgirenes notes the uninhabited islets of Phournoi, located three miles
south of the coast of Ikaria, boasting natural harbors capable of accommodating various vessels. He further
mentions that at other times, corsairs from Malta and other Christian factions would lie in wait on these islands,
ambushing ships trading between Chios and Rhodes.
The daily routine of these corsair groups is vividly described by the English captive Mr. Roberts, who was
shipwrecked in Ios in 1692 and subsequently captured by pirates, forced to serve as a gunner on their ship.
­According to Roberts, the corsairs would spend the winter in Paros, Antiparos, Melos and Ios until early March.
They would then relocate to Phournoi, where they would lie in wait from early spring to mid-summer, with
lookouts stationed in the mountains overlooking the Samos-Ikaria strait, keeping watch for passing ships. They
would also venture into the southern part of Ikaria, Gaidouronisi and Leipsoi, before moving further south to
posts in Asia Minor, spanning from Cilicia to Cyprus. In autumn, they would return to the Aegean to sell their
plunder and deliver profits to their backers in Livorno, Malta or Marseille (Hacke 1699; Ormerod 1924, 17–8;
Krantonelli 1991, 89–93; Simopoulos 1994, 106).
This cyclic movement of ambush, aligned with the routes of convoys between Alexandria and C
­ onstantinople
or guided by intelligence from captured vessels, was undoubtedly a prevalent method of piracy during this era.
Similar tactics were employed by Jacopo Inghirami, the admi

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
diplomat Louis Deshayes, Baron de Courmemin, reported from neighboring Samos that its few inhabitants,
lacking the protection of a castle, were left vulnerable to pirate invasions originating from Phournoi (Deshayes
1624, 315–21).
From the 15th century onward, Phournoi remained virtually uninhabited according to almost all post-­
Byzantine sources. This assertion is supported by the absence of settlement remains on the island from this
period, with the oldest standing houses in Phournoi dating back to the mid-19th century. The initial attempt
to repopulate Phournoi is believed to have commenced around 1770, when the monk Nimphon (Nikolaos
­Nikolaras) departed from Patmos and, along with other monks, constructed the chapel of Evangelistria at
­Koumara. However, due to the persistent threat of pirate raids, he relocated to Ikaria, where in 1775 he oversaw
the construction of the monastery of Evaggelistria in Mounde (Stamatiadis 1893, 82; Viglaki-Sofianou et al.
2019, 74–5). Phournoi remained sparsely inhabited, with the population reaching only 120 families towards the
end of the 19th century (Viglaki-Sofianou et al. 2019, 77).
Reports of piracy based in Phournoi persisted well into the 19th century. E.D. Clarke, a traveler who visited
the islands in the early 19th century, affirmed that even during his time, a significant number of pirates lurked
in Phournoi and the neighboring island of Ikaria (Clarke 1814, 185; Tsagas 2003, 91–2). Disorder in the waters
around Phournoi persisted long after the widespread suppression of piracy by the newly formed Greek state.
In 1856, any act of raid (course) was declared illegal by law, and the Turkish administration of Rhodes granted
­English and French ships full freedom of action to eliminate the remaining pockets of piracy in the Eastern
Aegean and the Ikarian Sea (Dimitrakopoulos 1977, 184; Pamphilis 1980, 141–42; Bakirtzis 2007, 230).
Nineteenth-century historians and local press accounts from Samos extensively documented the activities
of Emmanuel (Manos) Mytikas, a native of Patmos, who lived and operated in Phournoi, and is often regarded
as the last pirate of the Aegean (Kritikidis 1869, 117–18; Stamatiadis 1893, 39; Viglaki-Sofianou et al. 2019, 76).
Mytikas was characterized as a robber (ληστής) or criminal (κακούργος), but the methods he employed, such
as traversing from island to island in a makeshift boat and engaging in robbery and murder, align closely with
the operations of a small-scale pirate. Upon his capture and subsequent trial in Samos in 1861, he was found
guilty of 48 murders and sentenced to death. The execution took place in Marathokampos on February 19, 1863,
following approval from the Sultan in Istanbul (Bakirtzis 2007, 319).

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
ARCHAEOLOGICAL FINDS
Regarding archaeological finds, during the ongoing archaeological research of Phournoi (2015 onwards),
no tangible archaeological evidence directly linked to piracy has been uncovered. While the presence of a
­significant number of shipwrecks along the coast could suggest heightened maritime activity, it is also attributed
to extensive exploration of the seabed. Among the 50 identified shipwrecks, 48 were discovered to be laden with
cargo, reducing the likelihood of piracy-related incidents. The causes of sinking, to the extent that they can be
determined, predominantly stem from adverse weather conditions.
Furthermore, the chronological distribution of shipwrecks in Phournoi reveals a notable scarcity of finds
from the period historically associated with piracy activity, beginning from the 15th century onwards (Fig. 5).
This discrepancy, however, should not be surprising. Shipwrecks identified during underwater surveys are primarily recognized by the visual imprint they leave on the seabed. Consequently, amphorae cargoes comprise the
majority of the wrecks discovered in Phournoi, as is common in Mediterranean underwater surveys. Galleys,
smaller rowboats or sailing ships that did not transport ceramic cargo present far greater challenges in terms of
detection, as their visual traces on the seabed are considerably less distinct. Smaller-scale piracy activities, akin
to those documented in the 1553 voyage of French doctor and botanist Pierre Belon in the Aegean, are highly
unlikely to leave identifiable archaeological remnants (Simopoulos, 1994, 391–92; Braudel 2002, 605).

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
However, both the chronological and geographical distribution of shipwrecks in Phournoi can provide
­insights into the utilization of the seascape from antiquity to the steam age. The distribution of shipwrecks
around Phournoi exhibits non-uniformity (Fig. 2). The highest concentration of shipwrecks is observed on the
northeastern coast of the central island of the complex (the homonymous to the complex island of Phournoi)
and on the northern coast of the island of Ayios Minas. Conversely, the northern and more exposed coasts of
Phournoi show a lack of wrecks. Similarly, another cluster of wrecks is located on the westernmost island of the
complex, along the northern coast of Thymena. This pattern suggests that vessels passing through the archipelago of Phournoi tend to navigate around rather than through the central area of the complex. Additionally,
variations in cargo size are discernible. The cargoes identified around the island of Kisiria, situated between
Phournoi and Thymena, indicate the transit of exclusively small vessels, whereas all larger cargoes are situated
on the perimeter of the complex. It is evident that large ships avoided passage through unsafe narrow straits.
The circumnavigation along the eastern coastline of Phournoi appears to have been the primary option for
ships traversing the Ikaria-Samos channel, a choice that seems to be corroborated by the Ottoman portolan of
the Walters Art Museum in Baltimore (Fig. 6). The existence of a small settlement dating back to Late Roman
times beneath the modern village of Kamari, which provided access to water supply, along with the safe anchoring conditions offered by the continuous bays to the south, may be linked to this preference. Evidence
suggests that this settlement persisted through Byzantine times, with a large collection of abandoned anchors
discovered in the sea area in front of it, dating mainly to the late Byzantine and the Ottoman era.
Isolated finds, primarily ceramics, on the seafloor of Phournoi indicate the ongoing utilization of certain leeward bays, where no shipwrecks were found. Substantial quantities of discarded material were documented in
the bays of Vlychada at the southernmost cape of Phournoi, as well as in the bays of Kariotika and ­Vathylakas on
the northern side of Thymena. Notably, small size stone cannonballs are frequently found on the western shores
of the island of Ayios Minas, particularly in Kambi Bay, some of which have been recovered and are currently
housed in the Town Hall of Phournoi. Recently, a bronze arquebus dating to the 16th century was snagged by
a trawler in deep waters between Ikaria and Phournoi (Fig. 7). The fisherman who retrieved it turned it over to
the Port Police of Ayios Kyrikos in Ikaria, speculating that it might originate from a shipwreck.
An isolated shipwreck (no. 23), sunk in front of the modern settlement of Bali in Phournoi, may be linked
to piratical activity, although the evidence it provides is somewhat limited. It comprises the hull of an ­elongated
ship discovered near the coast at a depth of 36 meters (Fig. 8). The wreck was found devoid of all cargo and
­nautical equipment, with an unusually large quantity of large-sized rough stones found inside the hull. This
quantity exceeds the typical ballast expected for a ship of its size. The wreck was dated to the early 19th
­century, primarily based on the discovery of a glass inkpot, the sole identifiable object found within the hull.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
The evidence suggests a deliberate sinking of the ship, possibly following its capture and looting, to erase any
trace of the incident, a common practice in the Aegean noted by travelers like Choiseul-Gouffier (Simopoulos
1999, 378). This timeframe aligns with accounts of pirate activity in the Phournoi archipelago as documented by
traveler E.D. Clarke (1814, 185). However, these hypotheses require validation through further archaeological
investigation of the shipwreck.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
CONCLUSION
The comprehensive evaluation of all available testimony regarding piracy in the Phournoi archipelago suggests
that archaeological findings align with historical accounts only to a certain extent. Underwater investigations of
Phournoi indicate that the island complex served as a vital waypoint and intermediate step-stone for maritime
traffic in the eastern Aegean. Throughout various historical periods, sailors recognized and utilized the strategic
advantages offered by Phournoi’s location and geomorphology.
Piracy, however, presents challenges in archaeological identification on the seabed. The traces left by pirate
activity often resemble those of regular merchant shipping, complicating the interpretation of archaeological
data. Consequently, distinguishing between the two can be ambiguous and the archaeological record alone may
not definitively confirm instances of piracy.
Furthermore, terrestrial archaeological research on the island is still in its early stages, particularly ­concerning
remains from the second millennium CE. As investigations expand to encompass terrestrial ­settlement remains,
there may be opportunities to establish clearer connections between archaeological evidence and historical
accounts.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
Searching for Traces of Corsair Activity in the Aegean during
Early Modern Times
From Historical Accounts to Archaeological Remains

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
ABSTRACT
The pirate phenomenon in the Aegean –and generally in the Mediterranean– is inscribed in the longue durée and formed
an economic activity that was not always illegal. Nevertheless, the difficulty to detect its traces is a commonplace among
historians and archaeologists. This paper attempts to respond to this challenge by focusing on the period of the extended
Venetian-Ottoman wars of the 17th century (1645–1669, 1684–1699). During this period, the pirate phenomenon, in its
corsair version, was manifested with particular intensity in the Aegean and was normalized. The normalcy with which
corsairing was vested is fragmentarily attested in various types of contemporary sources, and still echoes to this day in the
collective memory of islanders and the microtoponymy of the Archipelago. These testimonies, though few in number, show
that various monuments and architectural remains in the island complexes of the Aegean are or could be linked with the
needs of the corsairs to defend themselves, guard their captives, heal their bodies and strive for the salvation of their souls.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
INTRODUCTION
In the Mediterranean, the pirate phenomenon –which is “as old as history”, as F. Braudel writes (1973, 866)– is
an economic activity of island and coastal populations, tantamount to the banditry practiced by the inhabitants
of mountainous areas. In any case, the proximity of the islands to the mountains of the mainland allowed for
a switching of roles. The example of the bandits of Olympus, who also acted as pirates in the wider area of the
Northern Sporades, is fairly well known (Vasdravellis 1970). After all, pirate activity was not confined to the sea
and attacks on ships, but also developed in coastal areas, where settlements were assaulted by marauders and
people were captured on the coast.
Despite its brutality, this activity was not always illegal. In early modern times, corsairing was lawful, at
least insofar as the corsairs respected the terms of their license (patente). In any case, however, the success of
pirate or corsair operations, which depended on their ability to surprise their victims, required the same level
of planning and organization as any other economic activity, all the more so since the attacks were carried out
using ships as the main modus operandi, which in turn required regular maintenance and purveyance. The
cost of ­maintaining a ship and buying supplies could be covered by the sale of the spoils (ships, goods and also
people), thus creating a cycle of activities that replicated the pirate phenomenon. Therefore, it was the needs
of the ship that, first and foremost, determined the schedule of pirate or corsair operations and dictated their

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
interruption from time to time. During that cessation of activity, pirates and corsairs would come ashore and
certain ­anchorages would then become their safe havens and bases of operation.
Based on the above, is it possible for one to detect traces of the pirate phenomenon on land? We will attempt
to answer this question by focusing on the period of the extended Venetian-Ottoman wars of the 17th century
(1645–1669, 1684–1699). In doing so, we will not concentrate on traces of material destruction related to the
pirate phenomenon, which is a commonplace concern among both historians and archaeologists. Instead, we
will focus on traces of material construction on land that could be associated with corsair activity.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
THE MEDITERRANEAN CORSO
In the early modern period, and especially in the 17th century, a particular form of corsairing had developed
in the Mediterranean with endemic characteristics, which was not only manifested in times of war but also
in times of peace. This was the corso, a term coined by M. Fontenay (2010, 212–14, 341–42), waged by both
­Catholic Christians and Muslims of North Africa in the context of an alleged “war against the Infidels”. These
obtained licenses to practice the corso from their respective rulers in exchange for a portion of their loot. In
essence, this was an organized economic operation under a religious pretext, securely backed by investors with
access to the authorities, from whence they secured their licenses. For this reason, those who obtained such permits had at their disposal means (ships, equipment, capital) that contemporary pirates could not even fathom.
In addition to the “private” corso, there was also the “public” or “state” corso, which was practiced by the fleets
of Malta, Tuscany and the Regencies of North Africa (Fontenay 1997, 211–12; Calafat and Kaiser 2016). This
paper will concentrate on the former manifestation of the pirate phenomenon and, more specifically, we will
examine the activity of “private” Catholic corsairs, who mainly operated and sojourned for extended periods of
time in the Aegean (Fontenay 2010, 228–31, 357–406). As observed by S. Bono (1993, 54–71), several facets of
the ­activity of “private” Catholic corsairs remain unknown.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
THE ANNUAL CYCLE OF CATHOLIC CORSO
Various sources of the last three decades of the 17th century inform us that the activity of Catholic corsairs in the
Eastern Mediterranean followed an annual cycle, which was imposed by weather conditions and, ­consequently,
by the schedule of the Ottoman fleet. The fleet of Kapudan Pasha sailed in the Aegean to collect taxes from the
islands only when the weather was favorable, between the feast of Saint George and the feast of Saint Demetrius
(Hidrellez and Kasim respectively in Islam). More specifically, the corsairs acted as follows:
During the winter months, from mid-December until March or, according to another source (Deloffre and
Rougeot 1976, 233), until the end of April, they retreated to islands of the southern Aegean, where no Ottomans resided, mainly Melos, Kimolos, Paros, Antiparos, Ios and Astypalaia (Fig. 1). In the spring, the corsairs boarded their ships and headed eastwards to Phournoi and their environs, between Ikaria, Agathonisi
and Leipsoi, where, until the first summer months, they would ambush ships following the Asia Minor route,
namely those that sailed through the passage between the Dodecanese and the Asia Minor coast that connected
the ports of Syria-Palestine and Alexandria with Smyrna and Constantinople. Around the middle of July, they
sailed along the coast of Cyprus and, as soon as they received the slightest news about the presence of Algerian
or Ottoman vessels in Rhodes, they would head for the coasts of Alexandria and Damietta, where the shallow
waters would prevent these vessels from approaching. Around the end of the summer, the corsairs would approach the Syrian coast, where they could disembark their ships and go ashore in feluccas, capturing people in
and releasing them for ransom. In the autumn, they would return to the Aegean, where they would continue
their operations until the advent of winter (ANF, A.E. BI 862, f. 75v; Magni 1679, 292–95; Hacke 1699, 8–9).

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
MAINTENANCE OF THE PIRATE AND CORSAIR SHIPS
As already pointed out, pirate and corsair operations were interrupted from time to time to cater for the
­maintenance and supply needs of the ships. The success of the operations, after all, heavily depended on the
speed of sailing, which could only be ensured by regular maintenance of the keel, scraping it clean from marine
organisms and coating it with a mixture of grease and tar. These particular jobs, namely careening and graving,
were carried out at least twice a year. Another job that took place at regular but less frequent intervals was
caulking, namely the sealing of the hull with a tar-soaked oakum.
In order to complete all these maintenance operations, the ship had to be disarmed in a suitable cove (Jal
1848, 388–89, 423, 655–56; Jurien de La Gravière 1885, 219–20; Fennis 1995, 454, 491–92, 849–50). In the case
of pirates and corsairs, the cove in question had to fulfill a number of conditions in order to be considered
suitable. First, it had to allow the ship to approach the shore as far as possible; then, it had to be secluded, and,
finally, it had to provide opportunities for defense during the works, which we shall discuss below. The German
scholar Johann Michael Wansleben, who traveled in the Ottoman territories in the 1670s, notes in one of his
manuscripts that the corsairs graved their ships during the winter months in Astypalaia and Ios, while in June
and July in Porto Chevalier (Fethiye or Şövalye Adası) and one other anchorage on the coast of Lycia (BNF, MS
NAF 4193, f. 195v).1 Other sources, however, attest that the corsairs maintained their ships on Ios, Melos (­ Gazette
1668, 650, 660; Argenti 1954, 152) and evidently on other islands even during the summer months. I­ n­deed, a
text containing comments on maps of the Archipelago informs us that sometimes the corsairs careened their
ships at Arkioi (ANF, Marine, 3JJ 221, no. 4), in the wider area of which, as we have already ­mentioned, they lay
in wait to ambush passing ships from spring until early summer.
1 I am grateful to my colleague Alastair Hamilton for pointing out this unpublished note by J.M. Wansleben.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
In Astypalaia, French portolans of the same period specify that the corsairs maintained their ships in the bay
of Agrelidi and on the islets of Ligno and Chondro, otherwise known as Diaporia, on the bay of Maltezana (Fig.
2). Ligno was also called Espalmador or Despalmador by Western Europeans, a name derived from the verb “espalmar”/“despalmar”, which in the nautical lingua franca meant “to grave”. Other data has led me to hypothesize
that the bay of Vathy played a similar role (Koutzakiotis 2023).
On Ios, the corsairs are attested to grave their ships in the bay of Chora, called Gialos (Gazette 1668; Argenti
1954, 143, 152), while in the gulf of Melos, as is explicitly mentioned in various sources, they performed this
task exclusively in the bay of Patrikia, which was used for the same reason by non-corsair ships later on (Fig.
3; ANF, Marine, 2JJ 44, no. 2; ANF, Marine, 3JJ 219, no. 8, 49; ANF, Marine, 3JJ 221, no. 2; BNF, MS FR 14682,
7–8; Hacke 1699, 25–6).
As regards Paros, the Englishman Anthony Roberts, who was captured in 1692 by members of a corsair
crew, on whose ship he would serve for several months until his escape, informs us that the corsairs wintered in
the bay of Ayios Ioannis Detis but, more than that, they would stop by the bay two or three times a year (Hacke
1699, 47; Fig. 4). Also, according to Roberts, when the corsairs were careening their ships in the spacious gulf
of Naoussa, they would anchor “under a small Isle at the Head of the Bay” (Hacke 1699, 46–7), a location which
should be identified with the bay of Ayioi Anargyroi opposite the islet of Galiatsos, which is still mentioned
today as the former site of the shipyard of Naoussa.2

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
The abovementioned bays are characterized by either a narrow entrance or one blocked by an islet, which
allowed the placement of cannons at the edges of the bay and/or on the islet to prevent enemy ships from
­approaching during maintenance work. This was a common defensive practice that was not only followed by the
Catholic corsairs. For example, in 1681, it is reported that, when corsairs from Tripoli in Libya were informed
that a French squadron was pursuing them and intended to attack them in Chios, they made plans to take refuge
in Nea Phocaea (Yenifoça), in order to maintain their ships and place cannons at the entrance of its harbor
(Argenti 1954, 164, 166, 175). What interests us here, however, is not the practice per se, but the construction of
defensive works for the placement of cannons in sites frequented by corsairs. Indeed, French portolans inform
us that, in the gulf of Melos, at the cape of Patrikia, the corsairs had constructed “a fort” (un fort) or, at least,
“something like a fort” (comme une espèce de fort) to install their cannons (ANF, Marine, 3JJ 219, no. 5, 22 and
no. 8, 49). Roberts also attests that in the gulf of Naoussa, right on the bay of Ayioi Anargyroi, the corsairs had
constructed “a small battery” for the same purpose (Hacke 1699, 47).

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
CORSAIR DEFENSIVE WORKS
The preservation to this day of such simple and crude structures is most likely in places that are uninhabited
and, even more so, in ones that are remote and inaccessible. This is not the case for the bay of Ayioi Anargyroi,
which is located at the eastern end of the settlement of Naoussa on northern Paros. Nevertheless, at the edge of
the western side of the bay, there are visible remains of two dry-stone walls made of rocks and raw stones, which
form a corner with preserved dimensions of about 11 × 2 m (Figs. 4–5). This structure faces the entrance to the

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
gulf of Naoussa in the distance and, if it served as a cannon placement point, it could well have made the bay of
Ayioi Anargyroi impenetrable from the sea. It might be the case that this position was defensively reinforced by
a similar structure on the opposite islet of Galiatsos, if we take into account the fact that a century later, when
Naoussa served as a naval base for the Russian navy during the Orlov Revolt (1770–1774), the Russians had
installed a battery unit on the same islet and had constructed a five-cannon battery, as well as four buildings (see
“Plan du port de Naussa” in Choiseul-Gouffier 1782, 70–1). It must be added that on the islet of Galiatsos, and
much more so on the islet of Mavronissi, which lies a little further to the east, the inhabitants have located from
time to time many cannon balls of different sizes.3
Unlike the bay of Ayioi Anargyroi, the bay of Patrikia in Melos is to this day far away from settlements and is
approached by a path. The “cape of the harbor” (la pointe du port), on which it is said that the corsairs had built
something for their defense (ANF, Marine, 3JJ 219, no. 8, 49), must be the pointed, low strip of land stretching
to the northeast of the bay, facing the entrance to the gulf of Melos, rather than the higher cape that lies south
of the aforementioned strip and does not have a narrow tip; thus, it can hardly be described as a “pointe” (Fig.
3). Neither of these two sites, however, currently has any visible structure. Nevertheless, it is interesting to note
that impressive volcanic rocks rise in the middle of the strip in question, which are spaced sufficiently apart to
allow for the firing of cannons placed behind them. At the same time, the mass of the rocks themselves provides
cover from any shot coming from the sea (Fig. 6). It might be the case that some of these rocks were placed in
an upright position by the corsairs, which explains the description of the site as “something like a fort”. It should
also be added that at the easternmost point of the northern side of the bay, reached by a path, there is a (likely
natural) small plateau, which appears suitable for the placement of a cannon carriage that could be fired against
any enemy ship that would approach in the area (Fig. 7).
3 See the relevant testimonies in the documentary “The Russian presence on Paros”, edited by Tasos Kasapidis and Ioannis
Vasileiopoulos. Paros: Historical Folklore Museum – Othon Kaparis Collection.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
LOOKOUTS
Beyond the installation of cannons in the bays, where the corsairs found refuge for the maintenance of their
ships, another practice, which may have left its traces in the landscape of the Archipelago, is the lookouts they
placed on the highest points around the bays they used, either as ambush points or shipyards (Earle 2010, 158).
In the 17th century, this practice is attested in Ios (Gazette 1668, 652–53; Argenti 1954, 152), in Pharmakonissi
(de Contreras 1977, 67), and, of course, in Phournoi (Hacke 1699, 8), where even today the names of the island’s
bays indicate that they were once the lairs of famous corsairs: Pano and Kato Maneta bays and, possibly, Pavlos
bay (Fig. 9).
The sentries alerted the corsairs to the appearance of ships in the distance by hoisting or waving small flags,
thus giving orders to prepare for defensive or raiding operations. This practice should probably be associated
with the name Bandieres (or Padieres) of the hill on the south side of the bay of Vathy, as the present-day
­inhabitants of Astypalaia do not have any explanation for this place name (Fig. 2). Thus, the name of the hill is
probably not related to the relatively recent Italian occupation of the island, but to the practices of sailors of an
earlier time (Koutzakiotis 2023, 231–32).
Moreover, it is no coincidence that a similar place name is found in the narrow strait between Antiparos and
Paros, where corsair ships frequently anchored. More specifically, the southernmost islet of the strait is called
Pandieronissi and, as it is the largest of a cluster of islets and skerries, it lends its name to the entire cluster:
Pandieronissia (Fig. 1). It must be added here that one of the Pandieronissia bears the name Preza (Skandalidis
2001, 185), which in the lingua franca of the time denoted the spoils of corsairs or pirates, their “prize”. “Preza”
as a micro-toponym is also encountered today in Kimolos (Katsouros 1975, 326).

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
BAGNO
“Bona presa” for corsairs, namely their lawful loot, included people they captured to be sold as slaves for galleys
or to be exchanged for ransom. In the oldest surviving consular register of the Archipelago, the register of the
chancellery of the French consulate in Melos covering the years 1690–1695, various notarial acts related to the
purchase and sale of slaves and captives (Koutzakiotis 2016) have been recorded, as well as the entire cycle of
economic activities that had developed around the corso at that time. In the lingua franca of the Mediterranean,
the place where slaves were confined was called “bagno”, a term whose origin has long been debated (Audisio
1957).
In the Aegean, the term is found today as a micro-toponym on the eastern outskirts of Xobourgo in Tenos,
where the bagno of the Corsican Giorgio Maria Vitali was located. Vitali settled in the area in the middle of
the 17th century and launched an enterprise alongside some of his relatives that practiced the corso on behalf
of Venice (Krantonelli 1991, 217–23; Pelizza 2022, 129–31). Vitali’s contemporary, the English merchant Randolph (1687, 10), informs us that his bagno was located on the hill east of the Castle of Tenos and that it was a
square structure where Vitali had detained over 4,000 people, of which 1/10 had been delivered to the Venetian
Admiral of the Fleet.
Amanda Foskolou and Charis Koutelakis (1997, 30–1, 35–6 n. 7) have formed the hypothesis that Vitali’s
palace, which includes this bagno, may be the dwelling depicted in a late 17th-century view of Xobourgo and
appears to be located at the site of Pigadakia, where a Roman fountain is also found (Fig. 10). The teacher
Georgios Dorizas (1976, 106–7), however, mentions –evidently drawing from oral tradition– that the site of
Bagno lies opposite from the spring called Pigadakia, an assumption which seems to be confirmed today by the
inscription at the entrance to a farmstead located further down and opposite the Roman fountain. Within this

findings.evidence_excerpt:
CHURCHES
Despite the atrocities they committed, pirates and corsairs, like their contemporaries, never forgot the divine
­element and manifested their religiosity in various ways, either because they had genuine metaphysical concerns
or simply for reasons of social prestige and/or alliances with the religious authorities. The historical notes of
the Capuchin monks of Naxos, which also narrate events from the period under consideration, record, among
other things, donations from corsairs to the local Catholic Church, which were subsequently used by the clergy
to build and equip temples; these included captives (to be exchanged for ransom), sums of money, precious
vessels, textiles and quantities of metals (Zerlentis 1922).
The role of the corsairs in church-building, however, was not always discreet and indirect. The Vitali coat of
arms, which was mentioned earlier, bears at the bottom an inscription in Latin, which informs us that he was
the founder of the church of “Spyridon, the miracle worker” (Fig. 7). He probably erected the church after he
was spared from a plague epidemic, if we take into account the relevant traditions about this particular saint.
A second case of a church built by a corsair is found in the closed sea surrounded by Melos, Kimolos and
Polyaigos, which is interrupted by two straits, and where corsair ships frequently anchored, as, much like in the
strait of Antiparos, no enemy ship could entrap them (BSB, Cod. gall. 728, 77; Sebastiani 1687, 29). More specifically, from a study by the priest Ioannis Ramphos (1932, 31–52), we now know that the small monastery of
Ayios Georgios on the islet of the same name (Ayios Georgios, which was called Ayionissi until the 19th century)
was always Orthodox (Fig. 1). The surviving patriarchal sigils certify as early as 1700 that it had been erected
from the ground up by the grandfather of the then abbot on the previously deserted islet.
Ramphos, however, cannot explain why the church is presented externally as a two-aisled basilica, while
it is lacking in internal unity, adding that the right building of this essentially twin church was called by the
­Kimolians “Frangokklisia” (Ramphos 1932, 43–4). The local tradition of the Frankish origins of the church is
ultimately verified by the records of the French consulate of Melos, which refer to a 1695 decision of capitan
generale Antonio Zeno, acknowledging that the Tuscan corsair Francesco Barbieri had built a Catholic church
honoring Saint George in Ayionissi (CADN, Milo et l’Argentière 3, 216).

findings.evidence_excerpt:
BURIALS
The relationship of the corsairs with the Church followed them to the grave. In Paros, in 1679, the
­nineteen-year-old Augustin, son of the famous French corsair Hugues Creveliers, was buried with honors at the
center of the ­Catholic church of Saint George in Naoussa and, according to the historical notes of the Capuchin
monks of Naxos, the parish priest was instructed to engrave the insignia of the deceased on the tomb (Zerlentis
1922, 95–6). A search on the Internet asserts that within the church one can still see the “grave of the pirate” to
this day. However, this tomb is not preserved. The church was destroyed during the Orlov Revolt, it was rebuilt
shortly afterwards, its roof collapsed in 1974 due to cracks caused by the 1956 earthquake, and it was finally
restored in 1994 (Fig. 12; Kaparis 1987; Aliprantis 1994). Slabs or parts of slabs from four tombs unrelated to
­Creveliers were placed on the new floor of the church. The doctor Othon Kaparis (1987, 185), however, published a photograph of part of a burial slab that was preserved in the now closed Byzantine Museum of Naoussa,
which, according to him, depicts the “insignia” of the pirate (Fig. 13). This is certainly not the case. In the
early modern period, the skull and crossbones were a common motif on the tombs of Paros and beyond (e.g.,
­Aliprantis 1985, 68–9; Florakis 2001b), while the sundial is attested on tombs across Europe (Gagnaire, n.d.).
The corsairs had the same anxieties and fears about the hereafter as most people of their time, as evidenced
by the case of the undistinguished burial of a Maltese corsair, the knight Hocquincourt. At the same time, this
case shows that the manner of burial of a corsair does not always leave evidence that will stand the test of time.
In 1666, the twenty-four-year-old French knight drowned when his vessel was wrecked at night near an islet of

findings.evidence_excerpt:
Kassos. Three days later, his surviving companions buried him according to the Orthodox rite in the then small
chapel of Ayia Marina. One of them, who narrates the events in detail, made sure that the grave bore the dead
man’s name and circumstances. This consisted of a single sheet of paper briefly recounting in French the story
of the voyage and the death of the corsair, which was then pasted onto a plank and placed on the grave (Argenti
1954, 147).

findings.evidence_excerpt:
STEAMBATHS
As sailors, the lives of the corsairs often became unbearable “as evil [i.e., venereal disease] flared up”. Then, “the
best medicine” was what Nikos Kavvadias (1989, 17, 19) describes as “kapsa” (meaning heat). The thermal baths
of Melos were, thus, an additional reason why the corsairs frequented the island. And, however improbable it
may seem at first, even these habits, as we shall see, have left an archaeological mark. During the last four decades of the 17th century, travelers visiting Melos mention in their texts not only the island’s water baths, but
also a cavernous steambath. The following can be deduced from cross-referencing the information they provide.
This steambath was located on a hill at the central Melos, about 3.5 km southwest from Old Chora (Zephyria). It
could accommodate three to four people. In addition, during the final years of the Cretan War (1645–1669), the
corsairs had customized the space and had even built a small room right next to the bath and probably others
a short distance around it (BSB, Cod. gall. 728, 64; Pitton de Tournefort 1717, 168; Labat 1735, 332–33, 335).
There is no doubt that this steambath corresponds to the currently operational Provatas Steambaths (Figs.
3 and 14), which, after the damage caused by the 1992 earthquake, were restored in 2013 by the Municipality
of Melos. In fact, one can still discern today on the walls of the Steambaths graffiti in Latin letters, most likely
dating to the times when the facility was used by corsairs (Fig. 15).

findings.evidence_excerpt:
CONCLUSIONS
In conclusion, the above discussion reveals that the question posed at the beginning of this paper about whether
it is possible to detect traces of the pirate phenomenon on land is in the affirmative. It is that pirates and corsairs,
either deliberately or because of their way of life, did not leave any remains proclaiming their status or clearly
revealing their connection with their activity. Nevertheless, a thorough study of the relevant written sources
and its combination with field study may yield positive results. In this paper, it became evident that traces of

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
the ­pirate phenomenon can be identified in various categories of material culture, such as defensive works,
lookouts, structures for keeping captives and slaves, burials and churches, and even in structures of everyday
life, such as steambaths. In the cases examined, it is the written sources that reveal the association of certain
structures or artifacts with piracy, thus providing archaeological research with evidence and guidelines for
­investigating the pirate phenomenon.
The archaeology of piracy can turn to two general categories of material culture:
The first is that related to the pirate activities and the protection of the pirates themselves and their ships
(e.g., defensive works, lookouts, structures for the keeping of captives and slaves). In this category, it seems that
these are modest yet effective structures, characterized by practical design, and made exclusively with local
materials. The key point for associating such structures with pirate activity is certainly the geographical context,
i.e., they are located in areas where their presence cannot be explained otherwise and/or are suitable for this
type of activity.
The second category includes structures and artifacts of everyday life or religion (e.g., steambaths, churches,
burials, tombstones). In this case, it is difficult to identify evidence that would reveal a link between these
structures or artifacts and pirates, but archaeologists studying a site or a monument in an area and a period
favorable to the flourishing of pirate activity can keep in mind that pirates were part of the society of their time
and had the same problems and fears as other people. Their activity often allowed and/or required them to erect
­monuments for reasons of social prestige.
These remarks are based on the study of piracy in the early modern period, but traces of the pirate
­phenomenon in premodern times can be sought in roughly the same categories of structures and in places with
the same characteristics, because humans, in spite of any advancements in technology through time, think and
act in similar, if not identical, ways.

findings.evidence_excerpt:
ABSTRACT
This paper presents the educational program “Piracy in the Cyclades”, developed by the Museum of Cycladic Art as part
of the A.P.Pir.A. research project. Piracy is closely tied to Greek history through its association with the sea, ­maritime
­professions, travel, and the active participation of Greeks in seaborne trade. Grounded in archaeological evidence and
pedagogical theory, the program targets children aged 8 and above and promotes experiential learning both within the
museum and in the classroom. Through a specially designed museum kit, the material is also available for remote use,
ensuring accessibility for students and teachers throughout the country. The program is structured across multiple levels
of difficulty and includes diverse concepts and activities tailored to participants' age, knowledge, and learning needs.
­Designed for flexible integration into school curricula, it can support subjects such as History, Ancient Texts, ­Literature,
and Social Life. Featuring a thematic exhibition route and a range of interactive tools, the program fosters critical thinking,
creativity, and meaningful engagement with ancient maritime history.

findings.evidence_excerpt:
INTRODUCTION
Museums, as places of non-formal education, have nowadays expanded their educational and social role
through actions that can be carried out inside the museum, but also outside, i.e., in its natural habitat (Mouliou
and Bounia 1999). Museopedagogical actions are addressed to formal education institutions, such as schools,
as well as families and other groups of adults and children. A museum’s resilience helps serve its educational
purpose, as defined by the ICOM Code of Ethics for Museums (Kokkou et al. 2009).
Museums, in their effort to attract visitors and be open to everyone, start utilizing their collections in a
modern and multifaceted way. Therefore, museum collections are exhibited in a dissimilar way through a
­variety of educational activities and programs, covering various themes and allowing the active participation of
visitors, who will hopefully gain a satisfying experience that combines learning with entertainment. In recent
decades, museums have expanded their activities outside their premises and buildings to reach out to groups of
people, who are unable to visit their halls.
This chapter focuses on the presentation of the educational program “Piracy in the Cyclades”, created by
the Department of Educational and Social Programs of the Museum of Cycladic Art (MCA), as part of the
A.P.Pir.A. project (see also Samaras, this volume).

EDUCATIONAL PROGRAM AND EDUCATIONAL MATERIAL DESIGN
FRAMEWORK FOR THE “PIRACY IN THE CYCLADES” PROJECT BY THE
MCA
Museum of Cycladic Art
The MCA was founded in 1986 to house Nikolaos and Aikaterini (Dolly) Goulandris’ collection of Cycladic and
ancient Greek art. Since its foundation, the museum has evolved into a vibrant international cultural organization, focusing on the promotion of the ancient cultures of the Aegean and Cyprus, with particular emphasis
on the Cycladic art of the 3rd millennium BCE. The permanent collections of the museum have been formed
through donations of its founders, Nikolaos and Dolly Goulandris, numerous private collectors (K. Politis, L.
Eftaxias, T.N. Zintilis, etc.), foundations (Academy of Athens) and other bodies (Commercial Bank). Today,
MCA houses one of the most comprehensive private collections of Cycladic art, with typical samples of the
world-famous Cycladic marble figurines. The museum’s permanent collections include 3,000 objects of Cycladic
culture, ancient Greek and Cypriot art, as well as fragments of cultures that flourished in the Aegean and eastern
Mediterranean from the 4th millennium BCE to circa the 6th century CE.
The museum’s permanent collections as displayed in the main building (4 Neophytou Douka Street ­entrance)
are presented in a modern way and using interactive means in the following permanent exhibitions: (a) Cycladic
culture, (b) ancient Greek art – a story with images, (c) Cypriot culture, and (d) scenes from everyday life in
antiquity. (https://cycladic.gr/).
The founder of the Museum of Cycladic Art was Dolly Goulandris (†2008). Her vision was to house and
promote as a public good the private collection of works of Cycladic culture and ancient Greek art that she had
collected with her husband Nikolaos Goulandris (†1983). Since 2008, with the so-called baton passing of the
museum’s management to Mrs. Kassandra (Sandra) Marinopoulou, new strategic objectives have been set, such
as the emergence of international trends in contemporary art, the consistent production of periodic exhibitions,
inventive promotion of archaeology, as well as attraction and familiarization of a younger audience with art. The
vision of the new management had four main axes: (1) to boost the museum’s extroversion towards all social
groups, (2) to host multiple exhibitions that will foster a dialog between ancient Greek and modern or contemporary art, (3) to create the museum’s digital footprint in compliance with the physical one, and (4) to ­enhance
the museum’s international visibility through exhibitions and actions abroad, as well as via collaborations with
leading museums abroad. Through the adoption of a more direct and welcoming profile, MCA succeeded in
integrating new technologies into its content, created communities of users who love art and disseminated its
cultural message to a wider audience, while nurturing a relationship with it.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
THE “PIRACY IN THE CYCLADES” PROGRAM
The archaeological investigation of the phenomenon of piracy in antiquity provided the Department of
­Educational and Social Programs of the Museum of Cycladic Art with material for the design of the educational
program “Piracy in the Cyclades”. This program includes various levels of difficulty, concepts and actions, as well
as product production according to the participant’s age, knowledge and skills. It will be addressed to children
aged 8 and above and will be potentially included in History, Ancient Texts, Literature and Social Life courses.
The educational material can be used either on the museum’s premises or in schools, providing ­therefore access
to students and teachers throughout the country.
When the Museum received the proposal submitted by scholars to participate in the A.P.Pir.A. research
project by creating an educational program, we decided to adhere to the same principle and design specific
educational material for children and families that can be used within the museum, as well as lending material
for teachers who wish to use it in the classroom, as part of a lesson or a project.
The educational program was a challenging opportunity, as material for piracy in the prehistoric Cyclades
had to be designed from scratch relying solely on archaeological findings. Beyond any doubt, the study of piracy
over time and in contrast with other historical periods utilizing archaeological findings, historical texts and
other sources, contributed to the project’s success. The initial step was the information collection. Then, the
most difficult and demanding step followed, as specific information had to be adapted to be easily understood
by children. This way, tailor-made, informed material was created to cover children’s educational needs on a
very specific topic.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
All activities were designed for the permanent Cycladic culture collection of the MCA. The main objective of
the educational program is to provide cohesive and robust answers to questions related to piracy, such as what
piracy is, what is the definition of pirate, why would one become a pirate, “types” of piracy, piracy in the Greek
seas in antiquity, piracy during the Early Bronze Age II (ca. 2400–2200 BCE), etc. Children and families participating in this program will be able to retrieve information in an interactive and experiential way.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
INSIDE THE MUSEUM: THEMATIC ROUTE ON PIRACY
Museum visitors shall follow a route with selected exhibits from the permanent collection of Cycladic art
(Figs. 1–2). The route in the dedicated hall includes a floor plan with stops at selected exhibits and texts about
­navigation and maritime trade in the prehistoric Cyclades. With the help of the floor plan, students and children accompanied by their parents can in turn discover the map of the Cyclades, a wall text related to shipping
and trade with reference to bases and shelters for pirate expeditions, frying pans with reference to decoration
(sea, ships, etc.), a pig-shaped zoomorphic pyxis related to animal theft, the figurine of the hunter-warrior and
bronze age weapons, a female figurine of a pregnant woman with references to women abduction.
Exclusive labels and drawing representations have been designed for each exhibition station. Each label
contains information on piracy-related exhibits, as well as discussion topics to be debated either by students or
family members using the educational material. In addition to labels, exact copies of ancient exhibits or accessible 3D prints are located at different exhibition stations (Fig. 3). The aim is to offer an immersive and genuinely
interactive experience to all visitors. Also, a dedicated box is designed that includes a map of the Cyclades, a
floor plan with stations, information cards and labels, copies of selected exhibits, 3D prints of selected exhibits
as well as objects related to piracy, such as ships.

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
OUTSIDE THE MUSEUM: MUSEUM KIT
The lending educational material is addressed to children aged 8 and above. It is a museum kit containing
­material dedicated to teachers, an information brochure, educational classroom activities suggestions, ­illustrated
cards, a board game and 3D prints of selected exhibits from the exhibition of Cycladic art related to piracy.
The information brochure “Piracy in the ancient Cyclades: From the prehistoric to Roman times” contains
multiple questions and answers that stimulate both students’ and teachers’ investigative mind, enabling them to

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
discuss, reflect, investigate what was happening in ancient times and eventually learn in an interactive and fun
way (Fig. 4).
Illustrated cards are mainly for teachers and contain information on piracy from prehistoric to Roman times
(Fig. 5). Through these cards, teachers can create their own story to narrate to students and make a timeline with
information about the different periods of antiquity and piracy.
The board game “Pirates in the Cyclades” is an educational game that enables children and adults to learn
through play about the lives of pirates in antiquity, the origin of pirates and what were their motives, what was
the ­pirates’ modus operandi and how many types of piracy are there, what was the relationship between pirates
and ­authorities, etc. (Fig. 6).
The game contains a map of the Cyclades with steps and stops designed on a tarp. Pirate-sailors embark on a
journey full of adventures. Who will be the first to arrive at the destination? Cards with questions, obstacles and
rewards sometimes facilitate and sometimes make it difficult for pirates to travel (Fig. 7).
In this game, students are split into two (or more) teams or play individually. They take on the role of
­archaeologists and investigate various cases to find out whether it is a case a case of piracy or not. They are given
various clues from written sources, archaeological sites, objects, iconography, etc., and are asked to a­ nswer
which of these are potentially linked to pirates. Each clue will be discussed, and after being categorized as being

findings.title: Vol. 14. The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity: Proceedings of the International Hybrid Conference held under the auspices of the Department of History and Archaeology of the University of Athens (October 5-6, 2023)
findings.evidence_excerpt:
pirate or not, children will receive the correct answer along with an informed explanation. Each clue has a
­different score depending on the degree of difficulty.
Based on the clues provided, children will most likely consider that all ships belong to pirates, all ­fortifications
are to repel pirate attacks, etc., in this way the game gains a plain field. The board game offers young players
an experiential learning while enhancing their critical thinking. Children will familiarize themselves with informed historical and archaeological facts and data, they will develop their own reasoning and critical thinking
and get acquainted with the real work of an archaeologist (see also https://cycladic.gr/en/museum-kit-piracy-in-ancient-cyclades/).

“PIRACY IN THE CYCLADES” PROGRAM: ANTICIPATED BENEFITS
The “Piracy in the Cyclades” program offers a comprehensive hands-on experience. Children actively p
­ articipate,
explore and discover tangibly process objects, ask questions, answer questions and engage in an open and
­stimulating dialog. The enhancement of imagination and creativity leads all participants to answer ­questions
related to piracy in antiquity and to foster their own argumentation and conclusions (Agostinho et al. 2004).
­Children use their senses, collaborate, express themselves and acquire knowledge in a pleasant way h
­ appily
involved in multiple ways throughout this experiential learning that characterizes learning in the museum
(Nikonanou 2015). The educational material on piracy was the outcome of a seamless cooperation ­between
scientific team members. Through this cooperation, a significant milestone was achieved: d
­ issemination of
research results and information on piracy to young and old.

findings.title: Οι πολεμικοί κίνδυνοι και κίνδυνοι πειρατείας στο Ιδιωτικό Ναυτικό Δίκαιο
findings.evidence_excerpt: Στη πτυχιακή μου εργασία βασίζομαι πάνω στο Ιδιωτικό Δίκαιο και αναλύω ορισμούς όπως είναι η πειρατεία, οι πειρατικές πράξεις, οι πολεμικοί κίνδυνοι και οι κίνδυνοι πειρατείας,  σε σχέση με το δίκαιο της θαλάσσιας ασφάλισης. Στη συνέχεια, παραθέτω μερικές υποθέσεις πειρατικών πράξεων και μερικά case studies  πάνω σε περιστατικά πειρατείας που έχουν καταγραφεί σε περιοχές υψηλού πειρατικού κινδύνου, όπως για παράδειγμα στον  Κόλπο του Άντεν και στα Στενά της Μάλακκα καθώς οι περιοχές αυτές είναι γνωστές ως πειρατικά περάσματα λόγω της Σομαλικής πειρατείας από την οποία πλήττονται. Γίνεται, επίσης, λόγος σε πολλά σημεία στην πτυχιακή μου εργασία, για το έργο του Διεθνούς Ναυτιλιακού Γραφείου σε σχέση με το θέμα αυτό και αναλύονται και κάποια μέτρα αντιμετώπισης. Παρακάτω αναλύω τη περίπτωση των ‘’πλοίων-φαντασμάτων’’, όπου πρόκειται για εξαφάνιση ολόκληρου του πληρώματος και κλοπή του πλοίου και του φορτίου με εξαιρετικά υψηλά επίπεδα οργάνωσης. Επιπλέον απαριθμώ, τα νομοθετικά κείμενα και τις συμβατικές ρυθμίσεις  για την πειρατεία και τους πολεμικούς κινδύνους. Τέλος, κάνω μία αναφορά στην ναυτική επιχείρηση ΑΤΑLANTA.

findings.title: On the social base of Sextus Pompey's Sicilian state: The origins of Cilician piracy and its first encounters with Rome
findings.evidence_excerpt: Abstract: This article focuses on the social foundation of Sextus Pompey's Sicilian state and the role of Cilician piracy in Rome's history. Particular attention is given to the origins of Cilician piracy in the 3rd�2nd centuries BC and its initial encounters with the Roman Republic. Piracy in the Mediterranean significantly influenced the political processes during Rome's civil wars. The research is based on a systematic analysis of ancient literary sources, including Appian, Plutarch, Polybius, and Strabo, alongside archaeological data and epigraphic studies. These sources provide a comprehensive understanding of piracy and its significance in Eastern Mediterranean politics. Critical analysis of historical texts is employed to reconstruct military-political events involving Cilician pirates. The article demonstrates that Cilician pirates were not merely bandits but key participants in regional politics. It examines the campaign of Marcus Antonius Orator in 102�101 BC, the first major Roman effort to suppress Cilician piracy. Piracy weakened Seleucid power and contributed to the creation of the Roman province of Asia. The interactions of pirates with eastern monarchs, such as Antiochus III and Mithridates VI, who actively utilized their services in military campaigns, are also explored. Rome's attitude towards pirates shifted from utilizing their services to open confrontation. Despite Marcus Antonius' campaign, piracy persisted until Gnaeus Pompeius finally eradicated it in 67 BC. The struggle against Cilician piracy was a significant milestone in Roman imperial policy, consolidating control over the eastern provinces and playing a vital role in establishing Roman dominance in the Mediterranean.

findings.evidence_excerpt:
SUMMARY
DODECANESE, THE GENESIS OF A NAME
AND THE ITALIAN APPROACH
The islands, the islets, and the rocks of the Dodecanese prefecture united
with Greece in 1947. At the 2001 census 15 islands and 93 islets or rocks are
registered. In ancient Greece these were known as (South) Sporades, whereas
the name Dodecanese is known since the 8th century and was used later for
the Cyclades, which in the later ancient era (according to Stravon) acted
similarly as twelve islands (dodeca nesoi).
During the Ottoman domination (1522-1912), twelve of the South
Sporades islands, with the exception of Rhodes and Kos, were widely
privileged by self government. In the 19th century, when these privileges were
abolished, the inhabitants strived to maintain them. Their representatives in
1909, in a memorandum to the Ottoman Porte, named the islands Dodeca
(Twelve) South Sporades, using the name Dodecanese for the first time. In
1912, when Italy occupied all of the then 12 privileged islands, and after
distinguishing Lipsus as an island by appointing a government, the islands
were name Rodi e Dodecanese However, the same year, the Greek
representatives, at their congress in Patmos in which they declared their
independence, referred to the islands as the Aegean Islands or as (South)
Sporades.
Since 1913, when Gerasimos Drakidis a Rhodes lawyer published in
Athens the Dodecanese's Album, in which he included the results of the recent
référendums among the inhabitants of the twelve islands (Rhodes, Chalki,
Symi, Telos, Astypalea, Nissyros, Kos, Kalymnos, Leros, Patmos, Kassos, Karpathos), in favour of the unification with Greece, which had taken place
during the First Balkan War, the name Dodecanese prevailed immediately
both in oral and written communication/speech, in Greece and abroad.
Soon, when the Italians comprehended that the predominance of the
Greek name was against their interests, they reacted in two ways. On the one
hand, some clamed that the name was of Italian inspiration and was chosen as
being of classical or medieval origins, trying to declare their claims in the
Mediterranean as a movement to promote the new roman / latin civilization,

findings.title: Caesar and The Pirates: or How to Make (and Break) an Ancient Life
findings.evidence_excerpt: It is hard for biographers, ancient and modern alike, to resist the story of the young Julius Caesar's kidnapping by a band of pirates. Suetonius and Plutarch both include full versions of the tale, with specific details (Suet. Iul. 4; Plut. Vit. Caes. 1.4–2). Suetonius, for instance, writes that the kidnapping took place near the island of Pharmacusa (just off the coast of Asia Minor), while Plutarch, noting that too, also specifies that the ransom that freed Caesar came from the (nearby) city of Miletus. And while Suetonius writes that Caesar, after his release, launched a fleet, pursued the pirates, and punished them, Plutarch includes another phase in the story: having taken command of a fleet and set sail (again, from Miletus), Plutarch's Caesar captured nearly all the pirates but, instead of killing them right away, ‘he himself went to Iuncus, the governor of Asia, on the grounds that it belonged to him, as governor of the province, to punish the captives’. When Iuncus postponed a decision on the matter (evidently hoping to make a profit out of the situation), Caesar returned to Pergamum, took the robbers out of prison, and only then crucified them himself.

findings.title: E. Ziebarth, Beiträge zur Geschichte des Seeraubs und Seehandels im alten Griechenland (Hamburgische Universität, Abhandlungen aus dem Gebiet der Auslandskunde, band 30). Paul Cloché, La vie public et privé des anciens grecs. V. Les classes, les métiers, le trafic.
findings.evidence_excerpt: L'intérêt des études consacrées au commerce des sociétés antiques est double. D'une part, elles nous font assister à la naissance d'institutions appelées à de puissants développements, telles que les banques, qu'elles nous présentent sous des formes rudimentaires ; pareillement, elles nous font assister aux premières ébauches des sociétés commerciales. D'autre part, elles nous montrent déjà les lois économiques exerçant leur empire souverain avec la même rigueur que dans des sociétés plus évoluées : les ravages exercés par la hausse des prix, l'extrême minutie des variations du change, les conséquences de l'inflation monétaire, ces phénomènes auraient pu être observés par les anciens avec la même précision que dans nos propres sociétés ; à cet égard, nous aurions beaucoup plus à apprendre de la technique des banquiers athéniens que des théories des philosophes, si souvent aveugles aux réalités contemporaines. L'ouvrage de Mr E. Ziebarth 2 a collectionné avec soin toutes les données précises qui concernent le commerce maritime des Grecs. Les deux appendices de son livre, qui donnent le texte de toutes ces citations, forment comme les archives d'une telle étude. Archives déchirées, pleines de lacunes, difficiles à interpréter. D'après ces documents, Mr Ziebarth s'est d'abord proposé d'écrire une histoire de la piraterie dans l'antiquité grecque, depuis le temps d'Homère jusqu'au temps de Pompée, qui marque comme l'apogée de ce grand mal. Commerce et piraterie sont très difficiles à distinguer aux époques primitives. L'empire athénien du ve siècle fit régner provisoirement la sécurité, mais les dangers se multiplièrent de nouveau pour les commerçants au ive siècle, jusqu'au moment où Philippe, en 338, fit proclamer la liberté des mers. C'est alors la piraterie de la Méditerranée occidentale qui préoccupe surtout les Grecs. Puis, au me siècle, la piraterie ressuscita même dans l'Egée. La deuxième partie du livre est consacrée au progrès du commerce maritime, qui réussit à défier la piraterie. Nos sources ne deviennent abondantes qu'au ive siècle, grâce aux discours des orateurs attiques, et principalement à ceux qui concernent les prêts à la grosse aventure, qui paraissent avoir constitué pour les capitalistes d'Athènes le type de placement préféré. La procédure de ces procès est particulièrement curieuse en ce qu'elle nous montre combien les Athéniens accordaient aux commerçants étrangers de privilèges. La catégorie des « procès de commerçants » bénéficiait de règles particulières touchant les délais de l'instruction et les rigueurs de l'exécution.
